<note>The following notes provide context for the names and terms found in the ledger.</note>

**Paid** — <note>original: "Uplatil."</note> This confirms the ledger tracks completed transactions rather than debts.

**Public obligation** — <note>original: "kazennoy obyazannosti."</note> This likely refers to a poll tax or a specific communal obligation required of the peasantry or merchant class.

**Silver** — <note>original: "serebrom."</note> During this period in Russia, payments were specified in "silver rubles" to distinguish them from the less stable paper currency (assignats) used earlier in the century.

**Names** — The individuals listed (Potapov, Gerasimov, Mitrofanov, Kubarev, Prokofyev) are the taxpayers or heads of households. The use of the terminal "v" (ъ) in the original Russian is a feature of pre-revolutionary orthography.

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the introductory material of the 1518 Venice edition of the Hebrew Bible. While the previous page contained the title and later family ownership records, this page provides a scholarly and theological preface to the Book of Psalms (Tehillim), explaining its divine inspiration and its traditional attribution to King David and ten ancient elders.</meta>

### He Said:

David, the son of Jesse—for our Rabbis of blessed memory <note>original: "ז"ל" (Zichronam Livracha), a standard honorific for deceased sages</note> called upon and relied on the tradition that David, King of Israel, wrote his book through ten elders. And these are they: Adam the First, Melchizedek, Abraham, Moses, Heman, Jeduthun, Asaph, and the three sons of Korah—and he taught them to his sons. And it is written that all the prophets prophesied within their psalms: some in a "Psalm" <note>Hebrew: *Mizmor*</note>, some as "A Psalm of David," some as <unclear>To David, a Psalm</unclear>, some as "A Prayer," some as "A Praise," and some as "A Song." And in the *Mechilta* <note>An ancient collection of Jewish legal and homiletic interpretations</note> regarding his sons: at the hour when Moses descended to Sinai, the portions of the tribes fell to the Children of Israel. The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moses: "Tell Israel that they should say all the psalms, for they are [given] in prophecy." And they asked, "What shall become of you and us?" He said to them <unclear>to wait</unclear> for each and every generation, so that each one shall stand according to his generation; and this is what is meant by saying that each and every one wrote a book in his name. In the version of its construction in the Book of Psalms, he wrote at the end "In Prayer," written in the psalms in their order. And this is because they were spoken through the Holy Spirit <note>Hebrew: *Ruach Ha-Kodesh*</note>; therefore, this book was prophesied within the "Writings" <note>The *Ketuvim*, the third section of the Hebrew Bible</note> and not within the "Prophets" <note>The *Nevi'im*, the second section</note>. For its words were not spoken in [standard] prophecy, but rather through the Holy Spirit.

The clarification of the matter and the reason from the commentator regarding the difference between Prophecy and the Holy Spirit is as follows: Prophecy is a thing that comes upon a person who is a perfect sage in his Torah, and prophecy is possible for him through his integrity and the power of his service, by the strengthening of his cleaving to his Creator, may He be blessed, in vitality and life, being separated from all the ways of this world and living in the vision of prophecy as if a man were speaking with him today. This is a novelty to him, occurring with difficulty. For prophecy rests in that vision—either he sees no form at all, or he hears a voice speaking with him. 

But the Holy Spirit is an action that rests slightly from the engagement with the words of God on the day he cleaves to the will of his Master. Such a person is not cancelled from any of the delights of the world, nor from the <note>original: "מצורות זרעו" - likely referring to family/procreative duties</note> needs of his offspring, Heaven forbid; rather, it is a grace of a higher spirit. It adds words to his tongue—words of wisdom and praise to his Creator, and His song and His glorification. He also speaks of future events with Divine assistance through the power of speech and all the faculties of speech. With this power, he wrote the Book of the Torah, and the Prophets are explained by the true prophets as "Psalm." 

As for those psalms concerning David, to praise and to thank, I have written "David" and "To him." This name remained only for his sons. And regarding the "Psalm" in later generations, we have received it as the truth, and to the Lord. And when a man is sealed in the words of God. And as for the sons of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, and the sons and grandsons, and the sons of Joseph, and by the hand of Asaph—in any case, their path was in this manner, little by little. For the praise grows from a part to a greater whole, one level above the other. Sometimes, days of the Spirit rest upon them, strengthening them in dreams or while awake, though his power and knowledge did not reach those levels through the power of the source of the senses and the orders of the Glories. 

Therefore, his book was not written among the books of the Prophets, but was written among the Holy Books called "Writings" <term>Ketuvim: The section of the Bible containing Psalms, which are considered divinely inspired but distinct from the direct 'visionary' prophecy of books like Isaiah or Ezekiel</term>, to say they were written through the Holy Spirit. And this book is the praise of David. It is written according to the words of our Rabbis, those who say the psalms. And the sign of comforts which he composed, he entered into the psalms to awaken slightly that which belonged to the Lord, may He be remembered <note>original abbreviation: "ס"ל"</note>, and David put it in their hearts to sing to the Lord by the hand of Asaph and Jeduthun. And as for "To the Chief Musician upon Jeduthun, a Psalm of David"—David composed it and gave it to Jeduthun. And likewise, five psalms regarding the matter of the Torah for Israel with the compositions. 

Also, today is "Prayer" and "Praise," aside from those who remembered them. And the psalms in which "By permission of David" is written, David composed them. Likewise, those in which no author is mentioned, David composed them. There is also a need to sharpen the explanation because of these: such as "To the Chief Musician, a Psalm of David" and "The Servant of the Lord." "To David, a Psalm" implies the power of the psalm [the music] came to another first. And so it is written in the Book of Prayer that was written and exact; they received it as a bride from us for its own sake, our Rabbis. Like "A Prayer of Moses." These were things David composed. He spoke in them about the Babylonian exile and about this current exile, and the many comforts, and the prophecy, and the Geonim <note>The heads of the Babylonian academies, or simply "great ones"</note> and the kings. Some of them are obligated... and some without... and we do not know every single day the division of grace between these names to be said in the spirit of the psalm. 

And now, our Rabbis of blessed memory, in everything they gave for the future to come, it was arranged by Jeduthun. "To David, a Psalm" means the Holy Spirit rested upon him first and afterward he uttered song. "A Psalm of David" means he uttered song first and afterward the Holy Spirit rested upon him. There is more in the explanation of this matter in the fourth psalm. And now we shall begin to explain the Fifth Book <note>The Book of Psalms is traditionally divided into five smaller "books" or sections</note>; may it be with the help of Him who teaches man knowledge.

<summary>This preface explores the divine origins of the Book of Psalms, attributing its composition to King David and ten elders, while explaining that its inspiration stems from the "Holy Spirit" rather than direct prophecy. This distinction justifies why the book is categorized as part of the 'Writings' (Ketuvim) in the Hebrew Bible.</summary>
<keywords>Psalms, Tehillim, King David, Holy Spirit, Prophecy, Ten Elders, Asaph, Jeduthun, Ketuvim, Venice 1518, Biblical commentary</keywords>

# Happy is the Man

<margin>
and he is not
he intends
in its depth
chambers
depths of
the wise

goes
</margin>

Regarding life: The word "Happy" <note>original: "אשרי" (Ashrei)</note> is phrased as a plural reward, for it is not possible for a person in this world to have a portion of absolute success unless it comes through many good things that occur and persist for him beyond measure. David included in this psalm the nature of man, what is proper for him to do in this world, the ultimate end of the righteous, and the punishment of the wicked. This is a very distinguished psalm; therefore, he began his book with it. He said, "who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked." He first turns away from the path of evil, just as it is said elsewhere, "Turn from evil and do good." For a person initially learns from his base inclinations and the way of the world <note>The text uses "exile" or "habitual way" to describe the material world</note>, which is to eat, drink, and be merry, and he is led by them, as it says, "for the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth." When a man reaches maturity and begins to recognize good and evil, he is warned to turn from the way of the wicked and not walk in their counsel.

The "wicked" <note>original: "רשעים" (Resha'im)</note> are those who think only of acquiring wealth and worldly glory; they do not distinguish between good and evil, and they rob and steal because of the intense desire of their hearts. For their sinning is intentional <note>original: "מדעת" (from knowledge/intent)</note>, coming from the inner chambers of the heart. This is like the phrase, "perhaps my hand has found much." In everything he recognizes, he acts wickedly. It is said, "do not be overly wicked." Because of this, the text connects "walking" with the "wicked," and joins them with "counsel," for they sit and counsel people on how to acquire their wealth and destroy them in a single moment. To them, this is a matter of laughter, hidden and mingled. Usually, a man is counted in this category because he views his youthful desires as good and does not look toward the end.

And he said, "nor stood in the way of sinners." For the "sinner" <note>original: "חוטא" (Choteh)</note> stands in that path, remaining in his place, fixed in his depths. The meaning of "way" here is not just the act of walking, but the persistence and engagement in the forbidden act and its performance. This is like the verse, "and you shall make known to them the way they shall go." He remains in a place of deep desire. The phrase "did not stand" means he does not linger or become involved with them; he does not stand in their company so that he will not learn from their actions.

And he said, "nor sat in the seat of scorners." The "scorners" <note>original: "לצים" (Letzim)</note> are those who are cunning in knowledge for evil, who act arrogantly and speak ill of people, mocking others and sitting in places of leisure <note>literally "houses of kindness" or "gathering houses" used here ironically for social idleness</note>, wasting time with one another. This refers to those who are idle from wisdom and engage in trivial talk. Because of this, it says, "nor sat in the seat of scorners." Note the progression of "seat" and the person's posture: he did not walk, he did not stand, he did not sit. These encompass all movements and times. Furthermore, the text mentions these because while a person is moving from place to place, he may do neither good nor evil. By saying "Happy," the text warns him not to engage in their deeds.

All of this teaches a man to distance himself from the group and the depths of vanity. Our Rabbis of blessed memory <note>original: "ז"ל"</note> asked: If he did not walk, where would he have stood? And if he did not stand, how could he have sat? This is to tell you that if one walks in their ways, he will eventually stand; and if he stands, he will eventually sit; and if he sits, he will eventually scorn. The verse does not say this about one who "walks in the way of the innocent."

"But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord." Even if he turned from the way of evil but did not do good, he has not completed his task, and his happiness will not be permanent. Thus it says, "Turn from evil and do good." Although our Rabbis said that if one sits and does not commit a transgression, he receives a reward like one who performs a commandment—this applies when a person has the opportunity to sin and is saved from it. Through that strength, he merits and "does good." Turning from evil is for the purpose of doing good.

They also thought: who surrounds him? If one avoids sin because the opportunity didn't arise, that is one thing. But the text says, "Happy is the man... who does good." What should he do? "In the Torah of the Lord is his delight." "Delight" includes both study and action, as in "to do your delight." One should not count the action as separate from the study. "And in His Torah"—notice that "Torah" is mentioned twice in one verse. First, it is called "the Torah of the Lord," but after he meditates and labors in it, it becomes "his Torah" <note>the student's own Torah</note>.

And regarding "he meditates" <note>original: "יהגה" (Yehgeh)</note>: he meditates in his heart, as in "the meditation of my heart before You." For he has already merited to learn and to understand. Now the text mentions the intention of his heart and his thoughts day and night—his constant involvement in investigation and understanding. Since he places them upon every action according to his occupation, as the sages said, "let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven." "And in his Torah he meditates day and night"—that he should occupy himself with study. They said this refers to one who occupies himself with the wisdom of the Table <note>likely referring to the table of study/law</note>. Not all people are capable of constant study, but the Scripture considers it as if they meditate day and night if they set aside time for it morning and evening. In the simple sense, "meditating" refers to the speech of the mouth, which should be constant whenever he is free from his occupations, whether by day or by night.

# Psalms

<columns>

<margin>Chapter 1</margin> The goodness of the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, and in the path of sinners has not stood, and in the dwelling of mockers has not sat. Rather, in the Torah <note>original: "אורייתא" (Oraita), the Aramaic term for the Law or Instruction</note> of the Lord is his desire, and in His Torah he meditates day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, which gives its fruit in its time, and its leaf does not wither, and everything he does shall prosper. Not so are the wicked, but like the chaff which the whirlwind drives away. Therefore the wicked shall not arise on the Great Day <note>A traditional reference to the Day of Judgment</note>, nor sinners in the assembly of the righteous. For the way of the righteous is revealed before the Lord, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

<margin>Chapter 2</margin> Why do the nations stir, and the peoples meditate on vanity? The kings of the earth prepare themselves, and the rulers are joined together as one to speak before the Lord and against His Messiah <note>original: "משיחיה" (Meshichei), meaning His Anointed One</note>. "Let us break their commandments and cast their chains from us." He who sits in heaven shall laugh; the Word of the Lord shall mock them. Then He shall speak to them in the strength of His anger, and in His wrath He shall terrify them. And I have magnified My king and appointed him upon the mountain of My Sanctuary.

<column-break/>

<margin>Chapter 1</margin> Happy is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked, nor stood in the way of sinners, nor sat in the seat of mockers. But his delight is in the Torah of the Lord, and in His Torah he meditates day and night. And he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, which brings forth its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither, and whatever he does shall prosper. Not so the wicked, but they are like the chaff which the wind drives away. Therefore the wicked shall not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous. For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked shall perish.

<margin>2</margin> The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the Lord and against His anointed. "Let us break their bands asunder, and cast away their cords from us." He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord has them in derision. Then He shall speak to them in His wrath, and vex them in His sore displeasure. "Yet I have set My king upon Zion, My holy hill."

</columns>

---

**He shall be like a tree.** He compared the good, pious man to a tree planted by streams of water. Not only for the fruit, but even its leaf shall not wither. And it shall be available and prepared at all times. And this pious man merited...

**Happy**. Every "Happy" <note>original: "אשרי" (Ashrei), a word used throughout the Psalms to denote a state of fortunate blessing</note> in the Scripture is an expression of praise. And why does it say, "Happy is the man"? Rather, this is praise for the man... **In the seat of mockers.** Since he did not walk and did not stand, ultimately he did not sit... But since he did not walk and did not stand, is it not obvious that he did not sit? Rather, this is to tell you that if one walks, he will eventually stand, and if he stands, he will eventually sit <note>The commentator is illustrating the "slippery slope" of negative influence: it begins with a walk, leads to stopping, and ends with settling in with the wrong crowd</note>...

## Why

**The nations rage.** Our Rabbis <note>Traditional Jewish sages</note> interpreted this matter as referring to Gog and Magog <note>A prophetic reference to a great war at the end of days</note>. However, we will explain it as referring to David... for in neither of these <note>the first two psalms</note> is it written "To the Chief Musician" or "A Psalm"... and so we see in the first Psalm: "And he shall be like a planted tree," which corresponds to David...

<summary>This page contains the opening chapters of the Book of Psalms, featuring parallel Hebrew and Aramaic texts alongside a Rabbinic commentary that explores the moral growth of the righteous and the historical context of King David.</summary>
<keywords>Psalm 1, Psalm 2, Targum, Torah, King David, Righteousness, Gog and Magog, Hebrew Bible commentary</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the transcription of the Book of Psalms. <margin>To
Jeduthun</margin>
I will tell of the decree: the Lord said to me, "You are my son; today I have begotten you. Ask of Me, and I will give nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession. You shall break them with an iron rod; like a potter’s vessel, you shall dash them in pieces." And now, O kings, be wise; be disciplined, O judges of the earth. Serve the Lord with awe and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the son <note>original: "בר" (Bar); the commentator explores if this means 'son' or 'purity'</note> lest He be angry and you perish on the way, for His anger is soon kindled; happy are all who take refuge in Him.

---

A Psalm of David when he fled from his son Absalom: Lord, how many are my foes! Many are those who rise up against me. Many say of my soul, "There is no salvation for him in God, Selah." But You, O Lord, are a shield around me, my glory, and the one who lifts my head. With my voice, I call to the Lord, and He answers me from His holy mountain, Selah. I lay down and slept; I awakened, for the Lord sustains me.

<margin>24</margin>

**I will tell of the decree.** This is David's psalm, and he says that the story of his life is a statute <note>original: "חק" (Chok)</note> and a custom for him. What is this decree of the story? It is that "the Lord said to me, 'You are my son.'" By this, He granted me the kingship. Therefore, let no man challenge it, for the Lord gave it to me. This is as He said to Samuel, "For I have seen among his sons a king for Me." That is to say, the kingship was a decree for me, and my atonement was a decree and my custom. For anyone who prevents the service of God is called a "statute," as it is written, "a statute for you and food for their service." So too, my portion is a statute for you. It is a decree for them and a decree for me and my children. And He said, "You are my son," because David was pious and righteous. **Today I have begotten you.** This refers to the day he was anointed, as if on that day he was born into the kingship. Just as it says regarding the spirit of the Lord resting upon him from that day forward. From that day, David and Solomon fought by the Holy Spirit. A spirit of strength was added to him from the Holy One on high. Thus it is for generation after generation.

# A Psalm
**Of David when he fled.** Our Rabbis of blessed memory <note>original: "ז"ל" (Zal)</note> asked: when he was ascending the Mount of Olives, he said this psalm. As it says, "And David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went." If he was weeping, why is it called a "Psalm" <note>original: "מזמור" (Mizmor), implying a song of praise</note>? And if it is a "Psalm," why was he weeping? It is because when the prophet said to him, "I will raise up evil against you from within your own house," David feared it might be a slave or a bastard who would have no mercy on him. But once he saw it was his own son, he was comforted and sang a psalm, thinking a son might eventually have mercy. Others say David remembered the judgment of the Lord from old and was comforted. He realized that by fleeing, his sin was being atoned for. Therefore, he sang. 

According to the plain meaning <note>term: "Peshat" (plain literal meaning)</note>, these were not called "Psalms" at the exact moment they occurred, but rather when they were later recited in the Holy Temple. This applies to the psalms regarding Doeg the Edomite, the Ziphites, and those concerning the destruction of Jerusalem. They were all composed or arranged as songs of praise and thanksgiving to God later. Regarding the exile, they will be sung when the exile ends. It is possible this psalm was said to warn those rising against his kingship. Regarding the war of Gog and Magog, the sages asked: why is the section of Absalom placed next to the section of Gog and Magog? If someone tells you there is a slave rebelling against his master, you might believe it; but a son rebelling against his father? Yet both happened. **Lord, how many are my foes.** Because even his own son turned against him. Amasa, his nephew, was also with Absalom, and most of Israel followed Absalom. **Many are those who rise up against me.** All of them rose against him, including Shimei son of Gera, who cursed him.

<sig>23</sig>

<column-break/>

<margin>61
God</margin>
I will tell of the covenant: the Lord said, "You are as dear to me as a son to a father, as if I had created you this very day. Ask of me and I will give the assembly of the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth. You shall break them with a rod of iron; like a potter’s vessel, you shall shatter them. And now, kings, be wise; accept instruction, judges of the earth. Serve before the Lord with fear and pray with trembling. Accept the teaching lest He be angry and you lose the way, for His anger is easily kindled. Happy are those who trust in His Word."

<margin>3</margin>
A praise of David when he fled from before Absalom his son: Lord, how numerous are my oppressors; many rise against me. Many say to my soul, "There is no redemption for him in God forever." But You, Lord, are a shield for me, my glory, and the one who lifts my head. With a voice before the Lord, I will offer my prayer; He will answer from His holy mountain forever. I lay down and slept; I awakened, for the Lord sustains me.
<margin>31</margin>

...from the kings of men. Do you not see what it says: "Will you repay the Lord thus?" This is the reward you give Him for all the good He has done for you. He forgives the sin of your son. 

**I will give nations as your inheritance.** As He said to him, "I have cut off all your enemies from before you and made you a great name." And it was that "today" the nations became servants to David, and the statute was established. The Lord put the fear of him upon all the nations. This is the meaning of "ends of the earth." **You shall break them.** He said this regarding the nations rising against him. He will crush them like a potter's clay vessel, which shatters easily. **And now, O kings.** He speaks to the kings of every generation. Understand that you cannot cancel the work of God who made me king. **Be disciplined.** If you were foolish until now, take instruction and do not be haughty. **Serve the Lord.** Serve Him with awe. **Rejoice with trembling.** Do not let your joy be arrogant; rejoice but fear Him. 

**Kiss the son.** This is like "embrace all the brothers." Or it means "purity of heart." If it means "son," it refers to the one God has anointed. Some explain it as "accept the decree of the king." **Lest He be angry.** If you do not quickly turn from your evil way, God will be angry with you and you will perish. **For His anger is soon kindled.** Even a small amount of His great anger will consume you. **Happy are all who take refuge in Him.** This refers to David himself who trusts in God, or to anyone else who does so. Some interpret this psalm as referring to the Messiah, the King Messiah <note>term: "Mashiach" (Anointed One/Messiah)</note>, as our sages of blessed memory explained. This is a clear interpretation, though the literal sense refers to David himself.

**Many say of my soul.** This means they say *to* my soul, or regarding my person. Many rejoiced at David's downfall, thinking he was being punished for the incident with Bathsheba and that his kingship would never be restored. Therefore they said he has no portion in the World to Come <note>term: "Olam Ha-Ba" (the afterlife/future world)</note>. This is why it says "no salvation for him." **Selah.** Most commentators say this means "forever." In Aramaic, it is translated as "forever." Some say it is a musical term for raising the voice or the lifting of the heart in prayer.

**But You, Lord, are a shield around me.** This contradicts those who say I have no hope. You are a shield for me in this world and my glory in the World to Come. **The one who lifts my head.** Instead of the shame they spoke of, I will walk with my head held high. I called and He answered—the past tense is used here to indicate the certainty of the future event, as if it has already happened through the Holy Spirit. **From His holy mountain.** This could refer to Mount Moriah or Mount Zion. **I lay down and slept.** I slept peacefully, not like a person in terror. I was confident the Lord would sustain me. I was awakened by the words of Nathan the prophet, who told me the Holy Spirit had departed but then returned. I knew the Lord would support me through the prophet Nathan who announced my atonement.

O Lord, in the morning You hear my voice; in the morning I lay my plea before You and wait. For You are not a God who delights in wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You. The boastful shall not stand before Your eyes; You hate all who do iniquity. You destroy those who speak lies; the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man. But I, through Your great kindness, will enter Your house; I will bow down toward Your holy temple in awe of You. O Lord, lead me in Your righteousness because of my watchful foes; make Your way straight before me. For there is no sincerity in their mouths; their heart is destruction. Their throat is an open grave; they use their tongues for flattery. Declare them guilty, O God; let them fall by their own counsels. Cast them out for their many transgressions, for they have rebelled against You. But let all who take refuge in You rejoice; let them ever sing for joy. Spread Your protection over them, that those who love Your name may exult in You. For You, O Lord, bless the righteous; You surround them with favor as with a shield.

# For the leader, with stringed instruments, upon the eighth <note>original: "sheminith" — likely an eight-stringed instrument or a musical scale</note>, a Psalm of David.
O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger, and do not discipline me in Your wrath. Be gracious to me, O Lord, for I am languishing; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are shaken. My soul is greatly troubled; and You, O Lord—how long? Turn, O Lord, and deliver my soul; save me for the sake of Your kindness. For in death there is no mention of You; in the underworld <note>original: "Sheol"</note>, who can give You thanks? I am weary with my groaning; every night I drench my bed; I melt my couch with my tears. My eye is dimmed with grief; it grows old because of all my foes. Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping. The Lord has heard my plea; the Lord accepts my prayer. All my enemies shall be ashamed and greatly troubled; they shall turn back and be put to shame in an instant.

<column-break/>

O Lord, in the morning You shall hear my voice; in the morning I will arrange my prayer before You and I will look out. Because You are not a God who desires wickedness, evil shall not dwell with You. The mockers shall not stand before Your eyes; You hate all who perform falsehood. You shall destroy those who speak lies; the Lord distances Himself from the man who sheds innocent blood and the deceitful. But I, in the abundance of Your goodness, shall enter Your house; I shall prostrate myself toward Your holy temple in Your fear. O Lord, lead me in Your righteousness because of my beholders; straighten Your path before me. Because there is no faithfulness in the mouths of the wicked; their bodies are full of turmoil; their throat is like an open abyss; with their tongues they speak smoothly. God shall judge them; they shall fall from their counsels; for the greatness of their rebellion, He shall cast them away, for they have rebelled against Your Word. And all who hope in Your Word shall rejoice; they shall praise You forever; You shall rest Your Presence upon them, and those who love Your name shall be glad in You. For You shall bless the righteous, O Lord; like a great shield of good favor, You shall crown him.

---

To give praise with melodies on the eight-stringed lyre, a song of David. O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger, and do not chastise me in Your wrath. Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, O Lord, for my bones are terrified. And my soul is greatly terrified; and You, O Lord, until when will I wait for my rest? Turn back, O Lord, deliver my soul; save me because of Your goodness. For in death there is no memory of You; in the underworld, who will give You thanks? I have become weary in my sighing; I speak every night upon my bed; with my tears, I soak my couch. My eye is darkened from anger; it has grown old among all my oppressors. Turn away from me, all you who perform falsehood, because the voice of my weeping has been heard before the Lord. My supplication has been heard before the Lord; the Lord will receive my prayer. All those who are my enemies will be ashamed and terrified; they will turn back and be ashamed in an instant.

<column-break/>

**O Lord, in the morning You hear my voice.** The explanation is: in the morning, the time of prayer, before a person occupies himself with the affairs of the world. In the morning, I will arrange my prayer to You and wait and hope for You to grant my request and my petition. **For You are not a God who delights in wickedness.** Why did I hope for You? Because I know that You do not desire the wicked, and therefore, evil shall not dwell in Your presence <note>literally: "in Your palate"</note>, for there the wise thoughts reside. **Evil shall not dwell with You.** Evil shall not reside with You. And so it is written in the Gemara <note>Rabbinic tradition</note>: "Evil shall not dwell with me," and there are many such instances. **The boastful shall not stand before Your eyes.** The matter of "boastful" <note>Hebrew: "holelim"</note> refers to those who speak in folly, similar to the phrase "and he acted madly in their hands" or "My name is praised by the madmen." This refers to those who act foolishly and boastfully before Your eyes. **I will bow down toward Your holy temple in Your fear.** I will strengthen myself regarding the Temple of the Lord, for the longing I have is for the Temple, which is the sanctuary from which I am kept distant. "His holy temple" refers to the House where the Ark was kept. **O Lord, lead me in Your righteousness.** This is my prayer to You, that You guide me in Your righteousness. That is to say, that You strengthen me to walk in the path of righteousness and judgment and lead me so that I do not stumble. **Make straight.** <note>Hebrew: "Hoshar"</note>. This is a command to make the path level. **For there is no sincerity in their mouths.** This is the reason you should do this for me: because of my watchful foes, who are men of deceit whose mouths do not speak the truth of their hearts. **Their throat is an open grave.** For they are like a grave that hastens to swallow. They use their tongues smoothly, but the words are intended for evil. **Declare them guilty, O God.** Some interpret this from the language of "desolation" <note>Hebrew: "shamama"</note>, meaning they should be desolate and silent. The meaning is that they should not succeed in what they thought to do against me. **Let them fall by their own counsels.** For they have rebelled against You; when they harass me, it is as if they have rebelled against Your word. **But let all who take refuge in You rejoice.** In contrast to the enemies who are driven out, those who take refuge in You will rejoice.

# For the Leader.
**With stringed instruments.** We have already explained the meaning of "with stringed instruments" and "the eighth" <note>sheminith</note> in the previous Psalm. Some interpret "the eighth" as referring to a lyre that has eight strings. It is possible that David said this Psalm regarding his illness, or perhaps regarding the enemies who pursued him. Many Psalms are prayers and praises of David that were not said regarding specific enemies at specific times, but as general prayers. **O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your anger.** Do not rebuke me for my sins, but handle me with Your kindness. This is like the words of Jeremiah: "Correct me, O Lord, but with justice, not in Your anger." **Be gracious to me, O Lord, for I am languishing.** I am weak and frail. **My bones are shaken.** He mentions "bones" because they are the foundation of the body's structure. **My soul is greatly troubled.** Not just my body, but my soul is terrified. **And You, O Lord—how long?** How long will You leave me in this sickness without healing me? **Turn, O Lord.** Deliver my soul. Save me for the sake of Your kindness, not because of my own righteousness, for I know I am guilty. **For in death there is no mention of You.** For God, in death I cannot mention You or thank You; but if You heal me, I will thank You before everyone. This is like what King Hezekiah said: "For the grave cannot thank You, death cannot praise You." **I am weary with my groaning.** Because of my pain, I sigh all night long. **I melt my couch with my tears.** This is an exaggeration of his great weeping and distress. **My eye is dimmed with grief.** My vision is weakened because of the anger and the trouble caused by my enemies. **Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.** He speaks as if his prayer has already been answered through the Holy Spirit. He is confident that the Lord has heard his voice. **The Lord has heard my plea.** He repeats this for emphasis, that God will accept his prayer. **All my enemies shall be ashamed.** When they see that I have been saved and healed, they will be ashamed and terrified in an instant.

I shall not be afraid of the masses of people who have gathered all around against me. Arise, O Lord, save me my God, for You have struck all my enemies upon their jaws; the teeth of the wicked You have broken. From before the Lord comes salvation, and upon Your people is Your blessing forever. 
For praise, upon the melody, a song of David: At the time of my prayer, accept [it] from me, O God of my righteousness; in the time of distress, You gave me relief. Have mercy on me and receive my prayer. Sons of men, why is your heart heavy in its hardness? For salvation you seek falsehood forever. And know that the Lord has set apart the righteous for Himself; the Lord will receive his prayer when he calls to Him. Tremble before Him and do not sin; speak in your hearts and upon your beds, and be humbled in your hearts, and pray upon your seats, and honor Him as a sacrifice <note>original: "mochta" - an Aramaic term for a sacrificial offering</note> forever. "I shall not fear ten thousands of people," etc. These were those who were with Absalom, besides the number that were with David in Jerusalem who were sent with him. And those who gathered against him were those who turned their faces... <note>The commentary here explores the military and political reality of David's rebellion</note>. And so too the two "salvations" refer to the victory of the wheels of judgment. "Arise O Lord, save me my God," etc. and similarly "Arise O Lord" is missing [the letter He] elsewhere in the book, such as "Arise to the Lord for help" or "Azaryahu to me." "For You have struck"—this action refers to those who misled me, as if to say, "lest you answer." Its meaning refers to this specific war, and "You have smitten" is like a told story. "Cheek" (lehi) refers to a blow of disgrace. And so too: "The teeth of the wicked You have broken." Have mercy, for it is possible that his action was for the sake of the pious one... "To the Lord is salvation": The accuser should be turned back to the attribute of His mercy. Salvation belongs to the Lord, and for us it shall be a help to have mercy through His merit. "Upon Your people is Your blessing, Selah," meaning even in death Your people have the freedom of life.

# For the Leader 
**With stringed instruments.** David returned to this; it was in order in this psalm, and he said "with my cup" in the psalm and mentioned in it "with the melody" (neginah). The "Leader" (Menatzeach) is the one who oversees the singers. There were those who were expert in singing psalms and they would play... do not wonder why sometimes it says "to the psalm" and sometimes "to the leader." And so in the prayer of Habakkuk it says, "To the leader with my stringed instruments." And it is written "to oversee the work of the house..." and it is written "with harps upon the eighth" <note>original: "sheminith" - an eight-stringed instrument</note>. There is a living force in the instrument called "Neginot" and there are melodies called "Neginot," and there are compositions that teach these melodies. It is a great wisdom, for it awakens the soul. This wisdom exists in the song and story of the external wisdoms... in the Temple they would praise with harps, lyres, and flutes... and the Levites were divided into five groups for the melodies... every time they mentioned "Selah," it was a pause in the speech. And this is understood from the context of the psalm. 

**"Slaughter sacrifices of righteousness and trust in the Lord."** This means to sacrifice with the proper intention of the heart. One should not trust in their own strength but in the Lord alone. Many say, "Who will show us good?" This refers to those who look only for worldly goodness, but we say, "Lord, lift up the light of Your face upon us," seeking the light of the World to Come. "You have put joy in my heart"—even when they have grain and wine in abundance, the joy You gave me in my heart is greater than theirs. 

# For the Leader 
**Upon the Nehilot.** I have already explained the meaning of "Nehilot" as a form of plea or a musical instrument... some say it refers to the "inheritance" (nachalah) of the word of God. "My words hear, O Lord"—this is the prayer of the mouth, while "consider my meditation" is the prayer of the heart. "Hearken to the voice of my cry"—a loud voice is required when one is in distress... "My King and my God," for You are the King over me and the judge of my soul.

For You shall bless the righteous, O Lord; like a shield of favor You shall crown them.

To praise with stringed instruments on the lyre of eight strings; a song of David.
O Lord, do not rebuke me in Your fury, and do not chastise me in Your wrath.
Have pity on me, O Lord, for I am weak; heal me, for my bones have been terrified.
And my soul is very terrified; and You, O Lord, how long until there is relief for us?
Return, O Lord, deliver my soul; save me because of Your goodness.
For there is no mention of You in death; in the grave, who shall give thanks to You?
I have become exhausted in my sighing; I will speak with my weeping every night; on my bed with my tears I will soak my couch.
My eye is darkened from anger; it has worn out because of all my oppressors.
Turn away from me, all workers of falsehood, for the Lord has heard the sound of my weeping.
The Lord has heard my petition; the Lord will accept my prayer.
They shall be ashamed and terrified greatly—all my enemies; they shall return and be ashamed in an instant.
</columns>

---

**Lord, in the morning You shall hear my voice** — This is because the morning is the time of prayer, before a person involves himself in worldly affairs. As it is written: "I will arrange my prayer for You," and therefore "I will look forward" for You to grant my request and petition. **For You are not a God who desires wickedness** to pray to You; for it is known to us that You do not desire the wicked, and evil does not dwell with You. Since You hate the wicked person and the ways of wickedness, You will not turn toward their prayer because they are an abomination to You. Therefore, I trust that You will answer my prayer, for I am not among those wicked people. **The boastful shall not stand, etc.** — Evil and wickedness cannot stand before You. **The boastful** <note>Hebrew: "holelim"</note> are the fools who are ignorant and lack knowledge, yet they praise themselves with their vanities; thus they are called *holelim*, a term for madness or folly. **You hate all workers of iniquity** — even if they have not yet committed evil in action but only in thought and heart, as it is written: "In your hearts you work iniquity." This is why it says He hates those who "work" iniquity—those who devise evil thoughts in their hearts. **You destroy those who speak lies** — as mentioned above, He hates the wicked who are transgressors, and workers of iniquity are those as bad as a vicious dog. **Speakers of lies** refers to falsehood and hypocrisy <note>Hebrew: "chanifut"</note>. Our Sages teach that there are seven groups of hypocrites who reveal faces contrary to the law, and liars/hypocrites are one of these groups. **The man of blood and deceit the Lord abhors** — this is one who thinks evil in his heart (blood and violence) but speaks deceitfully with his mouth.

**But I, through Your great kindness, shall enter Your house** — meaning my refuge is in Your house and Your proximity. This refers to the House of Study <note>Hebrew: "Beit HaMidrash"</note> which is called "Your house." The psalm explains that because he trusts in God's kindness, he prays now, confident his prayer will be heard. It also seems to me that David prayed this psalm while his son Absalom was rebelling against him. He says, **Lord, lead me in Your righteousness** — meaning, since You have rebuked me now for the sin of Bathsheba, let it be **because of my watchful enemies**; let them see that I have repented so that they too might return. **For there is no sincerity in their mouth** — this refers to Doeg and Ahithophel <note>Historical figures who opposed David</note> and their faction, who have only deceit in their mouths. **Their inward part is destruction** — their internal essence is the ruin of all workers of wickedness. **Their throat is an open grave** — their throat is like a grave that receives all the dead and never says "enough." Thus, their throat is always open to swallow and destroy people. **They make their tongue smooth** — this is flattery, where they use smooth words to cover the truth. **Condemn them, O God** — let them be found guilty and punished for their evil deeds. **And all who take refuge in You shall rejoice** — when You punish them, everyone will see that You help the righteous, and they will rejoice in their rescue. **And You shall shelter them** — meaning You will protect them. **For You, O Lord, will bless the righteous... as with a shield** — just as a shield <note>Hebrew: "tzina"</note> surrounds a person and protects them from all sides, so You will crown him with Your favor to guard him. Like a crown <note>Hebrew: "atara"</note> encircles the head, You will encircle him with goodness. This is how Rashi and Jonathan <note>Classic commentators</note> explained it, and it is correct.

# For the Conductor
**With stringed instruments.** I have already explained the meaning of "with stringed instruments" <note>Hebrew: "Neginot"</note>, relating to books of melodies and psalms played on the lyre for the Holy One. Some explain these as songs of the Sukkot festival <note>The Feast of Tabernacles</note>. This psalm is meant to be sung with the eight-stringed instrument <note>Hebrew: "Sheminit"</note>. King David left these psalms for all generations and for everyone who is weak.

Some explain that this psalm was said regarding the Exile, for one suffers many sicknesses and pains in exile. **Have mercy on me, O Lord, for I am languishing** — I am weak and poor. **Heal me, Lord, for my bones are terrified** — heal the internal illness, the pain, and the fractures in my flesh and my strength. **And my soul is greatly terrified; and You, O Lord—how much longer?** — I cannot wait any longer, for I am terrified by these troubles. **Turn back, O Lord, rescue my soul** — turn from Your burning anger and save me. **Save me for the sake of Your kindness** — not for my sake, but because of Your grace, as it is written: "For the sake of My Name." **For in death there is no mention of You** — a person who is dead cannot mention You or praise You as a living person can. David did not say this out of despair, but to express that he wished to live a long life to praise God in this world, which brings honor to God. **I am weary with my groaning** — like a dog howling and crying from the intensity of its suffering. **I make my bed swim every night** — he washes his face with tears and soaks his bed with weeping. **My eye is dimmed from grief** — from great pain and worry, my vision has blurred. **It has aged because of all my adversaries** — his eyes have moved from their place or been damaged because of the grief caused by enemies. **Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity** — do not gather to do evil anymore, for the Lord has heard my weeping. **The Lord will receive my prayer** — I am certain it will be accepted favorably. **Let all my enemies be shamed** — when they see my prayer was heard and I was saved, they will retreat and be ashamed of their plots. **Let them turn back and be shamed in an instant** — let them repent quickly and feel shame. With this, the chapter is completed.

# Psalms
## Psalm 7

<columns>
**The Aramaic Translation (Targum)**
An interpretation of the Torah belonging to David, which he sang before the Lord concerning the friend of Saul, the son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin: O Lord my God, in Your Word I have hoped; deliver me from all my pursuers and rescue me. Lest he tear my soul like a lion, breaking it in pieces with no one to rescue. O Lord my God, if I have performed this song in an evil gathering, if there is injustice in my hands; if I have repaid my friend with evil, or if I have oppressed my enemies without cause; let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it, and let him trample my life to the ground and lay my honor in the dust forever. Arise, O Lord, in Your strength; be revealed in anger against my oppressors, and execute for me the judgment You have commanded. And let the assembly of nations surround You, and for their sake, return Your Presence <note>The Hebrew "Shekhinah," referring to the Divine Presence.</note> to the heights. The Lord judges the nations; judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness and according to the integrity that is within me. Let the evil of the wicked come to an end, and establish the righteous, for the righteous God searches hearts and kidneys <note>In ancient thought, the kidneys were considered the seat of emotion and conscience.</note>. My shield is with God, who saves the upright of heart. God is a righteous judge, powerful and indignant against the wicked every day. If he does not repent, His sword is sharpened, His bow is drawn and ready. For him He has prepared instruments of death; His arrows are made ready for the righteous.

<column-break/>

**The Hebrew Source Text**
A *Shiggaion* <note>original: "Shiggaion." A musical or literary term of uncertain meaning, possibly referring to a "wild" or "wandering" melody.</note> of David, which he sang to the Lord concerning Cush the Benjamite.
O Lord my God, in You I take refuge; save me from all who pursue me, and deliver me.
Lest he tear my soul like a lion, rending it in pieces, while there is none to deliver.
O Lord my God, if I have done this; if there be iniquity in my hands;
<margin>I have repaid</margin> If I have requited him that was at peace with me with evil; or if I have despoiled him that without cause was my adversary;
Let the enemy pursue my soul and overtake it; and let him trample my life to the earth, and lay my glory in the dust. Selah.
Arise, O Lord, in Your anger; lift Yourself up in the face of the rage of my adversaries; and awake for me the judgment You have commanded.
And let the congregation of the peoples compass You about; and over them return on high.
The Lord ministers judgment to the peoples; judge me, O Lord, according to my righteousness, and according to my integrity that is in me.
Oh let the wickedness of the wicked come to an end, but establish the righteous; for the righteous God tries the hearts and reins.
My shield is upon God, who saves the upright in heart.
<margin>Indignant</margin> God is a righteous judge, and a God who has indignation every day.
If a man turn not, He will whet His sword; He has bent His bow, and made it ready.
He has also prepared for him the instruments of death, He appoints His arrows against the pursuers.
Behold, he travails with iniquity; yea, he has conceived mischief, and brought forth falsehood.
</columns>

---

# Shiggaion

David "dug a pit and hollowed it out" <note>A reference to Psalm 7:15</note> for himself, and it is also found in the prayer of Habakkuk "upon *shigyonot*." Our Sages, of blessed memory, said that this psalm was recited concerning Saul, who is called "Cush" <note>The word "Cushite" usually refers to an Ethiopian. Here it is used as a cryptic nickname for King Saul.</note> because he was as distinguished in his beauty as a Cushite is distinguished by his skin; this is the opinion of all the commentators. They say he was called Cush because just as a Cushite is distinct in his appearance, Saul was distinct in his kingship and his youth. In this way, Saul is addressed as "Cush." Some suggest it refers to a "friend" who was a companion of Saul and then abandoned him. 

The sage Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Ibn Ezra." A major medieval Spanish-Jewish scholar.</note>, of blessed memory, upheld this interpretation. He suggests that the term refers to the "changing" of a melody or a specific musical arrangement. He notes that many people would hear this psalm. It refers to the service David performed for Saul and how David did not harm him even when Saul pursued him. David wonders why he is being fought when he has committed no crime. He asks the Lord to protect him from those who seek his life. 

The text mentions "concerning the words of Cush," referring to the speakers who incited Saul against David, bringing evil reports to him from within his own people. As it is written elsewhere, people would add "false words" to incite fear and reward. David prays for the wickedness of these people to end and for his own heart to be tested. 

Regarding the phrase "Lest he tear my soul like a lion," this refers to the enemy who pursues him. David uses the metaphor of a lion to describe the power of the king who could trample his life to the ground. If David had truly repaid evil for good, he says he would deserve to be overtaken. But he insists: "If I have repaid him who was at peace with me with evil..." He reminds the reader of the incident in the cave where he only cut the corner of Saul's cloak and did not kill him, showing he did not return evil for evil. 

"Arise, O Lord, in Your anger"—David calls for divine intervention. He asks God to "awake" the judgment that was already commanded, referring to the kingdom that was promised to him. He speaks of the "assembly of nations" surrounding God, meaning that all the tribes or nations will see God's justice when He returns to His high throne of judgment. 

David's defense is his integrity. He asks God to judge him according to his righteousness. He acknowledges that God knows the "hearts and kidneys" (the inner thoughts). While men might act one way outwardly, God knows the truth. Therefore, David relies on God as his "shield." He concludes that God is a righteous judge who is "indignant every day" at the behavior of the wicked. If the pursuer (Saul or his allies) does not repent, God's "instruments of death" and "flaming arrows" are prepared. The wicked man "conceives mischief" but will ultimately "bring forth falsehood"—his plans will fail.

### Psalm 9
For praise, concerning the death of the man who went out from between the camps <note>Refers to the Philistine champion Goliath, who is called a "middle-man" or "champion" in the biblical text.</note>, a song of praise by David. I will praise before the Lord with all my heart; I will make heard all Your miracles.

<meta>catchword: אֲחַדֵי (I will rejoice)</meta>

---

<margin>He dug a pit and hollowed it out</margin>
This is a repetition of the same theme using different words. The meaning is that he dug a pit and hollowed it out specifically so that his companion would fall into it, but instead, he fell into it himself. **His mischief shall return upon his own head.** The word "and he fell" <note>original: "va-yipol"</note> into the pit is used here in the future tense, similar to other prophetic descriptions of consequences. **His mischief shall return upon his own head.** The order is correct: his labor returns to his head and his violence is visited upon him, a repetition of the idea in different terms. **I will praise the Lord according to His righteousness.** Our Sages <note>Hazal: The Jewish Sages of the Mishnah and Talmud.</note> interpreted: "praise the Lord according to the righteousness of the deeds of my people." **And I will sing praise to the name of the Lord Most High.** For He is supreme over all; note the repetition of terms as explained below.

# To the Chief Musician
**On the Gittith.** We have already explained that the *Gittith* is a musical instrument played by the musician. Some say it refers to a specific musical box. Others say this Psalm was composed regarding Goliath the Philistine, and "Gittith" refers to the fall of Goliath, who was from the city of Gath. This entire Psalm focuses on the mighty power of the Creator, blessed be He, and the weakness of man.
**O Lord our Master, how majestic is Your name in all the earth.** To Him is Your thanksgiving, for all the heavens are the "work of Your fingers." Even though the heavens are at the level of the Crown <note>A reference to the *Keter*, the highest of the Divine emanations in Jewish mysticism.</note>...
**From the mouths of babes and sucklings.** This refers to the day the Torah was given <note>The revelation at Mount Sinai.</note>, when the People of Israel were like tender infants without worldly knowledge, and their faith in the Creator came through pure tradition... as if they were nursing from the breast.
**To silence the enemy and the avenger.** This refers to Pharaoh, Sihon, Og, and all the kings who rose against Israel.
**When I behold Your heavens.** This includes the entire expanse of the heavens, all of which are the work of Your hands.
**What is man that You are mindful of him.** What is the strength of this lowly human compared to the celestial bodies and the stars, which are all mighty and stand to perform the will of their Maker?
**You have made him a little lower than the angels.** These are the celestial beings.
**And crowned him with glory and honor.** This refers to the "Higher Wisdom" <note>Intellectual and spiritual capacity</note> that You placed within him.
**You made him ruler over the works of Your hands.** Over all the beasts of the earth and the birds of the heaven... **Glory and honor You crown him** with everything that is placed beneath his feet.

# To the Chief Musician
**A Psalm of David.** Some say that *Laben* <note>from the title "Muth-labben"</note> refers to Goliath the Philistine, who blasphemed the ranks of the Living God. Others say *Laben* refers to Nabal the Carmelite, whose sons stood in war against David, as we have already expounded...

### The Aramaic Targum

**To the Chief Musician**... on the death of the son, etc. For I have placed all my trust in my strength for the war with us, and no "victor" <note>original: "Menatzach," which can mean both "conductor" or "victor."</note> is effective; and according to this meaning, the matter of "Muth-labben" refers to the death <note>Muth</note> of the champion <note>Labben—interpreted here as Goliath, the "man between the camps"</note>... to sing and praise again. Concerning the surroundings, let him return. For all the Philistine ranks were ended by David, as it is written in Joshua, and all of them were Joshua's... for tomorrow at the time of this speaking in war, this shall be David... he shall run for safety. The wall <note>Chamot</note> shall be for escape, and there is no security except from David. "To the wall" means to merit. *And those who know Your name will trust in You*, meaning whoever hears Your name as a refuge from it, who would be pleased by the Philistine ranks we have seen and known to all... *You have rebuked the nations, You have destroyed the wicked.* *You have rebuked the nations and the ruins are eternal.* The Holy One, blessed be He, rebuked them at the time of the Temple. And so, *You have rebuked nations*, etc. And the "wicked" is hinted at in the "eternal sword." The memory of the divisions. The memory of the Philistines. Kindness <note>Chesed</note> is the price over death as a sign and wrath for His name. *And the Lord will be a high tower for the oppressed.* For the people and the matter will be a shield, a fence, and a safeguard for every single thing, and one must return to the Lord. Because from them came the destruction of His people like a mighty man of war, the dwelling of His glory from above—kindness—and destruction of houses and fences and the parched sword of the poor was bitter from them. And they taught to... the ruins are finished—the ruins that will return with them forever, the power of their destruction. For the sword of Esau <note>Esau represents Rome or the archetypal enemy in rabbinic thought</note> is the mouth of the bitter sword, and every thought and great kindness and the wisdom of Horeb <note>Mount Sinai</note> for everyone who serves in the synagogues. His praise, etc. *The Lord sits enthroned forever*... God is high, dwelling in the heavens, for God forbid that He should turn back the discipline and all the laws of vanity and all the lonely life without our shelter. *Be gracious to me, O Lord.* May the Lord be gracious to me and He will be for him, sitting forever. *I will rejoice*... *be gracious to me, Lord*... and so *He sits forever.* And may there be profit from the gift of kindness, and His power is exalted from the mountain of the vision, for God forbid that grace should be stirred. The matter of the "return" will be stirred from His people, the Lord, and He will have mercy on him. *And He shall judge the world.* The wrath and the secret of their trembling; may the Lord be gracious to us, for God forbid the trembling that branches out in the understanding from the vision of every time; for how can a judge, etc., and have mercy on us. For He will be for him at the end, and from every time the vision of His kingdom and His dominion shall run in every House of Study <note>Beit Midrash</note> as much as... the world and all kindness is brought before the refuge of kindness, and all power for the time; and it shall be for Him to give us our strength from Him, God forbid, for like the signs of the poor is kindness in a strong tower, for his high tower is in it for all... He strengthened and fortified His kindness to awaken those who will be strengthened by the kindnesses of grace with the help of the Lord, may He be blessed, with us in the distance; and He will be a high tower for us—a tower, a tower, a tower—the protecting shield and help, etc., and so a high tower, etc.
<margin>In pride</margin>
**Why** [do You stand afar?] The ways of the wicked are in his deep face, and the pious man has the strength to be endured by him. And since he denied the Lord, he who engages in his paths <note>lit. "hooves"</note> will trust; the end of the matter of evil is from the wickedness of his face, anger in the distance, and in the hiding of His face he lodges and a path for the desired thing from him, he trembled for him. And the explanation of "evil from life in the distance," etc., for the distance is the heat of trade and commerce, God forbid. And in every understanding is the throne of the sun from its times, the warmth of the world as the world in wisdom. Therefore, to the one who said his fellow's sons are his sickness... to aim for the day of the End. *O Lord, You stand far off*, for in the one who waits for the help of his refuge for the poor, and for what is written "as they waited for his kindness." Like from the bread of the close gleanings of his sickness. And when the pig <note>often a code for Rome/Esau in this period</note> prevails, he waits for his kindness in the distance and hides His eyes from the poor. Therefore he said, *Why, O Lord, do You stand far off?* And the house in my spirit stands in the place of... great in a distant place. *You hide Yourself in times of trouble.* To hide from his eyes in the... in pride.

**In the arrogance of the wicked.** This means that in his spreading out, he pursues the poor to gather them in. **Let them be caught.** This is missing the letter *aleph*. <note>The commentator notes a grammatical irregularity in the Hebrew word "yitapsu" (let them be caught)</note> And let the wicked be caught in the schemes he intended for the gathering of the poor. This is like saying "that which they planned." **For the wicked boasts.** Because he has profaned himself for the sake of his monetary desire, and there is no one to prevent him; he concludes that everyone will be punished according to his judgment. **And the greedy man blesses.** The wicked man praises and glorifies the one who makes unjust profit, showing that his way is successful, and thereby spurns the Lord. That is to say, he attempts to cancel the depth of divine law. These are words of judgment against him. Like saying in his heart, "You will not require it." **The wicked in his haughtiness.** Haughtiness of heart is reflected in the face... like the phrase "his countenance fell." **The helpless.** This refers to those who are downcast. **All his thoughts.** From him come his sproutings and his vitality; he does not seek God nor pray before Him. **"There is no God" are all his thoughts.** All the thoughts of the wicked are that there is no divine judgment. And all the retribution that comes to the world is accidental in his eyes. Therefore, he does not seek God. **His ways prosper.** The word "yakhilu" (prosper) relates to waiting or enduring. Even though his ways are wicked, he remains firm and successful in the world at all times. **Your judgments are far above.** They are not upon him, therefore he is haughty. **He snorts at all his adversaries.** He blows away his enemies with his breath, as if they are nothing before him. That is to say, he considers them weak. **He says in his heart, "I shall not be moved."** He thinks he will never stumble, and his greatness will last for generations. **I shall not be in adversity.** From generation to generation, no evil will befall him. Therefore, he thinks he is secure. **His mouth is full of cursing.** This is the way of the wicked: his mouth is full of deceit and filth. For whenever he is angry, he speaks deceit and fraud. **Under his tongue are mischief and iniquity.** He hides within his speech the desire to cause harm and trouble. This "mischief" is hidden under the tongue like a secret. Just as the Tabernacle was filled with the Glory of God, his mouth is filled with these things. **He sits in the lurking places of the villages.** He waits in the open cities, on the roads, to rob people and their daughters. **He murders the innocent.** In his hidden heart, he will not refrain from doing evil in secret, but sits in ambush to steal from others. **His eyes are stealthily set against the helpless.** Like a spy who hides and watches the ways of the humble and poor. The word "yitzponu" (stealthily set) is an intransitive verb; he places his eyes in a hidden spot to watch the roads. **He lies in wait in secret like a lion.** Just as a lion stands in his thicket to snatch whatever passes by, so the wicked sits in ambush. And it says "he catches" twice to show the intensity of his action. He catches the poor by drawing him into his net. This is the way of the wicked: he acts in secret so that people do not see him, and he acts with strength and power. And regarding the poor, who are the broken among people, he rejoices over them. **He crouches, he bows down.** It is written "ve-dakhah" (he crouches) with a *vav*. He humbles himself to catch his prey. "Atzumav" (his mighty ones) refers to his strong limbs or his gathered strength used to crush the poor. **And the helpless fall.** This is written as one word but read as two: *chel* (army/strength) and *ka'im* (broken). It refers to the brokenness of the poor. Through all these ways, the wicked says in his heart that God does not see. **He says in his heart, "God has forgotten."** If he knew God saw him, he would not act this way. He thinks God has hidden His face and will never see. Therefore, the psalmist prays: **Arise, O Lord.** Since the wicked says there is no judgment, the psalmist asks God to arise and judge. **Do not forget the humble.** For the wicked thinks God has forgotten. **Humble.** It is written "aniyyim" (the poor) but read as "anavim" (the humble). **Why does the wicked spurn God?** Why does he provoke? Because he says in his heart that You will not require an account. **You have seen it.** You have seen the hidden things. Even though the wicked says You do not see, You see everything. For You alone behold the mischief and anger the wicked causes to the poor. **To requite it with Your hand.** To take up the judgment of the oppressed. **The helpless commits himself to You.** Because You are the helper of the fatherless and the one who has no power. **Break the arm.** Break his strength. **Seek out his wickedness.** Since he said You would not seek it, the psalmist asks God to seek it out until no wickedness remains. **The Lord is King forever.** When judgment is executed upon the wicked, the Lord is recognized as King. Then the nations—the wicked—will perish from the land of Israel. **You have heard the desire of the humble.** You heard their prayer. Even before they spoke, You knew their desire. **You will prepare their heart.** To pray with intention. And then You will incline Your ear to their prayer. **To judge the fatherless.** To take up the cause of those who are oppressed by others. **So that he may no longer strike terror.** So that the wicked man, who is but mortal from the earth, shall no longer act with violence.

# For the Leader

**Of David. In the Lord I take refuge; how can you say to my soul, "Flee."** It is written "nudu" (flee, plural) and read as "nudi" (flee, singular). David says: when I was in distress, my enemies said I should flee to the mountains like a bird. But I said that my refuge is in God.

->For the Leader<-
A psalm of David. How long, O Lord? Will You forget me forever? How long will You hide Your face from me? How long shall I take counsel in my soul, having sorrow in my heart daily? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me? Consider and answer me, O Lord my God; enlighten my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death. Lest my enemy say, "I have prevailed against him," and my adversaries rejoice when I am moved. But I have trusted in Your mercy; my heart shall rejoice in Your salvation. I will sing to the Lord, because He has dealt bountifully with me.

**For behold the wicked.** I have already explained this. And the Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, 1160–1235, a preeminent medieval grammarian and commentator from Provence</note> explains this matter as referring to the people of Israel in the days of King Hezekiah when Sennacherib <note>the Assyrian king who besieged Jerusalem in 701 BCE</note> came, and Rabshakeh <note>the Assyrian messenger</note> sent insults and blasphemies against the Lord. This is the meaning of what is written regarding the arrows... specifically the weapons of reward and punishment. In the heavenly realms, when the connection between the living beings of Glory was separated from their place—God forbid!—the sword of war appeared. The arrows are drawn from the source of strength... a material power... words of destruction... He sought to comfort his merits with grace and kindness, which is why the servant of the King is mentioned. It is written that Israel will be despoiled according to their laws unless they remain pious... to strengthen the heart of Hezekiah and his pious followers. **When the foundations are destroyed.** What are these foundations? They are the principles upon which the world is established. They represent the protection of the world's laws against the burdens of the wicked. What has the righteous person done? What has the one who prospers before the Lord achieved through merit? The "foundations" are the laws of mercy and the hidden treasures... This is a metaphor for the thoughts and counsels of men. **What has the righteous done?** For the thoughts of the wicked will be destroyed and they will not achieve what they planned, but the righteous will have his will fulfilled—meaning God will grant him success in his righteousness. **The Lord is in His holy temple.** His holy temple refers to the heavens. **The Lord’s throne is in heaven.** That is to say, even though His Presence is above, His eyes see and test the depths, testing the children of men. This is metaphorical, for the Lord sees and brings lightning and thunder to each person according to their deeds. **The Lord tests the righteous.** In the way of the law of mercy, he shall live. But upon the wicked He brings destruction... to show the purity of the heart... He will not spare the honor of His name... but the wicked person hates violence and His soul hates to be rebuked, though he should accept rebuke. He tests His people and refines them from the world. **He shall rain coals upon the wicked.** Derived from the word for a "snare." Some explain "coals" as carbon for fires... others as a burning heat. **The portion of their cup.** Just as one is given a portion or a lot. **For the Lord is righteous, He loves righteous deeds.** A language of embracing and prayer. **The upright shall behold His face.** Some interpret this as "they shall behold His face" similar to "we have seen His face." The word *panemo* means "His face." The faces of the wicked will be shamed... but the upright will behold the vision of His face, as one sees a flash of lightning.

**For the leader: Save, O Lord, for the godly man ceases.** That is to say, the pious have gone and vanished... and most of the sages of this generation are wicked and plot against the poor and weak. Therefore, the righteous man prays to the Lord of the Eight <note>referring to the *Sheminith* instrument mentioned in the psalm's header</note> to save them from the flood. **For the godly man ceases.** Because these children of men act from a divided heart. **Flattering lips.** Describing a smooth or deceitful tongue. **With a double heart.** He presents himself in their words with one heart for good but another heart for lies. **May the Lord cut off all flattering lips.** This is a form of prophecy or prayer. **Great things.** Words of arrogance and haughtiness... speaking as if they are superior to commoners. **Because of the oppression of the poor.** From the cry of the poor... because of the heat and sickness of those who love to stay with us... God says in a prophetic way: **I will set him in safety.** I will place the righteous in salvation and protect them from the snares the wicked set to trap them. **The words of the Lord are pure words.** Do not think that what the Lord promised is a mere puff of air; God’s word is pure and entirely true, like refined silver... refined sevenfold. **In a crucible <note>original: "ba'alil"</note> on the earth.** This refers to a place of supreme clarity and understanding. The number seven indicates a great number, as in "seven times for your sins" or "the righteous falls seven times and rises." It means many times over. **From this generation.** From this generation where the wicked act with violence in every age. **The wicked walk on every side.** For the wicked surround the righteous to harm them... **Vileness is exalted.** When lowliness and vileness are raised up among men, and the wicked and the base are honored, everything is lost.

**How long, O Lord? Will You forget me forever?** This is a psalm of David from when he was fleeing from Saul... or it speaks of the Assembly of Israel. He asks: How long will You hide Your face? Meaning, You do not wish to see my suffering. The Radak explains that this fourfold repetition—"How long?"—corresponds to the four exiles. How long will You forget me? How long will You hide Your face? How long shall I take counsel? How long shall my enemy be exalted? Against these, he offers prayers for salvation. **Sorrow in my heart daily.** Even during the day when one is busy with the affairs of the world, he is still struck by sorrow... **Lighten my eyes.** Lest I be consumed by the darkness of exile... **Lest my enemy say: I have prevailed.** If I fall, they will rejoice. **But I have trusted in Your mercy.** Even if You seem to forget me, I trust in Your kindness to save me... **I will sing to the Lord, because He has dealt bountifully with me.** When my salvation comes, I will sing to the Lord for the bounty He has bestowed upon me and upon all Israel.

Behold, the wicked decree the bow and prepare their arrows on the string to shoot in the darkness at the upright of heart. Because, behold, the foundations were broken, and the righteous man, because he did good deeds, was spared. The Lord is in His holy temple; God is in the high heavens, His throne is there. His eyes see, His eyelids test the children of men. God tests the righteous, but the wicked and the lovers of theft His soul hates. He shall bring down the rain of retribution upon the wicked—coals of fire and sulfur—and a storm-wind upon the arrogant shall be the portion of their cup. Because the Lord is righteous, He loves righteousness; the upright shall see the light of His face.
