->While they were dwelling in Egypt, the children of Ephraim were destroyed; though armed and carrying bows, they turned back in the day of battle.<-

**I will remember** (*Ezkor*). It is written with a *Yod* <note>original: "אזכיר"</note> meaning "I will mention," but it is read as "I will remember" with a *Nun* <note>meaning "let us remember"</note>. This refers to when he mentions the deeds of the Lord: **For I will remember Your wonders from of old.** These are the wonders performed of old in Egypt, as mentioned below, regarding the plagues and the miracles done for our ancestors in the wilderness. For they lived for fifty years and it did not occur to them that His power had diminished or that the wonders the Holy One, Blessed be He, did for them when they left Egypt had ceased. This refers to the narrative of the wonders sent to them from plague to plague, and the Manna, and the Well, and the clouds, and the Great Assembly at Mount Horeb and the giving of the Torah. **And I will meditate on all Your work.** Through my speech, I will reflect on Your actions and meditate on them. That is to say, You changed the face of nature for me as a testimony to teach grace to my children. This refers to the works and deeds You did in Egypt and at the splitting of the Red Sea in the depths of the sea and at the standing at Mount Sinai and in the Torah. **And Your work.** The *Yod* of the plural is missing. **And in Your deeds.** In all the many deeds You did for our fathers. **Your way.** Some explain this word as "peace." Its meaning is "from Your way come Your wonders," meaning apart from the natural way. This is like saying "Who is like the Creator of all life, who is like the one chosen among all gods?" These "gods" are not gods but kings and rulers. For kings, on the day they fall, their goodness descends, and their weakness shows they are but men. 

**The waters saw You and trembled.** Since he says "You ascended," the text uses "trembled." For the springs of water trembled and were terrified. **The waters trembled in the wilderness at Sinai.** Also the clouds, as it is written that they were in their midst, and on Mount Sinai, and it is written: "And all the people saw the voices." And further, as He showed him and descended on Mount Sinai with thunder and lightning. **Whirlwind.** A great thunder and the rotation of the heavens. According to the plain meaning <note>term: "Peshat"</note>, this refers to the heart of kings; from the Red Sea to the shore, they trembled from within. **The depths also quaked.** Fear of the deep waters; the depths were agitated and trembled from within because of the fear that surrounded them. **The clouds poured out water.** As if He wrote "mighty and strong." Because they trembled, the waters in the heavens opened, as did the Manna. And from a distance, they heard the voice of the thunders of the clouds of heaven, and this is "like the voice of thunder." This is evidence for what is written, that they did not see anything but the voices. As it is written: "And fire came out from before the Lord and consumed them." For they were a sign and symbols for them. As it is said: **The skies sent out a sound.** 

The end of the matter alludes to the Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> which was agitated because all of that generation remembered this choice. We learn this from the casting of idols before Him. This is how they call one who transgresses their testimony from generation to generation. **The voice of Your thunder was in the whirlwind.** In the opening of the celestial sphere. **And they turned back in the day of battle.** This belongs to the first part of the matter. So too, the sound of the sphere over them, and at the sound of His footstep, the world shook. The fear of the waters from the Presence had already fallen, for it fled from the day of the giving of the spheres and was quick to pass. Before Him was the fear of the seas and the Presence, and they denied the denial of the seas in the whirlwind of the new path, the path of holiness and the Manna. So too the fear of the seas like water, and **His footprints were not known.** For the rocks in the whirlwind were not like a new thing that weakens without order, which congeals the sea. And before the water, the water was a whirlwind. Because He broke through and led them through the end. He trod on the floor of the sea as it is written, and walked in a channel as it is written, and they suffered illnesses. 

**You led Your people like a flock by the hand of Moses.** Jacob and Joseph according to the Midrash <note>interpretive tradition</note>. "I led you by the hand of Moses" because the children of Joseph were with them in the wilderness, as it is written "And Joseph took," and Joseph went before your fathers. **By the hand of Moses and Aaron.** As it is said: "You led Your people in kindness by the hand of Moses and Aaron."

# **Maskil**

**To Asaph. My teaching.** What is "my teaching"? It is one who merits the Torah through the stories of the good things God did for the generation. The words of the Lord shall be, for there is much to learn from them and to understand, despite His word and His Torah. **I will open my mouth.** Even if I were exempt due to the smallness of their sin and only spoke of the good days, my companions have merited to rule and to rebuke... **I will utter riddles.** This refers to the Manna... **And our fathers told us.** Our fathers are those who told us of the forgiveness and pardoning of their sins. **We heard and we knew them.** Also from the written word of the Torah of Moses our teacher. **We will not hide them from their children.** Our companions, who are our generation, and the testimony and Torah are known and famous. **So that they might know.** So they are not hidden from them until they too are living and telling their children, and their children to their children's children, until the last generation tells the praises of the Lord. **He established a testimony.** As mentioned above, the foundations, and this was for the children... **And they shall set their hope in God.** As you have made known to your children. This refers to the children yet to be born, when they grow in knowledge, they too will tell their children. **And they shall set their hope in God.** Our longing for the wonders... and they shall place their trust and not rebel... unlike the generation of the wilderness... **The children of Ephraim, being armed and carrying bows.** This happened in the wilderness. It is considered as missing from the Torah but mentioned in the book of Chronicles. The intention is to give hope. This story appears in Chronicles, for in the wilderness this event took place... The meaning of "carrying bows" is that they increased in their military strength and their deeds, and they became angry and did not trust in God. **And they turned back.** They turned their backs before their enemies. This is "they turned back in the day of battle." They turned their back on the day of war. "Armed and carrying bows" means they were skilled in drawing and shooting arrows with the bow. Some explain this verse and the verse in Chronicles as referring to the children of Ephraim who left Egypt before the appointed end <note>A midrashic tradition that a group of Ephraimites tried to escape Egypt 30 years too early and were slaughtered by the Philistines.</note>, and this incident befell them. But investigate this verse and story...

# Psalms

<column-break/>

They did not keep God’s covenant and refused to walk in His law. They forgot His deeds and the wonders He had shown them. Before their ancestors, He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan <note>Zoan was an ancient city in the eastern Nile Delta, serving as a royal residence.</note>. He split the sea and let them pass through, making the waters stand like a wall. He led them with a cloud by day and all night with the light of fire. He split rocks in the wilderness and gave them drink as from the great depths. He brought streams out of the crag and made water run down like rivers. Yet they continued to sin against Him, rebelling against the Most High in the parched land. They tested God in their hearts by asking for food to satisfy their cravings. They spoke against God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness? Look, He struck the rock and waters flowed, and streams overflowed—but can He also give bread? Can He provide meat for His people?” Therefore, the Lord heard and was enraged; a fire was kindled against Jacob, and anger rose against Israel. For they did not believe in God or trust in His salvation. Yet He commanded the skies above and opened the doors of heaven. He rained down manna for them to eat and gave them the grain of heaven. Mortal man ate the bread of angels <note>original: "Abirim," literally "mighty ones," traditionally interpreted as angels.</note>; He sent them provisions to their fill. He set the east wind in motion in the heavens and by His power guided the south wind. He rained meat upon them like dust, winged birds like the sand of the seas. He let them fall in the midst of His camp, all around His dwellings. So they ate and were well filled, for He gave them what they craved. But before they had satisfied their craving, while the food was still in their mouths, God’s anger rose against them; He killed the sturdiest among them and brought low the choice young men of Israel.

They did not keep the covenant of the Lord and refused to walk in His Torah. And the deeds were forgotten by the community of the House of Israel, along with His wonders that He showed them. In the presence of their fathers—Isaac, Jacob, and the tribes of their ancestors—He performed wonders in the land of Egypt, in the field of Tanis <note>Tanis is the Aramaic and Greek name for the city of Zoan.</note>. He split the sea with the rod of Moses the merciful and brought them through, and he made the water stand upright like a goatskin. And He brought forth flows of water from the rock and brought them down like flowing rivers. And they continued further to sin before Him, to provoke the Most High in the thirsty desert. And they tested God in their hearts to ask for food for their souls. And they murmured before Him, saying: “Is there power before God to set a table in the desert? Behold, when he struck the flinty rock, waters flowed and streams overflowed; but can He also provide bread, or prepare meat for His people?” Therefore it was heard before God and He was angry, and fire was kindled against the house of Jacob, and even a strong wrath rose against Israel. Because they did not believe in God and did not trust in His redemption. And He commanded the clouds from above and opened the doors of heaven. And He brought down manna upon them to eat, and gave them the grain of heaven. Food that descends from on high, man ate the bread of the mighty; He sent them provisions to satisfaction. He cast the east wind into the heavens and led the south wind by His strength. And He brought down meat upon them like dust, and winged birds like the sand of the sea. And He let it fall in the middle of his camps, surrounding his dwellings. And they ate and were very satisfied, and He brought them their desire. And they did not turn away from their desire, even while their food was in their mouths. And the anger of God rose among them and slew their mighty ones, and the youths of Israel were laid low.

<insert>
The order of these praises follows the sequence of the Torah <note>The Five Books of Moses</note>. Since the Torah was given to them after the Exodus from Egypt, the text mentions the miracles that occurred then. It notes that concerning the destruction of Shiloh <note>The sanctuary that housed the Ark before the Temple in Jerusalem was built</note>, it is said that the verse “strengthened my heart to tell.” As is known, the master of Israel increased in Shiloh. This interpretation is somewhat difficult, for it mentions the destruction of Shiloh in the sequence after mentioning the divisions. Furthermore, why did the sons of Ephraim fail to have the strength to fight in the battle, as it is written, “And the word of Samuel came to all Israel”? They did not keep the covenant of God. This refers to the covenant He made with them at Mount Sinai. They were accustomed to fighting the wars of the Lord with honor. Two priests died, and the Ark was captured in the land, and the whole earth shook. He mentions here the “Field of Zoan,” which was the royal city in Egypt. **In the presence of their fathers:** This is the reason He brought them into the wilderness and performed wonders for them. As it is written: “the waters were like a heap” <note>original: "ned"</note>, referring to the flowing waters standing still. He led them with a cloud and darkness.

**He split the rocks:** The word “split” is in the future tense but used here for the past, as is common in biblical poetry. He mentions the wonders because after the first rock provided for them, they complained again. In the wilderness of Zin, He gave them manna, and He gave them drink from the depths. **He brought streams out of the rock:** This refers to the rock that was high up. **But they continued to sin against Him:** They added sin to sin even after the miracles. **To rebel against the Most High in the desert:** The term "Most High" <note>original: "Elyon"</note> is used because He is above all, and it was in His power to bring water from the rock. They, however, did not have the vision to see this and argued against Him at the Graves of Craving <note>Hebrew: "Kivrot HaTa'avah," a site of rebellion mentioned in the Book of Numbers</note>.

**They tested God in their hearts:** In their thoughts, they harbored disbelief. The manna was good and pleasant, and they did not truly lack food, but they spoke out of a desire for more. They did not speak this with their mouths at first, but in their hearts they belittled the glory of the King. **Can God spread a table in the wilderness?** They claimed that while He could strike a rock to produce water, He could not prepare a full meal or bread from the rain. They doubled their words, asking for both bread and meat. **Therefore the Lord heard and was enraged:** Because of what they thought in their hearts, His anger burned. The fire refers to the event at Taberah <note>A place named "Burning" where God's fire broke out against the people</note>.

**Anger rose against Israel:** This refers to the Graves of Craving. The verse includes two events: the fire at Taberah and the plague at the Graves of Craving. They did not believe that God could bring them into the Land without a war, and their request for meat was a lack of faith. **He commanded the skies:** He opened the "doors of heaven" to rain down manna. This is a metaphor for the abundance of manna, similar to the "windows of heaven" in the story of the Flood. **Mortal man ate the bread of angels:** The word for "mighty ones" <note>original: "Abirim"</note> refers to the angels. Some interpret this to mean food that is absorbed into the limbs <note>a play on words: "Abirim" (mighty) and "Evarim" (limbs)</note>, leaving no waste. **He sent them provisions to their fill:** Wherever they went, their provisions were with them. **He set the east wind in motion:** This brought the quail. He guided the south wind to bring them in abundance like dust. **And He let it fall in the midst of His camp:** Just as it is written, "it lay all around the camp." They ate until they were overfilled, until it became loathsome to them. **While the food was still in their mouths:** Even as they were eating, the anger of God rose against them and He killed the sturdiest and healthiest among them.

<column-break/>

Despite all this, they sinned again and did not believe in His wonders. And He ended their days in vanity and their years in terror. When He killed them, they sought Him; and they returned and prayed before God. And they remembered that God was their strength and their rock, and the children of Isaac <note>The Aramaic translation often adds specific ancestral references, here linking the "Redeemer" to the merit of the Patriarchs.</note> [remembered] the Most High God. And they flattered Him with their mouths and lied to Him with their tongues. For their hearts were not faithful with Him, and they did not believe in His covenant. But He, the Merciful One, atones for iniquity and does not destroy them; He frequently turns away His anger and does not stir up all His wrath. And He remembered that they are but flesh, a spirit that passes and does not return. How often they rebelled against Him in the wilderness and provoked Him in the desert! They turned back and tested God, and they brought sorrow to the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember His hand, the day He redeemed them from the oppressor. How He set His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the fields of Tanis <note>original: "Ma'anis," the Aramaic name for the Egyptian city of Zoan.</note>. Despite all this, they sinned still and did not believe in His wonders. So He ended their days in futility and their years in terror. If He slew them, they would seek Him, and return and look for God. They remembered that God was their Rock, and the Most High God their Redeemer. But He, being compassionate, atoned for iniquity and did not destroy <margin>in His...</margin>; He many times turned His anger away and did not stir up all His wrath. He remembered that they were but flesh, a wind that passes and does not return. How often they rebelled against Him in the wilderness and grieved Him in the wasteland! They turned back and tested God, and provoked the Holy One of Israel. They did not remember His hand, nor the day He redeemed them from <margin>His signs... foe</margin> the foe. How He set His signs in Egypt and His wonders in the field of Zoan. And He turned <margin>swarms</margin> their rivers to blood, and their streams they could not drink. He sent swarms among them which devoured them, and frogs which destroyed them. He gave their crops to the caterpillar and their labor to the locust. He sent against them His burning anger, wrath, indignation, and trouble—a band of evil angels. He paved a path for His anger; He did not spare their souls from death, but gave their life over to the pestilence. He struck all the firstborn in Egypt, the first of their strength in the tents of Ham. But He led forth His own people like sheep and guided them like a flock in the wilderness. ---

**Despite all this, they sinned still.** This refers to the sin of the spies, the rebellion of Korah and his assembly, and the Waters of Strife. **And they did not believe in His wonders.** Despite all the miracles He performed, they did not believe He would actually bring them into the Land.

**He ended their days in futility.** They died in the wilderness. **In terror.** In sudden panic. There is a tradition regarding the fifteenth of Av: every year, the people in the desert would dig graves for themselves and sleep in them. In the morning, those whose time had not yet come would arise. But in the fortieth year, when they dug their graves and no one died, they thought they had miscalculated the calendar. They continued to sleep in graves until the fifteenth of Av, when they saw the full moon and realized the decree of death had ended, so they made it a holiday. Thus it says their days ended "in futility," for they lived in constant dread of death. **Their years in terror.** Because they died suddenly without prior illness, with their shrouds already prepared.

**If He slew them.** God slew the rebels like Dathan, Abiram, and the spies. **Then they sought Him.** The survivors would return to seek the presence of the *Shekhinah* <note>The Divine Presence</note>.

**And they remembered that God was their Rock.** When they saw Him showing mercy and not ending their days in terror, they acknowledged Him as their fortress. **They flattered Him with their mouths.** They were hypocrites; their hearts were not whole. Three types of "flattery" are noted here—heart, mouth, and tongue—corresponding to the three parts of the human constitution.

**But He, being compassionate, atones for iniquity.** The Psalmist notes that even though God knew they were lying, He acted with mercy and atoned for them even without perfect repentance.

*Translator's note on liturgy:* Our Rabbis instituted the recital of this verse (*V'hu Rachum*) in the evening prayer because it contains fifty-three words, corresponding to the fifty-three letters in the various holy names of God <note>The commentator here explores mystical numerology linking the prayer to the protection of the night</note>. Reciting it at night is essential because night represents the "Attribute of Judgment," and we must invoke the "Attribute of Mercy" to sweeten the bitterness of judgment.

**A wind that passes.** Their days are short and troubled, like a flower of the field.

**How often they rebelled.** Specifically referencing the sin of the spies. **The wasteland.** A dry place, the wilderness of the nations. **Provoked the Holy One of Israel.** They made a sign or "mark" (*tav*) of idolatry. Some associate this with a specific pagan symbol called a *Skampa*.

**This mountain His right hand had acquired.** This refers to the Temple, which God "planted" firmly. **He paved a path for His anger.** The plagues were not delivered in a measured, predictable way, but with overwhelming force. **Evil angels.** The plagues themselves acted as God's messengers or heralds. The grammatical structure of these verses is explained in the *Michlol* <note>A famous 12th-century Hebrew grammar and dictionary by Rabbi David Kimhi (Radak)</note>.

**Every firstborn.** The destruction of the "first of their strength" in the tents of Ham <note>The biblical ancestor of the Egyptians</note>. **He led them in safety.** Just as He led them through the sea, He led them through the desert without fear, while their enemies were covered by the waters.

**He allotted them an inheritance.** Dividing the land by cord and line, settling the tribes of Israel where the nations once stood. Yet even after entering the land, they continued to test God.

**And they turned back.** The children of Ephraim, who were armed with bows, turned back like stragglers. **Like a deceitful bow.** Those who fight like a deceitful bow. They explained "deceitful bow" as a matter of trickery. **And the meaning of a deceitful bow:**
For the archer who aims his arrow, if the wood of the bow is warped, he aims to one side but it shoots to another side. Thus, they sin against Him; they aim in one direction but it turns in an instant to another side. So **they provoked Him with their high places.** For with various types of idol worship, as explained previously...

# A Psalm
**Of Asaph: O God, the nations have come into Your inheritance.** This psalm was said regarding the destruction of Jerusalem and the wrath of God upon them, similar to the people of Ammon and Moab who came with Sennacherib against Jerusalem. **They have given the corpses of Your servants.** This matter of Asaph can be understood in several ways: whether regarding the first destruction, the second destruction, or the troubles caused by various kingdoms...

<header>Psalms</header>

<margin>Among the nations</margin> Do not remember against us the iniquities of our ancestors; let Your mercies quickly meet us, for we are brought very low. Help us, O God of our salvation, for the sake of the glory of Your name; and deliver us and atone for our sins for Your name’s sake. Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let the retribution for the shed blood of Your servants be known among the nations <margin>May it come</margin> before our eyes. Let the groaning of the prisoner come before You; according to the greatness of Your arm, <margin>With greatness</margin> release those condemned to death. And return to our neighbors sevenfold into their lap the reproach with which they have <margin>reproached</margin> reproached You, O Lord. And we, Your people and the sheep of Your pasture, will give thanks to You forever; to generation <margin>We will tell</margin> and generation we will tell of Your praise.

# For the conductor; on "Lilies." A testimony of Asaph. A Psalm.

Give ear, O Shepherd of Israel, You who lead Joseph like a flock; You who are enthroned upon the cherubim, shine forth. Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up Your might, and come to our salvation. O God, restore us; cause Your face to shine, and we shall be saved. O Lord God of Hosts, how long will You be angry against the prayer of Your people? You have fed them the bread of tears, and given them tears to drink in great measure. You make us an object of strife to our neighbors, and our enemies mock us. O God of Hosts, restore us; cause Your face to shine, and we shall be saved. You uprooted a vine from Egypt; You drove out nations and planted it. You cleared the way before it; it struck deep roots and filled the land. <margin>Beast</margin> The mountains were covered by its shadow, and its branches were like the mighty cedars. <margin>Its branches</margin> It sent out its boughs to the sea and its shoots to the River <note>The "River" usually refers to the Euphrates, marking the ideal boundaries of Israel.</note>. Why have You broken down its fences, so that all who pass by the way pluck its fruit? The boar from the forest ravages it, and the creatures of the field feed on it.

<column-break/>

Do not remember against us the former iniquities; quickly may Your mercies meet us, for we have become very poor. Assist us, O God of our redemption, because of the glory of Your name; and deliver us and atone for our debts for the sake of Your name. Why should the nations say, "Where is their God?" Let it be revealed among the nations before our eyes—the revenge for the blood of Your servants that was poured out like a slaughter. And let the prayer of the captives enter into the Presence of Your Shekhinah <note>original: "Shekhintā" — the Divine Presence</note> before You; according to the greatness of Your power, release the children who are delivered over to death. And return to our neighbors sevenfold into their bosom the retribution for the insults with which they insulted You, O Master. And we, Your people and the sheep of Your flock, will give thanks before You forever; from generation to generation we will recount Your praise. To give praise for the members of the Sanhedrin <note>The Targum interprets "Lilies" (Shoshannim) as a reference to the scholars of the high court who are "beautiful as lilies."</note> who occupy themselves with the testimony of the Torah; by the hand of Asaph, a song of praise. O Provider of Israel, listen, You who lead like a flock the Ark of Joseph; You whose Presence dwells between the cherubim, shine forth! Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, stir up Your might and go and walk before us for our redemption. O God, bring us back from our exile; let the light of Your countenance shine and we shall be saved. O Lord God of Hosts, how long have You not accepted the prayer of Your people? You have fed them the bread of tears in the pouring out of weeping, and You have given them tears to drink in three-fold measure. You have set us for contention among our neighbors, and our enemies mock us. O God of Hosts, bring us back from our exile; let the light of Your countenance shine and we shall be saved. The people of Israel are compared to a vine that You brought out of Egypt; You drove the nations out of the Land of Israel and planted it. You cleared the way before it, and it took root and filled the land. The mountains were hidden by its shadow, and its branches were like the mighty cedars. It sent out its harvest to the sea and its shoots to the River Euphrates. Why have You breached its fences, so that all who pass the way pluck from it? The boar from the forest ravages it, and the wild beast of the field grazes on it. <meta>catchword: God</meta>

---

And when the land was settled and its fruit and boughs flourished, the Sanctuary was good within it; and the fellow-scholars and rabbis say there are seventy rows of disciples within it until the day they come, and its shoots reach the Euphrates River. Why have You breached its fences and all who pass by the way pluck it? The boar from the forest ravages it, and the wild beast of the field grazes on it. O God...

---

**Do not remember against us the iniquities of our ancestors.** This refers to the former sins committed in the days of our youth. That is to say: "Hasten to help us and remove our yoke, lest our enemies mention our sins." At the end, he calls their sins "the iniquities of our fathers," and this is also correct. For sometimes children continue the sins, and He visits upon them the iniquities of their fathers through the Attribute of Justice <note>term: "Middat HaDin" — God's strict justice as opposed to mercy</note>. He explained "the iniquities of the fathers upon the children" as being when the deeds of the fathers are still in their hands. Therefore he said, "Do not remember against us the former iniquities." **Let Your mercies quickly meet us.** The word "quickly" is associated with "meeting" here. **Meet us.** This carries the sense of a thing being ready and prepared to be placed before the sun. Similarly: "For You meet him with the blessings of goodness." May He quickly prepare for us what is to come. **Help us... for the sake of the glory of Your name.** Consider that if we are remembered among the nations as those who are crowned, Your name will be honored. **Why should they say.** This was understood regarding the children, according to the custom of praising the blood of Your servants. **Let the groaning of the prisoner come before You.** Meaning, on account of our suffering. To bring the prisoner out of the dungeon. That is: "In exchange for the sufferings of our poverty, remember the pit of our supplication from the prisons of our exile." He mentions the merit of those "condemned to death"—those who are destined to die in life <note>A poetic way of describing those whose lives in exile are a living death.</note>. Some specify these as those who are trapped in exile, whom we call "captives" or "those combed/scraped" in exile. **And return to our neighbors... the reproach with which they reproached You.** They spoke against Your portion. **And we, Your people.** Whether in exile or in our land, we will praise You for generation and generation.

-> ## To the Conductor <-

**On lilies (Shoshannim), a testimony of Asaph, a psalm.** Some specify this refers to the Second Temple, and some specify it as a testimony of the community of Israel. For the essence of these psalms serves as a witness to our House <note>The Temple</note> that it will be roused from the sea of our destruction. This psalm was said concerning the entire exile. **Shepherd of Israel, give ear.** Since the kingdom was sold and Joseph and the others were separated from us. For the Glory happened in this place. He says "Joseph" and calls him "his help," meaning Israel as a whole is called by the name "Joseph," just as they are called by the name "Israel." After this, Joseph is a provider and leader of the flock, just as Joseph was in his life, providing for all the children of Rachel. And the essence of "Israel" is sent forth. And he says all of Israel is like the son of Joseph, for sometimes this whole name is applied to all of Judah. He invites the "Shepherd of Joseph" and hints at it. Joseph is the seal of the companions to the prayer of the King in exile. Like the opening of the day, "You who dwell between the Cherubim, give ear," meaning to hold fast and draw near to the Glory before it shined forth. **Before Ephraim... and come to our salvation.** Therefore, hasten to our rescue. **O God, restore us.** That is: "Prepare for our children to go and return before You." For in a time of trouble, He hides His face, and in a time of mercy, He returns His face and meets us for good. **The Lord God.** He lacks for nothing; "God" refers to the power of trust. And so, "God of Hosts" refers to the God of the armies, as in "He will do." **You have fed them the bread of tears.** Just as it says "My tears have been my bread day and night." Meaning, from the mouth of their food... and You give them to drink... day and night, so the tears are their constant portion. **In great measure (Shalish).** Some explain this as "three-fold" <note>Hebrew: "Shalish" can mean a third-part measure or triple.</note>. Others explain it as the rivers of Babylon... some say they are the best quality of choice drinks. It is possible to explain that until this exile, they were... and gave tears... between us and them... and gave between the horse... the wicked one returned with him. And he said this verse three times in the manner of a refrain to focus the heart on the intensity of the supplication. **You make us an object of strife.** For your presence is always with us, like a "man of strife and a man of contention to the whole land." **They mock us.** For themselves. Meaning, they mock You and rejoice over our destruction. **O God of Hosts.** He said this verse three times because the one praying doubles his words in the manner of a supplication. **You uprooted a vine from Egypt.** Israel is compared to a vine. And so it says, "For the vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are His pleasant plant." **You uprooted, You drove out.** The future tense is used in place of the past, as in many places. The "uprooting" refers to the vine, as in "He leads His people like sheep." **You cleared the way before it.** So that no man could stand before you. **And it took root.** From the root... to uproot... "And He will uproot you from the land of the living." **The mountains were covered by its shadow.** Like a canopy. **And its branches were like the mighty cedars (Arzei El).** Like the cedars that are very high. Therefore he called them "Cedars of God" (Arzei El). For everything that is great in its size is called "of God," such as "a city great unto God." It was so great until its harvest reached the sea. The "harvest" (Katzir) refers to the hard branches, and the "shoots" (Yonekot) are the tender branches. He says "to the sea," meaning the Mediterranean. **And to the River.** This refers to the broad reach of Israel, as it is written "from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines and from the wilderness to the River [Euphrates]." And so it is written "to the River Euphrates... shall be your border." **Why have You broken down.** Its fences are breached... and all who pass the way pluck it, as it is written "and I will remove its hedge and it shall be eaten." **The boar from the forest ravages it.** The Targum says "it is cut down." In the word *miya’ar* (from the forest), the letter 'Ayin' is suspended <note>In many Torah scrolls and manuscripts, the letter Ayin in the word "mi-ya'ar" (from the forest) in Psalm 80:14 is written smaller and higher than the other letters. The commentary discusses the symbolic meaning of this.</note>. This refers to this: when Israel is worthy, it is like "from the river" (*mi-ye'or*)—meaning nothing can harm them—but when they sin, the boar "from the forest" (*mi-ya'ar*) rules over them. These people mock the name [of God]... and these from the forest... **And the creatures of the field (Ziz Shaday).** This refers to the birds... "and the Ziz of the field is with me." He says it is from the hand of fate. He returns and says that all the nations of the world... the boar of Israel... and the boar from the forest refers to the wicked Roman Empire (Edom). Just as the boar shows its cloven hooves to say "I am pure," so did the wicked Edom/Rome act, showing their "hooves" and pretending to be righteous while being thieves and violent. O God... let us return from the deeds... and he said "O God" to return... at their end... **The boar from the forest ravages it.** And if "from the forest" is said about a man... because the face... **And the creatures of the field (Ziz Shaday).** These are the people of Israel... for the Ziz is a giant bird, and when it spreads its wings it covers the orb of the sun. As it is written "As an eagle stirs up its nest... spreads its wings." And why is it called Ziz? Because it has many different tastes (Ziz) in it. God...

**God of hosts:** Our rabbis of blessed memory explained this as the Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note>. Return now and see, and remember with Your favor, and take note of this vine. **And the root which Your right hand planted, etc. and for the King Messiah whom You strengthened for oneself:** That is to say, at that time when You said to Moses, "Go, say to them: I have surely remembered <note>original: "pakod pakadeti"</note> you," may He see and remember us. **And upon the son of man You strengthened for Yourself:** Meaning, at that hour You said, "Behold, I send an angel before you, etc." and as it says, "and he shall be to you as a mouth and you shall be to him as a god <note>referring to Moses and Aaron</note>." **Burned with fire, cut down:** Similar to the matter of "when He has washed away... by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning" (Isaiah 4). And the Midrash says: Israel said to the Holy One, Blessed be He, "Yesterday You said, 'Let Israel set up a Tabernacle for Me and let their flags be around it,' and now it is burned with fire and cut down." **At the rebuke of Your countenance they perish:** Because the Divine Presence departed from them, the enemies sent their hands into the Sanctuary. The Midrash interprets the verse as referring to the arrogant Romans who would destroy the Holy Temple. **Let Your hand be upon the man of Your right hand:** Meaning the name that was delayed <unclear>rendered inactive</unclear>; they will say to Him: do not forget the Egyptians whom You went out against. So let Your hand be upon me. **Then we will not turn back from You:** Meaning, when we pass through with Your help, we will not retreat. **Revive us and we will call upon Your name:** That You should revive us and redeem us from the exile. All this is the language of prayer. **O Lord God of hosts, restore us, etc.**

# For the Conductor
This psalm was said concerning the exile of Babylon and the kingdoms of Media and Greece, and all the exiles they passed through, and it serves for the salvation of the fourth exile <note>Commonly identified in medieval thought as the Roman/current exile</note>. It is said "on the Gittith" and in the name of Asaph, as understood in Psalm 8. In the Midrash of Psalms, it is explained that "on the Gittith" refers to those who are destined to be redeemed and will sing a perfect song like the one at the Exodus from Egypt; these were spoken by the sons of Korah who sang about their prophecies in their exile. In this psalm, the liturgical poets <note>original: "payyetanim"</note> differ as to when it was said: some say at the time Israel went up from Egypt they sang this song; some say it was said regarding the Babylonian exile; and some say it was said regarding the fourth exile which shall come speedily in our days. Asaph spoke this psalm through the Holy Spirit regarding this exile of ours, which will be followed by the fourth exile.

**Sing for joy to God our strength:** Meaning, a day will come when we sing to the Holy One, Blessed be He, for His salvation, for He saved us from the hand of our enemies—those of the fourth exile who will soon be redeemed. **Shout for joy to the God of Jacob:** Rabbi David Kimchi <note>Radak</note> explained that because all the seed of Jacob was in the Babylonian exile and other exiles, they sang to Him. **Raise a song:** He explained this psalm in his house, etc. **And beat the timbrel, the sweet lyre with the harp:** Musical instruments with which they sang in the Holy Temple. **Blow the shofar at the New Moon:** He explained that this psalm was said regarding Rosh Hashanah <note>The Jewish New Year</note>. **At the full moon** <note>original: "ba-keseh"</note>: Its meaning is "the covered one," which is the day the moon is covered, being the New Moon and a festival. **For the day of our festival:** The holiday of Rosh Hashanah.

**For it is a statute for Israel:** That is, it is a day of judgment for Israel, on which the world was created and on which the Name, blessed be He, created it; it is His custom to judge His creatures on this day. **An ordinance of the God of Jacob:** Meaning a judgment for the God of Jacob, who judges them on this day. **He appointed it as a testimony in Joseph:** This testimony that the Holy One, Blessed be He, gave regarding Joseph, who was appointed as a prince and ruler over the land of Egypt; it was on the day of Rosh Hashanah that Joseph went out of the prison house. **When he went out over the land of Egypt:** When Joseph left the prison and became ruler over Egypt. **I heard a language I did not know:** He heard the language of Egypt which he did not know until the angel Gabriel taught him seventy languages. As it is written, "The house of Jacob from a people of strange tongue." Our sages of blessed memory said the angel taught him the Arabic language and condensed it <unclear>mastered it</unclear>, and they understood it, and the kings and princes said to him, "Teach us." The scripture says: **I heard a language I did not know:** Meaning he did not know the Egyptian tongue until that day.

**I removed his shoulder from the burden:** I removed from him the yoke of Egyptian servitude. **His hands were freed from the basket:** The "dud" is the mortar tub in which they made bricks; the children of Israel worked in Egypt with such tubs. **In distress you called and I rescued you:** A hint to the distress in Egypt when they cried out to the Lord and He answered them. **I answered you in the secret place of thunder:** A hint to Sinai where the sound of thunder and the sound of the shofar were heard. **I tested you at the waters of Meribah:** As in the matter of "there He made for them a statute and an ordinance, and there He tested them." **Hear, O My people, and I will warn you; O Israel, if you would but listen to Me:** Listen to My voice and I will testify to you and warn you. **There shall be no strange god among you:** One should not worship idols. **Nor shall you worship any foreign god:** This refers to idolatry. **I am the Lord your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt:** He reminds them that He is the one who brought them up from Egypt, and therefore it is proper for them to listen to His voice. **Open your mouth wide:** He explained the psalm in this way, etc. **And I will fill it:** All your needs; whatever you ask of Me, I will give to you.

### 82

**A Psalm** of Asaph. God stands in the assembly of the Almighty; in the midst of the judges <note>original: "elohim", which can refer to God or human magistrates</note> He judges. ### 83

**Of Asaph.** O God, do not keep silence; do not be deaf and do not be still, O God. For behold, Your enemies are in an uproar, and those who hate You have lifted up their heads. They take crafty counsel against Your people and consult together against Your hidden ones. They said, "Come, let us cut them off from being a nation, so that the name of Israel shall be remembered no more." For they have consulted together with one heart; they have made a covenant against You: The tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites; Moab and the Hagrites; Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek; Philistia with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assyria also has joined them; they have been an arm of support for the children of Lot. Selah. Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the brook of Kishon.

<column-break/>

"I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt; open your mouth with the words of the Torah, and I will fill it with all goodness." But My people did not accept My voice, and Israel did not want My Word. So I cast them away in the stubbornness of their hearts; they went and wandered in the counsel of the wicked. If only My people had listened to Me, if Israel had walked in My ways! In a little while I would have humbled their enemies, and against their oppressors I would have returned My stroke. The enemies of the Lord would lie to Him, and their strength would be [lost] forever. And He would have fed him from the best of the wheat bread, and from the rock I would have satisfied you with honey.

A praise by Asaph. God, His Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> dwells in the assembly of the righteous who are strong in the Torah; in the midst of the judges of truth, He judges. How long will you wicked ones judge falsely and show favor to the wicked forever? Judge the poor and the orphan; justify the afflicted and the destitute. Rescue the poor and the needy; deliver them from the hands of the wicked. They have not become wise, nor have they looked into the Torah; they walk in darkness; the foundations of the world are shaken because their feet stumble. I thought, "You are counted like angels, and all of you are like the angels of the heights." But in truth, you shall die like men, and like one of the princes you shall fall. Arise, O Lord, judge the judgment of the earth, for You shall take possession of all the nations.

A song and praise by Asaph. O God, do not be silent; do not be deaf and do not be still, O God. For behold, Your enemies are in a stir, and those who hate You have raised their heads. They have plotted a secret against Your people and take counsel against those hidden in Your treasury. They said, "Come, and let us destroy them from being a people, and the name of Israel shall no longer be remembered." For they have consulted with a pure heart against You; they have made a covenant and gathered: the tents of the Edomites and the Arabians, the Moabites and the Hagrites; Gebal and the Ammonites and the Amalekites, the Philistines with the inhabitants of Tyre. Also, the Assyrians have joined them; they have become a help to the children of Lot forever. Do to them as [You did to]

<column-break/>

My pious ones, I am your God. Recognize your evil ways and remember the good I have done for you since I cut your path out of Egypt. **But my people did not listen to my voice.** This refers to the time in the wilderness, in the days of the Judges, and also in the days of the Kings after David and Solomon until they went into exile. Then the scripture returns to say to them: **If only my people would listen to me.** This was when evil began to come upon them through Sennacherib and the kings of Egypt, and suddenly the oppressor thought to <unclear>beseech</unclear> them. **And they followed their own counsels.** As it is written, lest they go into evil and therefore be destroyed. **Suddenly their enemies.** In an instant, I would have been wise for them and suddenly I would humble them. **And against their foes I would turn my hand.** Against those who strike them, I would return my hand to strike them back. The "Kaph" <note>the Hebrew letter 'K' used as a prefix</note> here denotes compassion... <unclear>text corrupted</unclear>. This hints that if they had been worthy, Sennacherib would not have brought about the exile, and the time of their blessing would have been forever. As it is written: "Behold, today the Lord shall give life to his mouth." **And they would eat.** And since they would eat the "fat of the wheat" <note>referring to the highest quality grain</note>... **And from the rock honey I would satisfy you.** As it is written: "Behold, I satisfy you with honey." This refers to milk, butter, and the summer produce from the rock and the Temple. It is written "honey and the produce of the field." These are types of grains over which we bless, to see the "fat" or "cream" which is the most excellent of all.

# Psalm [82]
**Of Asaph. God stands in the assembly of the Almighty; in the midst of the judges He judges.** This psalm was said concerning the judges, that they should be judges of truth. This occurred in the days of Jehoshaphat <note>King of Judah, 9th century BCE</note>, for we see that he appointed judges in all the fortified cities of Judah and warned them greatly. He said to them: "Consider what you are doing, for you do not judge for man but for the Lord" (2 Chronicles 19:6). He said: "Now let the fear of the Lord be upon you... for there is no injustice with the Lord our God, nor partiality, nor taking of bribes." There were judges before this, but in the time of Jehoshaphat, they returned to warn them with the words of this psalm. It says **God stands in the assembly of the Almighty**, meaning His Glory stands before them more than in other places to stir their hearts toward justice. **In the midst of the judges.** In the midst of the magistrates. They began to judge for bribes... **How long.** How long will you favor the wicked? **Selah.**... **Judge the poor.** Take up their cause and justify them in their needs. **Justify.** According to the law... **Rescue the poor.** Take the judgment out of the hands [of the oppressors]... **The foundations of the earth are shaken.** Because the judges are the measure of the world... **In darkness they walk.** For judges who do not act for God move the throne of heaven into darkness... the Holy One, Blessed be He, allowed them to be struck in the world... you are **sons of the Most High**... **But like men you shall die.** Therefore, I desired your deeds, that you should return a gift for your actions... and you shall fall like the **princes.** These princes are the leaders of men in their exile... **Arise, O God.** Because of the greatness of the poverty and the oppressors... **For You shall inherit all the nations.** You shall settle the neighbors... this verse speaks of the judge standing in his place.

# Song
**A Psalm of Asaph.** This psalm was said regarding the war that occurred in the days of Jehoshaphat, when the children of Moab and Ammon came against him (2 Chronicles 20). There were other nations with them who were not mentioned there specifically, but here they are identified as those who joined them, similar to the war of Uzziah with the Arabians. They are called the "Meunites." Also in the Book of Judges and in Josephon, Amalek and Meun and others are mentioned as surrounding them. All those mentioned here stood with the children of Ammon, Moab, and the inhabitants of Mount Seir... **O God, do not keep silence.** Do not be still. **For behold Your enemies.** For many nations have gathered against us... **Against Your people.** They take counsel and a secret, nation with nation, in craftiness against You. **Your hidden ones.** Israel, who are Your treasure... they say "let them no longer be a nation"... **For they have consulted.** They have set their hearts together to cut a covenant against God and Israel. **The tents of Edom.** The camps that join them... **The Ishmaelites, Moab, and the Hagrites.** These are the children of Seir... **Assyria also.** This is the beginning of our hope... Assyria joined them to destroy Israel. **For the children of Lot.** Namely, Ammon and Moab. **Do to them as to Midian.** Like the defeat of Midian... **At the brook of Kishon.** Like the war of Sisera which took place at the brook of Kishon.

**Who were destroyed at En-dor.** This refers to the defeat of Midian. Previously, it mentions the "star that rose in the book of Judges" <note>a reference to the Song of Deborah, Judges 5:20</note>. Know that this refers to the war of Sisera and the generation that lived in the portion of Manasseh near Taanach and Megiddo, where the "stars fought from their courses." **They became as dung.** Like refuse that fertilizes the ground, they became food for the earth. **Make their nobles.** Like Oreb and Zeeb <note>Midianite princes mentioned in Judges 7:25</note>, for they thought they would be the inheritors of the Land of Israel and Jerusalem. The kings and officers intended to seize the "dwellings of God" for themselves. **O my God, make them like a tumbleweed.** Like the rolling straw that is blown before the wind. **As fire consumes the forest.** Some say this refers to the parched state of the forest on a day of wrath. **Pursue them with Your tempest.** As in the war of Deborah. **Fill their faces with shame.** Meaning they should be covered in the darkness of their disgrace until they are forced to seek Your name. **Let them know that You alone are the Lord.** Just as it says, "On that day the Lord shall be one and His name one." This emphasizes that everything is under Your hand and authority.

Who were destroyed at En-dor; they became like dung for the ground. Make their nobles like Oreb and like Zeeb, and all their princes like Zebah and like Zalmunna, who said, "Let us take for ourselves the dwellings of God as a possession." O my God, make them like a tumbleweed <note>original: 'galgal', referring to the rolling thistle or dry vegetation</note>, like chaff before the wind. As fire consumes the forest, and as a flame sets the mountains ablaze, so pursue them with Your tempest and terrify them with Your storm. Fill their faces with shame, that they may seek Your name, O Lord. Let them be ashamed and terrified forever; let them be disgraced and perish. And let them know that You—Your name alone is the Lord—are the Most High over all the earth.

### 84

For the conductor, on the *Gittith* <note>a musical instrument or a melody from the city of Gath</note>; a Psalm of the sons of Korah. How lovely are Your dwelling places, O Lord of Hosts! My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh sing for joy to the living God. Even the sparrow has found a home, and the swallow a nest for herself where she may lay her young—at Your altars, O Lord of Hosts, my King and my God. Happy are those who dwell in Your house; they will ever praise You. Selah. Happy is the man whose strength is in You, whose heart is set on the highways. Those passing through the Valley of *Baca* <note>often translated as "weeping" or "balsam trees"</note> make it a spring; the early rain also covers it with blessings. They go from strength to strength; each one appears before God in Zion.

<column-break/>

They were destroyed at En-dor; they became like dung spread upon the earth. Make them and their leaders like Oreb and like Zeeb, and like Zebah and like Zalmunna, all their kings, who said, "Let us seize for ourselves the land of God." My God, make them like a rolling wheel that wanders and does not rest on a slope, and like chaff before the gale. Like a fire that burns in the woods, and like a flame that singes the edges of the mountains, so shall You pursue them in Your whirlwind, and in Your gale You shall terrify them. Fill their faces with disgrace, and they shall seek Your name, O Lord. They shall be ashamed and shaken for all eternity; they shall be humiliated and perish. And they shall know that You—Your name is the Lord—You alone are the Most High over all the inhabitants of the earth.

### 84

For praise, upon the harp that came from Gath, by the hands of the sons of Korah, a song. How beloved are the dwellings of Your mercy, O Lord of Hosts! My soul yearns and even pined for the courts of the Lord; my heart and my flesh sing to the living God. Even the bird has found a house, and the swallow <note>Aramaic: 'shoshpala'</note> a nest for herself, where she has placed her fledglings to be prepared upon Your altar, O Lord of Hosts, my King and my God. Happy are the righteous who dwell in Your Sanctuary; they shall praise You again forever. Happy is the man whose strength is in Your Word <note>term: 'Memra', the personified Word of God in Aramaic theology</note> and in whose heart is faith. The foolish who pass over the depth of Gehenna <note>hell</note> in weeping, He shall make it like a fountain; even blessings shall cover those who teach the Law <note>Torah</note>. The righteous go from the Sanctuary to the House of Study; their Torah shall be seen before the Lord, whose Presence <note>term: 'Shekhinah'</note> dwells in Zion.

# For the Conductor

<margin>
**On the Gittith, for the sons of Korah.** This psalm was composed concerning the generation of Korah's atonement, the Babylonian exile, and the prayers of the Levites who used to sing in the Temple.
</margin>

For there was the standing place of Israel in the Holy Temple during prayer, and not just in the inner hall. **My heart and my flesh.** Because a person’s whole body and all their inward parts praise and sing. **Even the sparrow.** If this psalm is said regarding the exile, it means: in the time of our exile, the bird <note>the people of Israel</note> finds a home, but Your house is destroyed. Or, it is a metaphor: the birds find a nest in the ruins of the Temple, while we cannot enter there. Others explain that in the Temple, birds were not allowed to nest because of the holiness, but now that it is ruined, they do. **Happy are those who dwell in Your house.** Referring to the priests or the sages and students who were constantly there. **Highways in their hearts.** They have the paths of Your wisdom in their hearts; they walk upon these paths and add strength every day. **Passing through the Valley of Baca.** This is a metaphor for the sages who pass through the depths of wisdom and turn it into a fountain. **The early rain also covers it with blessings.** Those who teach the right path receive blessings. **They go from strength to strength.** Meaning the students go from the House of Assembly to the House of Study, increasing in wisdom until they see the God of gods in Zion. In a homiletic sense <note>original: 'derush'</note>, the "Valley of Baca" refers to Gehenna; the wicked weep there, but if they return in repentance, they make it a spring of blessings.

**They go from strength to strength.** We have already explained this previously regarding **His pious ones**. In the homiletic interpretation <term>Midrash: an interpretive act of seeking deeper meaning</term>, the reason is connected to **those who dwell in Your house** mentioned above. It means they go from the Temple to the House of Study. Jonathan <note>original: "יונתן", likely referring to the Targum of Jonathan</note> also explained it this way for Torah scholars, saying that scholars have no rest even in the world to come, as it is said, "They go from strength to strength." Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, also taught that one who goes from the synagogue to the House of Study merits seeing the Divine Presence, as it is said, "He shall appear before God in Zion." **O God in Zion.** This is explained as the beginning of the answer to my prayer, meaning "God of gods." Similarly, the phrase **my soul longs** refers to the God of Jacob, for Jacob is the "portion of the tribes of Israel" and possesses merit. **Our shield, behold, O God.** God is our strong shield because of the covenant and his merit... **Your anointed.** This refers to the King Messiah and his qualities... the Psalm refers to David returning to himself. **For a day in Your courts is better than a thousand.** That is to say, it is better because he prayed to offer the daily sacrifices... he said one day in Your courts is better, for I have learned that one day of life in the future is better... **I would rather stand at the threshold of the house of my God.** "To stand at the threshold" means sitting at the entrance. It is better to be on the outskirts of the House of God than to dwell in the assemblies of the wicked... Some explain **tents of wickedness** as referring to the belongings of the wicked... I would rather choose to sit at the threshold of the book of God to engage in the words of wisdom than to be in the palaces of the world and its concerns... **Sun and shield.** God gives light and protection... this Psalm was given by the sages to describe the world... **Grace and glory.** The Lord will give grace and glory before the nations... He will not withhold good from those who walk in integrity... **O Lord of hosts, happy is the man who trusts in You.** He will not be put to shame, for You will bring him back from exile and he will trust in Your sanctuary.

# To the Chief Musician
For the sons of Korah. Some explain this Psalm regarding the Babylonian exile. It is possible it refers to the entire exile, including the Roman exile <note>original: "גלות חריף", likely referring to the harshness of the current diaspora</note>. As it says, **Will You be angry with us forever?** Furthermore, it says that in the goodness of the exile You shall comfort us... **You have been favorable.** This refers to the kingdom... the prayer of the children of the exile... He promises them concerning the entire exile... Some explain "You have been favorable" and "You have forgiven the iniquity" as a request: just as You were favorable in the past, so may You continue now. **You have brought back the captivity of Jacob.** "Shabat" (brought back) is the verb form... Some say this refers to the land... from the concept of "rest." Similarly, "Return, O Lord, to the ten thousands of the thousands of Israel." This is the opinion of Rabbi Judah Hayyuj <note>A 10th-century grammarian</note>, explaining it as resting and being quiet from the tribulations of exile. **Captivity.** Written with a 'Yod' but read without it... **Forgiven... Covered.** I have already explained the meaning of "lifting" and "covering" in the Psalm... **You have taken away.** Like gathering and removing... **You have turned from the fierceness of Your anger.** "Haron" (fierceness) is a noun... as in "Turn from Your fierce anger." The word "Turned" is a transitive verb, meaning He turned His anger so it would not burn... **Restore us, O God of our salvation.** Because our salvation depends on You... **Cause Your anger to cease.** Remove it from us... **Forever.** Will You be angry for so long?... **Will You not revive us.** For there is none other than You to save and comfort us from the exile... **Show us, Lord, Your mercy.** If our sins prevent us from receiving grace, do not repay us according to our deeds, but show us Your kindness... **I will hear what God the Lord will speak.** The prophet says: I am listening to what God will say... He will speak **peace to His people**, to those returning from exile, and **to His saints**, the righteous among the nations who dwell with Israel... **Let them not turn back to folly.** They shall not return to the way of evil, as it is written, "Your people shall all be righteous, they shall inherit the land forever." This proves it refers to this long exile... **Surely His salvation is near.** If all Israel are God-fearing, their salvation will be near, for redemption depends on repentance... **That glory may dwell in our land.** This also proves it refers to the exile, for in the Second Temple the Divine Glory did not dwell there <note>Rabbinic tradition holds that the Second Temple lacked five things present in the First, including the Shekhinah or Divine Presence</note>. As the Rabbis said, the word "I will be glorified" is written without the letter 'He' to hint that five things were missing: the Ark, the Mercy Seat, the Cherubim, the Fire, the Shekhinah, the Holy Spirit, and the Urim and Thummim. But in the future house, the Glory will be there... **Mercy and truth.** When the Glory dwells in the Temple, mercy and truth will be in the world, for all Israel will follow one path of truth... there will be righteousness and peace... **Truth shall spring out of the earth.** When men act with truth, righteousness will look down from heaven... for blessings descend from heaven according to the deeds of men on earth... **Yes, the Lord will give what is good.** As a reward for their deeds, He will give rain... **And our land will yield its increase.** For they will no longer lack good... **Righteousness shall go before Him.** Peace shall walk before him on the way... righteousness will be before his face always... and he will set his footsteps in the way of righteousness. **Prayer.**

# For the Sons of Korah
**A psalm, a song; its foundation is in the holy mountains.** I have already explained at the beginning of this book the five reasons why the sons of Korah are mentioned. This psalm concerns the praise of Zion and the love of its dwelling place. The sons of Korah wrote it to be recited, or perhaps they composed it themselves. The meaning of "its foundation" refers to the foundations of the holy city. The text uses "mountains" in the plural because Mount Zion is more precious than the other mountains in the kingdom that surround it. As it says elsewhere: "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem." Zion is mentioned because it is the center of holiness and the glory of Jerusalem.

**The Lord loves the gates of Zion.** He loves the gates because the elders and the sages sit within the gates. This is like the verse "he who goes up to the gate." It mentions that He loves these more than all the "dwellings of Jacob," which refers to the synagogues and houses of study throughout the land. Zion is superior because it is the place of the Great Sanhedrin <note>The supreme religious and judicial council of ancient Israel</note> and the Temple.

**Glorious things.** Great virtues are spoken of you. Some explain that Jerusalem was situated in the "fifth climate" <note>In medieval geography, the 'climates' were latitudinal zones; the fifth was considered the most balanced and ideal for intellectual and spiritual development</note>, which is the most balanced of environments, producing wisdom and physical health. This is why our Sages said that ten measures of wisdom descended to the world, and Jerusalem took nine. 

**I will mention Rahab.** The commentator explains <insert>that this refers to the great nations. When God counts the nations, He will mention the great ones like Egypt and Babylon, but Zion's residents will be noted for their personal merit.</insert> In other places, a person might be praised just for being born in a famous city, but in Zion, "this man and that man"—every individual—is born into wisdom and greatness. 

**The Lord will count when writing up the nations.** When God records the history of the world, He will note the birthplaces of the wise. While other nations might produce one wise man, Zion produces many. 

**And singers and dancers.** All will sing of their joy in you. "All my springs are in you" means that all my thoughts and desires are focused on the holiness of the city. 

# A Song, a Psalm for the Sons of Korah
I have written many times that the titles of the psalms are not always literal. This psalm was written regarding the troubles of the exile. **To sing (Leannoth).** This refers to "affliction" (Inui). The psalmist asks God to remember the suffering of the people. **Heman the Ezrahite.** This Heman was a famous sage, one of the sons of Zerah, son of Judah. He is the one mentioned in the book of Kings as being incredibly wise, though Solomon was wiser still.

**O Lord, God of my salvation.** The psalmist cries out by day and night. In the darkness of the exile, which is compared to night, he remains before God. **For my soul is sated with troubles.** This is a poetic way of saying he has had more than enough of suffering. His life is so miserable it is as if he is already in the grave (Sheol). 

**I am counted with those who go down to the pit.** In the exile, the Jewish people are like the dead who have no strength. **Among the dead I am free.** This is a bitter irony; the only "freedom" the exile feels is the freedom of the dead, who are no longer under the obligations of the living or the protection of God's active providence. 

**You have placed me in the lowest pit.** This describes the depth of the captivity. Just as a pit is dark and deep, the exile is a place of darkness and "depths" (the metaphorical drowning in national sorrow).

The commentary highlights Jerusalem's unique geographic and spiritual standing as a place where wisdom is born.</summary>

Upon me You have leaned Your wrath, and with all Your waves in the flood You have afflicted me, Selah. You have shut me up from my speech, and those outside have distanced me; I am in a prison house and cannot go out. My eyes grieve with tears from affliction; I have called to You, O Lord, every day; I have spread my hands toward Your hands. Is it possible that You will perform wonders for the dead? Or shall the bodies that have crumbled in the dust rise and praise You forever? Is it possible that Your goodness shall be seen in the house of the grave, or Your truth in the house of destruction? Is it possible that Your wonders shall be known in the darkness, or Your righteousness in the parched land? And I, the righteous, stand before You; may I not be crushed, and in the morning may my prayer reach You. Why have You abandoned my soul? You hide Your face from me, and this is my plight in my chosen youth. I am afflicted and weary from my youth, I have carried the burden of Your terror. Your anger has passed over me; Your terrors have changed me, they have struck me down. They have surrounded me like water all day; they have encompassed me together. You have distanced from me friend and companion, and I know only darkness because of them. An elder captive <note>original: *shibya saba*</note> that was said by the hand of Abraham, whom You desired. I will praise the kindness of the Lord forever; to every generation I will make known Your truth with my mouth. For I said, the world shall be built in kindness; in the heavens You shall establish Your truth. I have made a covenant for Abraham My chosen; a covenant for David My servant. I will establish your children forever, and I will build the throne of your kingdom for all generations, Selah. And the heavens shall praise Your wonders, O Lord, and also Your truth in the assembly of the holy ones. For who in the skies is equal to the Lord, who can inherit the angels? God is mighty in the assembly of the holy ones, great and awesome over all who surround Him. From the heights You bring strength; who is like You, the mighty Lord? And Your truth surrounds You.

<margin>28</margin>
Your wrath lies heavily upon me, and You have afflicted me with all Your waves. Selah. You have put my acquaintances far from me; You have made me an abomination to them; I am shut up and cannot come out. My eye wastes away because of affliction; I have called upon You, O Lord, every day; I have spread out my hands to You. Will You perform wonders for the dead? Shall the departed rise and praise You? Selah. Shall Your lovingkindness be declared in the grave? Or Your faithfulness in destruction? Shall Your wonders be known in the dark? And Your righteousness in the land of forgetfulness? But as for me, unto You, O Lord, have I cried; and in the morning shall my prayer come before You. Lord, why do You cast off my soul? Why do You hide Your face from me? I am afflicted and ready to die from my youth up; while I suffer Your terrors I am distracted. Your fierce wrath goes over me; Your terrors have cut me off. They came round about me like water all day long; they compassed me about together. Lover and friend have You put far from me, and my acquaintances into darkness.

->**Psalm 89**<-

A <term>Maskil</term> <note>A musical or contemplative poem</note> of Ethan the Ezrahite. I will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever; with my mouth will I make known Your faithfulness to all generations. For I have said: "Mercy shall be built up forever; in the very heavens You will establish Your faithfulness." I have made a covenant with My chosen, I have sworn unto David My servant: "Your seed will I establish forever, and build up your throne to all generations." Selah. And the heavens shall praise Your wonders, O Lord; Your faithfulness also in the congregation of the saints. For who in the heaven can be compared unto the Lord? Who among the sons of the mighty can be likened unto the Lord? God is greatly to be feared in the assembly of the saints, and to be had in reverence of all them that are about Him. O Lord God of hosts, who is a strong Lord like unto You? Or to Your faithfulness round about You?

---

**Your wrath lies heavily (Samcha) upon me.** *Samcha* implies closeness and surrounding, as in "the King of Babylon leaned (Samach) against Jerusalem." Our Sages of blessed memory <note>original: *R.Z.L.*</note> were quite uncertain about this expression, connecting it to "poured out" or "molten." This is a very deep sickness of the soul. **And with all Your waves (Mishbarecha) You have afflicted [me].** The commentators and grammarians are also entangled here, comparing it to the storming of the sea. Like the verse "all Your waves (Mishbarecha) and Your billows passed over me." According to the secret of the "shattered ones" <note>original: *poskei chomer*</note>, this refers to the weight of the exile. **You have distanced my acquaintances.** Some explain "my acquaintances" as referring to the seals of the heart or those who are close. Every member of the exile feels the weight of his own wounds; because of the greatness of the exile's burden, they cannot even find comfort in one another. Every person says that his brothers, friends, and acquaintances are distant from him, and he has become an abomination to them. **Why, O Lord, do You abandon my soul?** He pleads for mercy and the removal of the hiding of the Face.

## Maskil
Therefore, all our hope stands upon the word of the King, which was made known to David by this hand. **I will sing of the kindnesses (Chasdei) of the Lord forever.** Kindness <note>original: *Chesed*</note> is what comes before the promise, and Faithfulness <note>original: *Emunah*</note> is what follows the promise. He promises to give praises for His kindness in choosing [David], making it known for all generations. **For I said.** I am certain that the world will be built on kindness. Just as the heavens are established with Your faithfulness, so You will establish Your faithfulness with David and his descendants, never to be cut off as long as the days of heaven are above the earth. **I have made a covenant with My chosen.** To give him an inheritance, and his throne shall be like the stars forever. **I have sworn.** For His word is His foundation. **Forever... and I will build for all generations.** As it was said to him, "I will build you a house," a house that will stand forever. **And the heavens shall praise.** Just as the heavens testify to Your wonders and faithfulness, as it is said "the heavens declare the glory of God," so the movement of the celestial spheres never ceases to testify that Your word is true. **Also Your faithfulness.** The faithfulness You promised is known in the assembly of the holy ones, which are the angels. For in their existence, the existence of the spheres is maintained. Faithfulness is the foundation; they exist forever because they are without physical bodies. **For who in the skies.** They descend and say, who in the skies can compare to You? They acknowledge that among all the powers of the heavens, there is none with Your value or likeness. They themselves admit that their power comes from You. The "sons of the mighty" <note>original: *Bnei Elim*</note> are the angels, and they are called "sons" because their movement and judgment come from the First Cause. **God is awesome (Na'aratz).** This means He is powerful and feared, hidden within the council of the holy angels. This council is a company, like "the council of the upright." He is great and awesome, meaning His greatness is infinite and His fear is upon all who surround Him—meaning the angels who serve Him. **Lord God of hosts.** He is the Lord who rules over the heavenly hosts. **Mighty (Chasin) Lord.** *Chasin* means strong and certain. **And Your faithfulness surrounds You.** Just as it says "Your faithfulness is in the assembly of the holy ones," for the holy angels surround Him and stand upon His foundations—that is, upon Your existence. **Who is like You?** Among the upper beings who maintain and hold power, who is like You? For they testify that their own existence comes from You forever.
