### Book Four

->A Prayer of Moses, the Man of God<-

<margin>81 to 74</margin> Lord, You have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were born, or You had formed the earth and the world, even from everlasting to everlasting, You are God. You turn man back to dust, and say, "Return, O children of men." For a thousand years in Your sight are like yesterday when it passes, and like a watch in the night. You sweep them away; they are like sleep; in the morning they are like grass that grows up. In the morning it flourishes and grows; in the evening it is cut down and withers. For we are consumed by Your anger, and by Your wrath we are terrified. You have set our iniquities before You, our secret sins <margin>behold</margin> in the light of Your countenance. For all our days pass away in Your wrath; we finish our years like a sigh. The days of our years are seventy years; and if by reason of strength they be eighty years, yet their pride is but labor and sorrow; for it is soon cut off, and we fly away. Who knows the power of Your anger? Even according to Your fear, so is Your wrath.

<column-break/>

Who is the man who is made of flesh, this or that, and sees the Angel of Death who overpowers him because of his sins, and will not see the house of his burial forever? Where are Your former goodnesses, which Your Word <note>original: "Memra" — a technical term in the Targum for the Divine manifestation</note> desired for David in Your faithfulness? Remember, O Lord, the scorn of Your servant; I have carried in my lap all the blasphemies of many nations. Which Your enemies have scorned, O Lord; which they have scorned the end of the delay of Your Messiah's footsteps. Blessed be the name of the Lord in this world, Amen and Amen; blessed be the name of the Lord in the world to come, Amen and Amen.

A prayer that Moses, the Prophet of the Lord, prayed when the people of the House of Israel sinned in the wilderness; he answered and said: O Lord, the dwelling of Your Divine Presence <note>original: "Shekhinah"</note> is in the heavens; You have been our support in every generation. Before the mountains were revealed or prepared to be brought forth, You established repentance; before the earth was made and the world was built, and from this world to the world to come, You are God. You shall bring man back for his sins until death, and You said, "Return, children of men." For a thousand years in Your sight are accounted as a day that has passed, and like a watch of the night. You shall cast them out from the world to come as if they were asleep; in the morning they are like grass that passes away. In the evening at the time of the shadows, it withers and dries up.

The pious are consumed by Your anger, and we are terrified by the destruction. You have set our sins before You, our hidden iniquities before the light of Your glory. For all our days turn away in Your anger; we finish the days of our lives like the breath of the mouth in winter. The days of our years in this world are seventy years, and if by strength eighty years, and the majority of them are toil and falsehood, for they pass in haste and we fly away. Who is the one who knows the strength of Your anger? According to the fear of You, Your wrath is created.

---

Remember the kindness. It speaks of the kindness that was promised to David during the exile. He says that he is afraid of death and will not see the salvation. If he does not live to see it, it will be as if the kingdom has ceased. God lives in every generation, and why should David be prevented from seeing the days of salvation? This refers to the voice of the King Messiah. He says, "Remember the kindness," for life is like a shadow, a brief end to the life of man. He mentions the fear of death for all children of men. He finds comfort in the life of the world to come. "Who is the man who lives and shall not see death?" This means no one can rescue his soul from the hand of the grave.

Strengthen Your former kindnesses. These are what You swore to David in Your faithfulness, and there are many who find comfort in this during the long exile. "Remember, Lord, the reproach of Your servants." The enemies reproach us and say, "Will there ever be salvation for us?" "I bear in my bosom the reproach of many nations." I hear and endure the insults of many nations who mock me. This is said by every individual in the exile. "Footsteps of Your Messiah." These are the delays of the Messiah who tarries so long that they say he will never come. Just as "heel" <note>original: "akev"</note> is the end of the body, so this is the end of time. "Blessed be the Lord forever." These are the words of the singer, concluding the third book. Just as the first two books ended with "Amen and Amen," so here.

->Prayer<- to Moses. This begins the fourth book. This prayer is very ancient. Our Sages of blessed memory <note>original: "Raza" or "Hazal"</note> said that Moses composed eleven psalms which are included here. "Lord, You have been our dwelling place." David mentioned this because he relied on the mercy of the ancient ones. "Dwelling" <term>Ma'on: a place of refuge or a habitation</term>. He says that for the righteous of Israel in every generation, God is their refuge. "Before the mountains were born." He mentions the mountains and the earth to emphasize that man stands but a short time in the world compared to the ancient foundations. The mountains are the highest parts of the earth. "You turn man back to dust." This refers to the return to the earth, but the Sages also interpret it as "Return in repentance." Even if a man lived a thousand years like Adam, it would be but a day in Your eyes. Therefore, do not be surprised if You prolong the days, for they are all like yesterday. "You sweep them away." The singer compares the life of man to a flood of water that passes quickly, or to a dream during sleep. "In the morning it flourishes." Like grass that is wet with dew in the morning but by evening, under the heat of the sun, it is cut down and dried up. "We are consumed by Your anger." Now he speaks in the tongue of the exile. Even the little bit of life we have is consumed by the anger of the exile. "You have set our iniquities." He places our sins before Him to punish us. "Our secret sins" <note>original: "alumenu"</note>. Some explain this as the sins of our youth which are hidden from us but revealed before God. "The days of our years are seventy." This refers to the average lifespan in the exile. Even if one reaches eighty, the extra years are filled with "labor and sorrow." "Who knows the power of Your anger." Who can properly fear the extent of Your wrath?

<note>The following text transitions to a single column layout with commentary in Rabbinic (Rashi) script.</note>

**To number our days:** Regarding the count of our days, how many they are; in simple terms, make known to us so that we may apply a heart of wisdom. That is, we shall bring wisdom into our hearts and look further into wisdom as we recognize our own smallness. And so it is said: "Make me know, O Lord, my end" (Psalm 39:4). It is also possible to interpret this as referring to the end of the exile, which is hidden. Is it not revealed when it will be? For the Sages refrained from calculating the end. And even the angel said to him <note>Daniel</note> to seal the words that were hidden from him. He says: "Make us know when the end will be," and from then on our hearts will be set. And let there be wisdom to say, just as the angel said to Daniel. Know that quickly the rebuke will be heard, for there will be a heart of wisdom for us. As it is written: "For the vision is yet for an appointed time" (Habakkuk 2:3). **Return, O Lord, how long:** Turn back from Your anger; how long will You delay? And likewise **have compassion:** Have regret over them... **Satisfy us in the morning with Your mercy:** The time of salvation is called "morning," even before its time. **In all our days:** For even if he lives a long time, our lives are filled with Your mercies. Just as we waited in the years You afflicted us, like the days of suffering... as we saw evil, so may You gladden us. **Let Your work appear:** The work of salvation. **Upon their children:** Their fathers see the exile and their children see the salvation. In every generation, they hand down the traditions of the coming salvation... **And let the beauty of the Lord our God:** This verse is not said except concerning the days of salvation. When the days of salvation come, the work of our hands will be established. As it is written: "They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth for trouble" (Isaiah 65:23).

---

# **HE WHO DWELLS**

**In the secret place of the Most High:** Let us mention here the ethical words of the Sages, of blessed memory, in the book *Menorat HaMaor* <note>original: "The Candelabra of Light" — a 14th-century work of Jewish ethics by Isaac Aboab</note>. It is written in the words of our Rabbis that these psalms were said by Moses, corresponding to the eleven tribes. **A Prayer of Moses** corresponds to the tribe of Reuben... **He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High** corresponds to the tribe of Levi, who dwelt in the service and guarded the sanctuary. **It is a good thing to give thanks to the Lord** (Psalm 92) corresponds to the tribe of Judah, the tribe that first gave thanks to God. **The Lord reigns** (Psalm 93) corresponds to Benjamin... **O Lord God, to whom vengeance belongs** (Psalm 94) corresponds to Gad... **O come, let us sing** (Psalm 95) corresponds to Issachar... **He who dwells in the secret place:** Some say this refers to Moses, for when he went up to the thick cloud he said these verses... **For He will deliver you from the snare of the fowler:** Do not fear, for He will save us from sufferings... **With His pinions He shall cover you:** Wings of the hawk <note>or "fledge"</note> so that they do not touch you. **Shield and buckler:** These are types of defensive armor... **You shall not be afraid:** The changes of time and its mishaps, which come by chance, whether by day or by night. And he says **of the terror by night** because the destruction of the night is feared... **A thousand may fall at your side:** In war, men will fall... and you shall pass through them in peace and no evil shall touch you. Or it refers to a plague, that people fall during the time of pestilence... but it shall not come near you. **Only with your eyes:** You shall see the death of the wicked who did not dwell in the secret of the Most High like you, while you are in peace. **Because You, O Lord, are my refuge:** The logic of the psalm is to say: all this success will be yours because You have made the Lord your dwelling. **No evil shall befall you:** No plague shall harm you, neither you nor your children. **For He shall give His angels charge over you:** For your sake. Just as it says in the Torah: "Behold, I send an angel before you to keep you in the way" (Exodus 23:20). **Upon their hands they shall bear you:** A verb describing the action... as if the angels lift you up so you do not strike a stone... **Upon the lion and the cobra:** You shall tread upon them and be strong. **Because he has set his love upon Me:** God says about you: "Because he desired Me, I will deliver him," for he has known My name with great love... I will give him a refuge and a place where no damager can touch him. And "knowing the Name" refers specifically to the Tetragrammaton <note>original: "the four letters"</note>... **He shall call upon Me:** In every time of trouble I will answer him... **And I will honor him:** I will give him grace and honor in the eyes of all men. Rabbi Levi said: Throughout this world, people pray and are not answered because they do not know the explicit Name, but in the future, God will make it known, as it is written: "Therefore My people shall know My name" (Isaiah 52:6)... **With long life:** In this world, I will satisfy him with long life, and in the world to come, I will show him My salvation through the resurrection of the dead. Some say "My salvation" refers to the days of the Messiah... for this psalm is essentially a protection against damaging forces and spirits. Our Sages called it the "Psalm of Plagues." This is a great secret for those who understand.

<note>Commentary Section</note>

**They shall still bring forth fruit in old age.** In the days of the Messiah, the days of Israel shall be long, as it is written: "As the days of a tree are the days of my people" <note>Isaiah 65:22</note>. And those who were old in this world shall be like the days of youth; they shall live like young men and give birth, being vigorous and fresh—the opposite of how the elderly are now. Like a grandmother <note>The text likely means "the youth shall die at a hundred years," implying extreme longevity</note>, for a youth of a hundred years shall die. This means in their old age, even a hundred-year-old will be called "young" when he passes. 

**To declare.** Then they shall declare that the Lord is upright. For in this present time, the hearts of men are blemished in the service of God when they see the success of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous. But the King Messiah will explain the reasons... so that the suffering of the righteous is understood. In the future time, when the Messiah comes, all will see and praise and glorify, living with a joyous and good heart, and there will be no more iniquity or turning away for the righteous. Just as the verses in the Book of Psalms testify, the whole world will recognize that they must serve Him with their whole heart to reach the Most High. All will learn and seek that "there is no injustice in Him" and all His deeds are with wisdom. This is unlike the current human understanding, which asks "why is this?" and "who is this?" regarding the suffering of the righteous in this world. 

<margin>iniquity</margin>
-> **Among the many thoughts, all are joined together.** <-

**The Lord reigns.** All these psalms, like Psalm 92, are intended for the days of the Messiah. This psalm is said because currently the whole world does not recognize that He is the Most High. But in the future, as the psalm says: *The Lord reigns, He is clothed in majesty.* He is "clothed" because the whole world will recognize His supremacy, and His memory will never depart. He is King over all, and humanity will not forget Him as they do now. He is described as girded for battle to fight against the nations. The world will be "established" because there will be no more wars on the earth. This book chooses this theme because of the great wars that precede the end. *Your throne is established of old*—they will recognize that His throne has been prepared from the beginning, even before the world was created. 

**The rivers have lifted up.** This refers to the kings and rulers who gathered to fight against Jerusalem. They are compared to "rivers" because of the great noise of their many chariots. Their noise is like the "noise of many waters." But the Lord is mightier than these kings who come against Israel. 

**Your testimonies are very faithful.** Your testimonies are the words written by Your prophets regarding Your redemption; they will be fulfilled without fail. 

<margin>Your testimonies<br/>is becoming</margin>
**Holiness is becoming to Your house.** This means Your house (the Temple) will be beautiful and pleasant in holiness for length of days, and it will never be destroyed again. The future Temple will be the final one, established at the end of days. As it is written: "The mountain of the Lord's house shall be established at the top of the mountains" <note>Isaiah 2:2</note>, and all nations will flow to it to prostrate before the King, the Lord.

<margin>knowledge</margin>
**O God of vengeance.** This is a prayer to bring the vengeance closer—vengeance against the wicked who have acted with cruelty. The psalmist calls Him "God" (*El*), meaning He is powerful enough to exact the retribution that is rightfully His. The wicked speak "hard things" <note>original: "atak" — meaning ancient or arrogant words</note>; they grow great and arrogant against us. They crush "Your people"—Israel—and "Your heritage." They kill the widow and the orphan because these have no one to plead their cause before the government. They think that since these people are weak, no one will avenge them. They say, "The God of Jacob does not see," for they believe God is only the God of Israel and does not concern Himself with the deeds of all men. 

**Understand, you brutish among the people.** This is addressed to the fools among every nation. How can you say He does not hear your words or see your deeds? He who fashioned the ear and the eye—did He not do so with the intent to know everything? The Lord knows the thoughts of man, that they are vanity. He knows their plans are but a breath; they think they can do as they wish, but their thoughts will not stand unless He wills it.

### **Commentary**

**Happy is the man.** The wicked desire that we lose the grace and kindness God has given us <note>An interpretation of the "discipline" mentioned in verse 12 as a protective measure</note>. You have thought about how many years we have spent in exile, in shame and in evil. But we fight for our foundations. Your discipline, O Lord, is for our good. **And from Your Torah You teach him.** We learn from the Torah that God disciplines those He loves, just as a father disciplines his son <note>referencing Deuteronomy 8:5</note>. This is meant to benefit you in the end.

**To give him rest from days of evil.** This means to provide safety while the wicked are facing their end. The righteous person remains calm while the pit is being dug for the wicked. It is like a traveler waiting for the heat to pass.

**For the Lord will not abandon His people.** He will not leave us in exile forever. **For judgment shall return to righteousness.** A time will come when justice and righteousness, which have been separated by the wicked, will be joined together again. **And after it all the upright in heart.** They will merit this restoration. Some explain this as: once justice descends upon the earth, all the people of the world will follow it.

**Who will rise up for me.** Who will stand for me against the "workers of iniquity"? **Unless the Lord had been my help.** If not for God, my soul would have been lost. **Dwelt in silence.** "Silence" <note>original: "dumah"</note> refers to the grave, the place of stillness.

**In the multitude of my thoughts.** These are the troubling thoughts I have about the length of the exile. **Your comforts delight my soul.** The promises found in the words of the prophets provide joy and hope, for I know they will come true.

**Shall the throne of destruction be allied with You.** Can a corrupt human throne that "frames mischief by statute" compare to God's throne? Human kings create unjust laws to seize property or life, but God’s throne is established in truth. **They band together.** The kings of the earth gather to kill the righteous. Some relate "band" <note>original: "yagodu"</note> to "troops" <note>original: "gedud"</note>.

# **O Come (Psalm 95)**

->O come, let us sing to the Lord; let us shout for joy to the Rock of our salvation.<-

Israel will say this to one another in the days of the Messiah. The word "Come" <note>original: "lechu"</note> is an expression of encouragement and urgency, not just physical movement. **Let us come before His presence.** Let us be early to thank Him for the good He has done for us. **For the Lord is a great God.** In the future, this will be clear to everyone, unlike now when some deny His power or His providence. He is a King over all "gods"—meaning the judges and rulers of the earth.

**In His hand are the deep places of the earth.** Just as the heights are His, so are the hidden depths. **The heights of the mountains.** The peaks. **The sea is His.** He gathered the waters into one place so the dry land would appear for the sake of living creatures.

**Come, let us worship and bow down.** There are three types of prostration mentioned here: **Worship** <note>original: "nishtachaveh"</note>, which is spreading the whole body on the ground; **Bow** <note>original: "nichra'ah"</note>, which is bending the body; and **Kneel** <note>original: "nivrechah"</note>, which is specifically on the knees. We do this before our Maker. **For He is our God.** He is our judge and leader. **We are the people of His pasture.** Like a shepherd who guards his sheep until the morning. **Today, if you would only listen to His voice.** Do not be like the generation in the wilderness.

->**Subject of the Psalm:** Concerning the worshippers of foreign gods who will be terrified of their gods' current state. They will say that all their fury was channeled through flutes <note>A metaphor for the vanity or hollowness of idol worship</note> because they used to worship them. But now, when God judges them, they will change and see that their fury was misplaced. The "oversight" and the "flutes" refer to the superior decrees of the constellations, the passing seasons, and the sick. "All gods shall bow to Him"—this refers to the idols and the bans placed on the "perfected" flutes, for everyone is destined to be surprised by the coming of the Messiah. "They bowed" is written in the past tense instead of the future <note>A common feature of prophetic Hebrew</note>. These "gods" are all the idolaters. Furthermore, the servants of God will take hold. "And they sang"—song in place of praise. "Five"—the sound of lightning, thunder, and rain. At the sound of the thunder they will hope and tremble, standing in the corners like those waiting for the hail and the bread of heaven to descend for the judgment of the wicked. If the changing winds of protection are lacking in wine, then great praise and song will burst from their hearts because they knew the judgment of the wicked by the lightning and the sentence. Therefore, he mentions the heart of the daughters of Judah: "The eyes of Judah were opened." Understand "kindness," for He has mercy on the kingdom of Israel. Moreover, "He guarded" so there would be no more false gods. These refer to the heavens, the drugs passing over the present time. "Pious ones of the Lord"—all who love the Lord will be guarded, and He will protect all life from great evil. When the foundation is established before the King, the Lord Messiah, the oversight of the wicked will begin. For He will distance all the wicked by His word, guarding the souls of His pious ones. He will rescue them from the hand of the wicked and their rest will be in peace. "Light is sown for the righteous"—in this world, it is sown and prepared for the righteous. "And for the upright of heart, joy"—light and joy will be given to them to delight in the future coming of the Messiah. "Rejoice"—for they will rejoice in Him because they see His judgment upon the wicked. "At the mention of His holiness"—that is His name.<-

# **Psalm**
# **The Lord**

---

"Shall be ashamed." And for whom shall all the worshippers of images be ashamed? From being proud of their gods now; they will say that all their fury was through the "flutes" they worshipped. But when God judges them, they will see that the law of their fury was for nothing. The constellations and "flutes" are merely decrees of the stars. "All gods bow to Him"—referring to the idols. All are destined to be surprised at the arrival of the Messiah. "Bow down" is used in the past to mean the future. This refers to all idol worshippers. "They sang"—song as a form of acclaim. "The sound of lightning and thunder"—those who wait for the hail and the judgment of the wicked. If they lacked the "wine" of divine protection, they would burst forth in song when they saw the lightning of judgment. Therefore, he mentions the "daughters of Judah." "Kindness"—He showed mercy to Israel. "Pious ones of the Lord"—He will guard those who love Him from evil. The Messiah will execute oversight on the wicked. He will rescue the souls of the pious from the hand of the wicked. "Light is sown"—prepared for the righteous in this world for the sake of the next. They will rejoice in the judgment of the wicked.

"Let the mountains sing." Above it says, "The Lord reigns, let the earth rejoice," and elsewhere, "The Lord reigns, the world is established." And it says, "The Lord reigns, let the peoples tremble." The earth will be established in a good and balanced foundation. "The world shall not be moved," for there will be no more destruction. "He sits upon the Cherubim," for He will lower His Presence <note>Shekhinah</note> to the building of the Holy Temple. "The Lord is great in Zion"—then He will be great in Zion because His judgments over the nations and the wicked will be revealed. "Give thanks to His name"—all nations will give thanks to His name for it is great and awesome. "The strength of the King"—His strength and power will be revealed as King over all. "You have established equity"—You have established the world in fairness. The judgment in Jacob will be revealed to the nations. Some interpret the verse as the laws of the Torah given to Jacob, which are the source of discipline that all nations will eventually acknowledge. "Exalt the Lord our God"—this is addressed to both Israel and the nations. "Prostrate yourselves at His footstool"—which is the Holy Temple, for He is holy. For the ancients who were holy in their prayers before Him were answered. "Moses and Aaron among His priests"—it mentions the High Priests. Moses was also considered a priest in his time. They were like those who offered sacrifices. Moses and Aaron were among His priests, and Samuel was among those who called upon His name in his time. Whenever they called to the Lord, He answered them. It is written regarding the staff <note>of Moses</note> and the staff <note>of Aaron</note>; this one shows the way and the other gives song. This one ruled over Israel and Judah. This one fought wars and that one fought wars. This one built an altar and that one built altars. This one sacrificed and that one sacrificed. Regarding one it says "The Lord called to Moses," and the other "The Lord called to Samuel." As for what is said in the Writings, Samuel was also a priest... <note>The text here enters a complex rabbinic discussion comparing the lineages and merits of Moses, Aaron, and Samuel, citing various Midrashic traditions about their status and the "cloud" through which God spoke to them.</note> "They called to the Lord"—"we have sinned against the Lord." "In a pillar of cloud He spoke"—this refers to Moses and Aaron. Rabbi Saadia Gaon explained that this was a sign of prophecy. At times the cloud would appear before them. It says in the Midrash Tanhuma that God also spoke to Samuel in a pillar of cloud. "They kept His testimonies and the decree He gave them"—Moses and Aaron kept the testimony and the law, and gave it to Israel without adding or subtracting. Samuel also gave the testimony and law to Israel and returned them to the proper path.

<column-break/>

"They kept"—we have already explained this. "His right hand delivered for Him"—as it is written, for His hands were strong. "He made known"—this refers to the last verse. "He remembered His kindness"—the kindness and faithfulness He had with the House of Israel. Before the war of Gog and Magog, He remembered His faithfulness to them and saved them in the sight of all. This is "All the ends of the earth have seen." "Shout to the Lord"—the nations are told to shout and rejoice in the salvation of Israel. For through their salvation, the state of the whole world will be stabilized, and there will be no more war between nations. "Sing with the lyre"—with the lyre alone, and with the lyre accompanied by the voice, which is vocal song. "With trumpets"—before the King, the Lord, meaning in the Holy Temple to praise Him. "Let the sea roar"—this is used as a metaphor. "Let the rivers clap"—this too is a metaphor; "clapping hands" is the way of those who are excited and joyful, as it is written "They clapped hands and said: Long live the King!" "Before the Lord"—His judgment will be through lightning and rain, giving good to the righteous and evil to the wicked.

**8) Our God. You answered them.** When they prayed for Israel. **To them.** This means on their behalf. **And took vengeance for their misdeeds.** For the deeds they did against Your will. **Exalt.** Explained as a reference to the blossoms and flowers <note>likely an allegorical reference to the Tabernacle ornaments</note>. **To them.** This means on their behalf. **And took vengeance for their misdeeds.** For the deeds they did against Your will. **Exalt the Lord our God.** And some explain it according to its plain meaning: **Our God, You answered them...**

# A Psalm
**For thanksgiving: Shout joyfully to the Lord, all the earth.** The meaning is that this psalm was said when the nations come and the wicked are destroyed from the whole earth. From the whole earth they shall rejoice. And they shall prostrate themselves for the festival of the Lord with joy. From every hope they shall come with joy to the altar of the Lord with joy. And it is written elsewhere: "Serve the Lord with fear," yet here it is written, "Serve the Lord with gladness." The explanation is that one should serve with fear except in certain circumstances, and with joy during the Sabbath and Festivals, from which fear is removed beneath praise. One might say that a person feels fear when there is no peace within. But on the Sabbath and Festivals, fear is taken away. This is the meaning of peace.
**Know that the Lord is God; He made us and we are His... and the sheep of His pasture.** The explanation is that the general rule is for my whole heart to think in the way of His goodness, to complete and fulfill His laws. And so it is with the peace offerings; I have come to the house of the Lord. The end of the verse refers to the Temple <note>original: "Ha-Bayit"</note>, where they will pray toward the House of the Lord, the Holy Temple. The Temple is their place forever, and for all generations, even when the Temple is destroyed.

# Of David
**A Psalm: I will sing of mercy and justice to You, O Lord.** David spoke in this psalm about the laws of his kingdom, as he walked in the holy way of the Blessed One. He recounts what he would answer according to the custom of kings; he would contemplate matters with great fear of Heaven. He would isolate himself from corrupt judges and those who work iniquity, and he would apply judgment to his own soul through the way of wisdom, conducting his worldly affairs from his heart to receive the holiness. **I will sing of mercy and justice.** Concerning the mercy and justice that a king performs to benefit Israel. **To You, O Lord, I will sing.** When will You come to me? As it is written: "And David executed justice and righteousness for all his people." The essence of mercy and justice is found when God is present in the judgment. Why was the singing of justice given to the Lord? 
**I will be wise in the way of integrity.** I will set my heart to understand the good and perfect way, for wisdom is a gift. That is to say: may the preciousness of holiness come to me. **I will walk in the integrity of my heart within my house.** "My house" refers to the general rule of the heart, to think in the way of His goodness and to keep His laws.

**A perverse heart shall depart from me. I will know no evil. Whoever slanders his neighbor in secret, him I will destroy.** Out of humility and submission, the perverse heart shall depart from me, for it shall never be in my company. **I will know no evil.** I will not see a "bad day," meaning the evil person will not be in my presence. **Whoever slanders in secret.** This refers to one who uses his tongue to bark like a dog. The word for slander <note>original: "meloishni"</note> is a four-letter root meaning to plot in thought. I would rebuke him. He is the opposite of those kings who bring close the flatterers who speak sweetly to them. But my heart was not occupied with such things. I would forget the slanderer and not hold a grudge in my heart. Our Sages of blessed memory said that one should not even leave a slanderer at the table... **He who has a high look and a proud heart.** One who is arrogant in his actions and looks only at worldly matters, his heart broadening with worldly desires. 

**My eyes are upon the faithful of the land.** He means that while the wicked are removed from my house, my eyes are upon the pious of the land to look upon them with favor. Our Sages said this refers to the place of the faithful. Therefore he said "in my presence." 
**He shall not dwell.** In my surroundings and my separation, he who has a haughty eye shall not dwell in my house. I cannot bear to see him, let alone have him serve in my house.
**Every morning I will destroy.** Day by day, continually. **All the wicked of the land.** In every place. Even from the city of the Lord, which is Jerusalem.

# A Prayer
**Of the afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his complaint before the Lord.** This psalm was said in the language of the people of the exile <note>original: "bnei ha-galut"</note>. Each individual in the exile says his prayer in the plural language of the psalm. **When he is faint.** For one who is weighed down by great trouble, as if burdened by his anger and grief, he wraps himself <note>original: "yitatef," same root as "ya'atof/faint"</note> in his restoration. **O Lord, hear my prayer.** May my prayer rise up. Let my grievance be revealed before You. **Hide not Your face.** I have already spoken and turned my face from them to forget. Do not hide Your face anymore, for I fear this greatly. Answer me.

<column-break/>

---

**For my days are consumed in smoke.** Like a burning object that turns into smoke and vanishes into nothingness, so too my days have vanished. My strength is consumed like smoke. **Like a hearth.** The place where the fire burns constantly is called a *moked* <note>hearth or fireplace</note>. Depending on the material being burned, the heat varies; so too my bones are charred. **Stricken like grass.** It is written with a *vav* <note>a grammatical note on the Hebrew spelling</note> and a dagesh <note>a formal emphasis mark</note>, as I have noted in my book *The Miklul* <note>This identifies the author as Radak, Rabbi David Kimhi, a 12th-century grammarian</note>. The meaning is that just as the sun beats down on moist grass until it dries up, so my heart has dried up. Why? **Because I forgot to eat my bread.** That is to say, from the greatness of my troubles. 

It is known in the **wisdom of nature** <note>medieval physiology</note> that physical illness combined with grief strikes the heart, and then the heat of the illness burns within. From the heart, this spreads to the whole body, causing a loss of strength and moisture. Without food, the body's internal heat would consume the natural fluids, and the heart would dry out. Food and drink provide the body with the moisture it needs to balance this heat. Therefore, because he does not eat, his heart withers. This is why he says: "My strength is dried up like a potsherd."

**From the sound of my groaning.** It is known that sighing and a troubled heart weaken the body. When there is silence, the flesh clings to the bone until the bone is visible through the skin. As it says elsewhere: "Their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as wood." 

**I am like a pelican of the wilderness.** The *ka'at* <note>translated here as pelican or cormorant</note> is a type of bird mentioned in the Mishnah. It is a desert bird with a bitter cry. Therefore, he says, "I have likened my voice to the pelican of the wilderness." So too with the **owl of the ruins**; its cry is bitter. Or, he may be thinking of himself as a lonely creature in exile, like a beast in the desert or birds that dwell in ruins, far from human habitation.

**I watched.** My "watching" refers to my solitude and hiding. Like a bird that stays awake on a roof, or a watchman at a door. In the exile, I am lonely like a bird separated from its flock, sitting alone on the edge of a roof, not entering the house because it is afraid. Even though I may physically be in a house, because I am in exile and not with my people, I am "on the roof."

**All day my enemies reproach me.** They curse me in my sickness. **Those who mock me.** Those who speak foolishly and mock me until they are "mad" with joy over my suffering. **Swear by me.** Meaning, they use my name as a curse-formula, saying: "May you become like that miserable man." 

**For I have eaten ashes like bread.** This is a metaphor. My bread tastes like ashes in my mouth. **I have mixed my drink with weeping.** My tears fall into my cup. Everything I consume is mixed with the "water" of my eyes, just as wine is diluted with water.

**Because of Your indignation.** For if not for Your anger, I would not be suffering like dust in the hand of this enemy. **For You have lifted me up and cast me down.** This is like a person who lifts an object high only to hurl it to the ground with greater force. The higher it is lifted, the harder the fall.

**My days are like a lengthening shadow.** When the sun is about to set, the shadow stretches out over the earth, but as the sun disappears, the shadow vanishes instantly. So my days pass like a shadow that is about to vanish. **And I wither like grass.** My days pass in an instant, and my heart dries up like grass.

**But You, O Lord.** Even if I die in exile, I know that Your years do not end. You sit forever. He mentions this because while he fears he will not live to see the redemption, he knows God is eternal and will eventually fulfill His promise. **Your remembrance is for all generations.** In every generation, people will pray to You to hasten the redemption.

**You will arise and have mercy on Zion.** For it has been desolate for many years. **For the time to favor her.** The appointed time <note>Hebrew: "moed"</note> for the end of the exile. Though we do not know the exact date, we know that God's mercy and judgment have a set limit.

**For Your servants take pleasure in her stones.** This is a beautiful image: even though the city is in ruins, the exiles still love and kiss its very stones and dust. They long to see it rebuilt. 

**So the nations shall fear.** When Zion is rebuilt, the nations will see God's glory and tremble. **For the Lord built Zion.** When it is rebuilt, His glory will be revealed. **He turned to the prayer of the destitute.** The word *ar'ar* <note>destitute</note> refers to a lonely tree in the desert; so too were the people lonely and stripped in exile.

**Let this be written.** This salvation should be recorded for the "final generation." Future generations, even those not yet born, will hear of these wonders and praise God for what He did for their ancestors. 

**For He looked down.** God looked from the heights of heaven to the earth. **To hear the groaning of the prisoner.** To release those "doomed to death," meaning the exiles who were close to death from their suffering and fear. **To declare in Zion.** So they can return and tell of God's praise in Jerusalem.

**He weakened my strength.** Now the psalmist returns to his personal plea. He feels the length of the exile has shortened his life. **In the way.** The travel and wandering of the exile have sapped his strength. Therefore he prays: **O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days.** Do not let me die before I see the redemption. You are eternal, but my days are few; let me live to see the end of this sorrow.

From the very beginning, when You first started creating, You founded the earth, and the work of Your hands are the heavens. **They shall perish, but You shall endure;** and all of them like a garment shall wear out; like a cloak You shall change them, and they shall be changed. **But You are He as You were, and Your years are not completed.** The children of Your servants shall dwell in the land, and their seed before You shall be established. | <margin>102</margin> Of old You laid the foundation of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands. **They shall perish, but You shall endure;** they shall all wear out like a garment; like clothing You shall change them, and they shall pass away. **But You are He, and Your years shall not** end. By the hand of David it was said in prophecy: Bless, my soul, the name of the Lord, and all the members of my body <note>original: "benei geviyati," literally 'the sons of my body,' an Aramaic idiom for internal organs</note>, His holy name. **Bless, my soul, the name of the Lord, and do not forget all His benefits.** Who forgives all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases. **Who redeems your life from Gehenna <note>The Hebrew text says 'the pit,' which the Aramaic translator interprets as the spiritual realm of punishment</note>, who crowns you with kindness and mercies.** Who satisfies with good the days of your old age, and you shall be renewed **so that you will be** like an eagle in all your youth. **The Lord performs righteousness and judgments for all who are oppressed.** He revealed His ways to Moses, His deeds to the children of Israel. **The Lord is merciful and gracious, slow to anger and abounding** in performing goodness. **He will not contend forever, nor will He keep a grudge for eternity.** He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor has He repaid us according to our iniquities. | <margin>103</margin> # <column-break/>

---

->For as<-

---

**Of old You laid the foundation of the earth.** Because it was said "Your years are throughout all generations," it means that just as You exist forever without a beginning, so You are merciful without end. To demonstrate this endlessness, he says that just as the heavens and earth were there from the start—not like the words of those who believe the world is primordial <note>original: "kadmon," referring to the Aristotelian view that the universe had no beginning</note>—everything is newly created by You; from nothingness You renewed them. And just as You renewed them, so You can end them if You wish, for everything is in Your hand. Because it says, "They shall perish," there are researchers <note>philosophers</note> who believe that the heavens are eternal and that, heaven forbid, the world cannot cease or come to nothing. For us, their words are all like a dispute. There is a dispute among them as to when the world will be destroyed and for how long. Some say it will never be destroyed, God forbid, and they try to bring proof from the sun for everything created. But the view of the Torah is that this verse is like its counterpart: if You wish, just as they were created anew, they shall perish, while You remain forever. **And they shall all wear out like a garment.** Like a cloak You shall change them and they shall be changed—meaning that in the life of the world to come, they will be transformed and a new Torah <note>or "order/nature"</note> will be renewed for them. If they perish, it is by Your will, like a garment, heaven forbid; they were not a primary law to Him. **But You are He.** Your attributes are eternally standing over them, and You are needed for eternity and for all worlds. **But You are He.** It is already known, while my companions are still living: **But You are He, and Your years shall not end.** And when will they not end? **The children of Your servants shall dwell.** They shall dwell forever in their lives, for the life of the world to come in the days of the Redemption, for a Comforter <note>The Messiah</note> will yet come to them and their children forever. This is praise for the discerning King. The meaning of "Before You" refers to His service, blessed be His name, for the eternity of the Living One for all days.

# **Of David**
**Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me.** This psalm is not spoken in the language of ordinary men, but refers to the soul and every part and life-force of the world, because all of this is regarding the good He has bestowed upon him in the building and life-force of the hidden world. He already said at the beginning, "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, etc." "All that is within me" means that every part of the vessel should bless Him. The explanation of "within me" <note>original: "keravai," literally 'my innards'</note> refers to the kidneys, the heart, and the liver; they are the "inner parts." It is not just saying "my inside" referring to the body, but it is by way of a metaphor, like "All my bones shall say, 'Lord, who is like You?'" The sage Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra <note>A 12th-century Spanish scholar</note> wrote that he mentioned the "glorious essence" <note>the soul</note> corresponding to the "glorious essence" <note>God</note>. For man's body was like "half a world" <note>a microcosm</note>. This is known from the "Day of the Torah," for there is a wisdom—the wisdom of the universe—within the world as a whole together with the Wise One, and they are His holiness together with His Holy One. "Every part and all my inner parts, His holy name"—he mentioned the inner parts as the visible essence, while the soul is the essence in the world. In my opinion, every part is needed for this. It is the way of the researcher to repeat a thought in different words. So it is here: "The Lord" and "His holy name." Furthermore, the Sage <note>Ibn Ezra</note> spoke in his books: "All my bones shall say, 'Lord, who is like You?'" Regarding the ten things in man that are an offering to the Holy One, blessed be He: Glory to Glory. The mouth of the wise is a gift of the holy ones. The sacrifice to the Glory. An offering to the One who strikes. The dwelling to the Place <note>HaMakom, a name for God</note>. The life-force to Existence. The kidneys advise. The heart completes. Therefore, King David said that all attributes are according to my actions. Thus, when he says "Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me," another explanation is that he blesses according to grace because he is a part of the whole. **Bless, my soul, and do not forget all His benefits.** Meaning, the rewards of the Creator upon you from the beginning, because the soul is a "part of the Holy One, blessed be He" <note>a spark of divinity</note> and is not a physical body. For so it is written, and the word is not the dwelling of the soul, but "as long as my breath is in me." The Holy One, blessed be He, was and will be—may His name be praised for glory—He fills the world. And the soul fills the body. The Holy One, blessed be He, is all-powerful and nothing is impossible for His glory; and this is "Glory," and the soul is "glory." The Holy One, blessed be He, is unique in His world, and the soul is unique in the body. The Holy One, blessed be He, neither slumbers nor sleeps, and the soul neither slumbers nor sleeps. The Holy One, blessed be He, sees but is not seen, and the soul sees but is not seen. The Holy One, blessed be He, is pure, and the soul is pure—and this is from its high level. Behold, how worthy and essential it is to give thanks to the Creator, blessed be His name. Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi</note> wrote: **And do not forget all His benefits.** Since it is a part of the Holy One, blessed be He, it should not be like anything else in this world; no action or kingdom has power over it from all of this. **Bless, my soul, and do not forget all His benefits... His holy name.** This is by way of a metaphor. Merciful and Gracious, the Holy One, blessed be He, is unique in His world...

The text argues against the philosophical idea of an eternal universe, asserting instead that God is the unique, eternal creator who mirrors the human soul in its invisibility, purity, and sustaining power.</summary>

### Psalms

**Aramaic Interpretive Translation (Targum)** | **Hebrew Masoretic Text**
---|---
For as the height of the heavens is above the earth, so His kindness has prevailed over those who fear Him. | For as the heavens are high above the earth, so great is His kindness toward those who fear Him.
As far as the east is from the west, so far has God removed our transgressions from us. | As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us.
As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has had compassion on those who fear Him. | As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him.
For He knows the evil inclination <note>original: "yitzra bisha"</note> that burns within us; He remembers that we are from the dust. | For He knows our frame; He remembers that we are dust.
As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he flourishes. | As for man, his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so he flourishes.
For a storm wind passes over it and it is no more, and its place shall not recognize it again. | For the wind passes over it, and it is gone; and its place knows it no more.
But the kindness of the Lord is from eternity to eternity upon those who fear Him, and His righteousness to children’s children. | But the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting upon those who fear Him, and His righteousness to children’s children.
To those who keep His covenant and to those who remember His commandments to perform them. | To those who keep His covenant and to those who remember His precepts to do them.
The Lord has established His throne of glory in the high heavens, and His kingdom rules over all. | The Lord has established His throne in the heavens, and His kingdom rules over all.
Bless the name of the Lord, you angels on high, you who are mighty in strength, who do His word, to obey the voice of His command. | <margin>Mighty ones</margin> Bless the Lord, you His angels, you mighty in strength, who do His word, obeying the voice of His word.
Bless the name of the Lord, all His hosts, His ministers who do His will. | Bless the Lord, all His hosts, His ministers who do His will.
Bless the name of the Lord, all His works, in all places of His dominion; bless, O my soul, the name of the Lord. | Bless the Lord, all His works, in all places of His dominion; bless the Lord, O my soul.

<meta>104</meta>

<column-break/>

**For as the heavens are high.** This is similar to the phrase "For Your kindness is great unto the heavens." Therefore, it is appropriate to emphasize the height to demonstrate the power of His kindness. The kindness of the Lord is "supernal," exceeding that of all other creatures, just as the heavens are high above the earth. The word *gavar* <note>meaning "prevailed" or "was strong"</note> implies "might" (*gevurah*), meaning that His kindness overcomes our sins and forgives them.

This is why the text immediately follows with **As far as the east is from the west.** The Great Master, the Guide <note>original: "Ha-Moreh," referring to Maimonides (Rambam) in his *Guide for the Perplexed*</note>, explained this by noting that the distance between east and west from any given point is not as great as the distance from the center of the world to the encompassing heavens. Through scientific proof, he demonstrated the vastness of the distance between heaven and earth. Thus, when the verse says "He removes our sins," it implies that His kindness is exceedingly great, removing our transgressions to the furthest possible distance. It says "He removed [them] from us," rather than saying His kindness moved away from us. On the contrary, His kindness "prevailed" (*gavar*) over us to be strong and enduring.

**As a father has compassion on his children.** His pity is like a father’s natural love for his children because His mercy toward us is abundant. **For He knows our frame.** This means the responsibility for us is laid upon Him, for He formed us and knows our "evil inclination" and its terrors. It is in the very nature of creation, for **we are dust.** He remembers that man is merely physical matter; what is he worth?

**As for man, his days are like grass.** The purpose of this parable is to highlight human frailty and smallness, and the fact that we are material, like the dust of the earth. His days are compared to grass—just as a flower of the field sprouts and blooms in beautiful glory, but then immediately dries up and withers, so too does man. **For the wind passes over it and it is gone.** This refers to a harsh, strong wind, like a storm. When such a wind passes, the flower withers instantly. This "wind" can be understood literally as a momentary breeze that passes. If the Blessed Name created him as dust and ashes, how could man survive if his Creator did not pity him?

**But the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting.** Having mentioned man’s frailty and his likeness to grass, the text now speaks of the kindness of the Creator, which exists forever. This kindness is for **those who fear Him.** It is not promised to every person indiscriminately, but to those who are worthy and perform His will. **And His righteousness to children’s children.** This means His merit extends for all eternity, to future generations.

Some interpreters explain **the kindness of the Lord is from everlasting to everlasting** as a reference to the excellence of the soul, which yearns for the World to Come and eternal life. They say this soul reflects the "might" of the King of Kings. Even after death, the kindness of the Lord reaches those who keep His covenant. Furthermore, a righteous person commands his children after him to keep the way of the Lord and perform acts of charity and justice, bequeathing this righteousness to all generations.

**The Lord has established His throne in the heavens.** This refers to the governance of the world through Divine Providence, which is directed from the heavens. The "Throne of Glory" is, so to speak, the place from which decrees and judgments emerge. Because the heavens are eternal, they serve as the foundation for the covenant explained by the prophets. Heaven forbid that the Creator would destroy His own creations!

**Bless the Lord, you His angels, you mighty in strength.** They perform His will, and their word is more honored than any earthly power. From their strength comes the power of souls, the celestial spheres, and the stars. These "mighty ones" are the angels and the souls. The text says **to obey the voice of His word** because unlike humans, who might hear a command but try to avoid it, these beings find their glory in the very act of hearing and doing.

**Bless the Lord, all His hosts.** These are the lower beings, for everything is made by Him. This includes the scholars, the men of understanding, and the researchers who serve the Lord through their thoughts. They are His "ministers" who serve Him through inquiry and the study of righteousness. The psalm concludes with **Bless the Lord, O my soul**, for the soul is the highest part of man, connected to the power of both the upper and lower worlds. It is within the soul's power to bless the Lord for everything.

<summary>This page concludes Psalm 103, contrasting human mortality (likened to grass and dust) with God's eternal mercy. The commentary integrates Maimonides' astronomical views on distance to explain the vastness of divine forgiveness and discusses the soul's eternal nature.</summary>

Bless the name of the Lord, O my soul! O Lord my God, You have shown Yourself great in seeing praise, and You have clothed Yourself in glory and splendor. | Bless the Lord, O my soul! O Lord my God, You are very great; You are clothed in glory and majesty.
Wrapping Himself in light like a garment, stretching out the heavens like a curtain; | Wrapped in light as with a garment, stretching out the heavens like a tent curtain.
He who roofs His upper chambers with water, who makes the swift clouds His chariot, and who walks upon the wings of the wind; | He who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters, who makes the clouds His chariot, who walks on the wings of the wind.
He who makes His messengers swift as the wind, His servants strong as flaming fire; | He makes the winds His messengers, flaming fire His servants.
He who founded the earth upon its foundations, so that it shall not be moved forever and ever; | He set the earth on its foundations, so that it should never be moved.
The abyss covered it like a garment; the waters stood above the mountains. | You covered it with the deep as with a garment; the waters stood above the mountains.
From Your rebuke they flee; from the sound of Your thunder they hasten to pour out. | At Your rebuke they flee; at the sound of Your thunder they take to flight.
They ascend the mountains and descend into the valleys, to the place that You established for them. | They went up the mountains, they went down the valleys to the place that You appointed for them.
You set a boundary for the waves of the sea that they should not cross, that they should not return to cover the earth. | You set a boundary that they may not pass, so that they might not again cover the earth.
He who sends springs into the streams; they flow between the mountains. | You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills.
They give drink to every beast of the field; the wild asses quench their thirst. | They give drink to every beast of the field; the wild asses quench their thirst.
Upon them the birds of heaven dwell; from among the branches they give forth their song. | Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell; they sing among the branches.
<meta>catchword: Who waters</meta>

<column-break/>

->**Glory and majesty You have clothed**<-

**Bless [the Lord]:** This psalm recounts the Act of Creation <note>Hebrew: *Ma'aseh Bereshit*, the traditional term for the account of the world's origins</note>, and how the Holy One, blessed be He, does everything with wisdom for the benefit of His creatures. It says, "Bless, O my soul," because among the lower beings <note>earthly creatures</note>, there are those who know how to bless God with the mouth and the heart. It says, "You are very great," meaning that His name is blessed by the mouths of His creatures, and His greatness is visible to all eyes. **Glory and majesty You have clothed:** This is like a person putting on their greatness; it is a language of honor and splendor. Through the investigation of nature, a person recognizes the immense splendor and honor of the Creator. Just as kings are recognized by their royal garments, so too is His greatness known.

The sage Rabbi Abraham Ibn Ezra wrote that "glory and majesty" refer to the heavens, for the greatness of Your honor is found in the investigation and depth of the kingdom. And in the Midrash of our Sages, it is said that He turned His face and revealed the light of the world—this is the meaning of "Glory and majesty You have clothed." Rabbi Moshe bar Nachman <note>Nachmanides, or Ramban</note>, of blessed memory, wrote concerning the secret of "Glory and majesty You have clothed," but we must be careful in explaining this, lest one misunderstand the ways of the Creator. However, it is certain that God possesses these two attributes: Glory and Majesty. It is also possible to translate this according to the established commentators; this is clear, and the order of the year follows it.

**Wrapped in light as with a garment:** He begins by mentioning the start of all things, at the very beginning of creation, after He has described the King's beauty. Thus it says in the Torah: "Let there be light." The word "wrapped" is like a garment of splendor. Some say this "wrapping" refers to the entire world being enveloped in His glory. **Stretching out the heavens like a tent curtain:** This refers back to the firmament that divides the waters. As it says, "He wrapped Himself in a garment to create the waters." The beginning of this creation was on the second day. It is not written "on that day" <note>referring to the phrase "it was good"</note> because the waters were not yet separated. Some prophets say that the heavens are His holy glory. On the first day, He created the heavens, the boundaries, the spheres, and the "Chariots." The spheres are given ten names, corresponding to the movement of the stars and the measurement of time. 

Regarding the phrase **He who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters:** Some explain this as referring to the "waters above the firmament." The scholars of research <note>medieval natural philosophers</note> agree that there are indeed waters above the heavens. Others explain it as the clouds being the "upper chambers." It says **He makes the clouds His chariot** because by His will, the clouds move and travel. Likewise, **He walks on the wings of the wind** refers to the movement of the wind and the hovering of the clouds. It is as if He is walking upon their wings. 

**He makes the winds His messengers:** The spirits and souls are His messengers and emissaries, for nothing happens by chance; everything is by the intent of the Intender. Likewise, **flaming fire** and all the combined elements are all within His blessing and power, and all are His servants. Now, having mentioned the upper things, He mentions the earth and the water. He mentions what was done on the third day regarding the gathering of the dry land. He first mentions the foundation of the earth. **He set the earth on its foundations:** He placed within the nature of the earth the tendency to sink to the lowest point, which is the center of the celestial sphere. It stays on its foundations so it will not move forever, for if it moved from its center, the foundations of the world would be destroyed. This is by His wisdom, that every thing stays in its place within the circle, and the earth remains in the middle due to the force of the "heaviness" <note>an early intuition of gravity</note>.

**The Deep (Abyss):** Now He says how the earth was covered in water at the beginning of creation. For the nature of water is to be above the earth, as they are lighter. But God, in His blessing and wisdom, gathered them to one side of the face of the earth. The word "Abyss" <note>Hebrew: *Tehom*</note> is compared to a garment. Originally, before the waters were gathered, the waters were the covering of the earth. "Abyss" can be treated as either masculine or feminine in Hebrew grammar. As it says: "A river went out of Eden to water the garden." Sometimes "Abyss" is feminine, as in "The great deep" (*Tehom Rabbah*), and sometimes masculine, as in "The deep said, 'It is not in me.'" The primary explanation is that the water was like a garment covering the entire earth. **The waters stood above the mountains:** Even over the highest mountains, the water stood. 

**At Your rebuke they flee:** They flee and scatter to their assigned place. The waters flee from His rebuke as if a person flees from a shouting voice. **At the sound of Your thunder they take to flight:** Just as a person is terrified by a voice of thunder and hastens to move, so did the waters hasten to the place of their gathering. **They went up the mountains... down the valleys:** By His power, the mountains appeared to rise and the valleys to sink until the water reached the place established for them. **You set a boundary:** After the gathering of the waters, He set a boundary so they would not cross over and return to cover the dry land as they did at the beginning. This is a sign of the Creator's power and His mercy on His creatures, for the water is gathered in one place despite being naturally higher than the land. 

**He who sends springs:** This is also for the benefit of the creatures. For when He gathered the waters, He left some in the earth. The gathered waters of the sea are salty so they do not putrefy, but the waters He sent through the mountains are sweet to give drink to the animals and to moisten the dry land. **They flow between the mountains:** The springs flow from the hills, and their benefit to human settlements is well known. Even in the deserts, they provide for the "wild beasts" so they may find water. **The wild asses quench their thirst:** Specifically mentioning wild asses because they live in the desert where water is scarce. **Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell:** Birds also benefit, for they live near water sources. **From among the branches:** Referring to the branches of the trees that grow by the riverbanks. **They give forth their song:** They chirp and sing.

### Psalms

**Hebrew Masoretic Text** | **Aramaic Interpretive Translation**
---|---
He waters the mountains from His upper chambers; the earth is satisfied by the fruit of Your works. | He waters the mountains from the house of His upper dwelling; the earth is satisfied by the produce of His labor.
<margin>for the service</margin> He causes grass to grow for the cattle, and herbs for the **service of man**, to bring forth bread from the earth; | He makes the grass grow for the cattle, and greenery for the service of man, to bring forth bread from the earth;
And wine that makes glad the heart of man, making the face shine with oil, and bread that sustains the heart of man. | And wine that gladdens the heart of man, to brighten the face more than oil, and bread that sustains the heart of man.
The trees of the Lord are satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon which He planted; | The trees of the Lord are satisfied, the cedars of Lebanon which He planted;
Where the birds make their nests; as for the stork, the cypresses are her home. | Where the birds nest; the <term>shoshilai</term><note>Aramaic: "shoshilai" - likely referring to a specific type of bird or the stork</note> makes her home in the cypress.
<margin>for the hyraxes</margin> The high mountains are for the wild goats; the rocks are a refuge for the **hyraxes**. | The high mountains are for the wild goats; the shelters of confidence are for the <term>tafneya</term><note>Aramaic: "tafneya" - the Aramaic equivalent of the Hebrew "shafan" or hyrax</note>.
<margin>for seasons</margin> He made the moon for **seasons**; the sun knows its setting. | He made the moon for times; in its time, the sun knows the season of its setting.
You make darkness and it is night, in which all the beasts of the forest creep. | You set darkness and it becomes night, in which all the beasts of the field creep.

<column-break/>

**He waters the mountains from His upper chambers.** After mentioning the gathering of the waters, the scripture mentions the benefit of the waters. The scripture mentions this as part of the blessing of the third day <note>original: "yom ha-shlishi"</note>, just as it says, "Let the earth sprout vegetation." Before the earth brought forth, a mist went up from the ground and watered the entire face of the soil, and afterward, the Lord God rained upon the earth. This is what is meant by "He waters the mountains from His upper chambers," which refers to the clouds. He mentions the mountains because they need rain more than the valleys and lowlands; the valleys drink easily as the rain collects and remains there. Furthermore, the water descends to water the valleys and lowlands from the rivers, and thus the mountains are prioritized for rain.

Afterward, he says, **the earth is satisfied by the fruit of Your works**, repeating the idea in different words. The "fruit of Your works" refers to the rain. He calls it "Your works" because the matter of rain is a work of wisdom, measured and weighed. Similarly, he mentions the heavens among the wondrous works of the Creator in providing the rain's decree. He says this to imply that there is no one else who can bring rain except the Blessed Name. Thus, the workings of the celestial spheres and the rain are His story.

**He causes grass to grow for the cattle.** With the rain, He causes grass to grow for the animals' food, and He also grows herbs. As written in the words of the sons of <unclear>A.S.</unclear>, everything comes forth to show the benefit of the greenery and herbs for both man and beast. Generally, he mentions the source of food; specifically, he describes how He gave them more strength and nourishment. The phrase **herbs for the service of man** refers to herbs that are human food, for we produce them through "human service" <note>original: "avodat ha-adam"</note>. Unlike the grass for animals which grows on its own, bread requires human labor to be brought forth from the earth. Human labor is required to extract for oneself grains like wheat, barley, and legumes. "Bread" is used here as a general term for all food, as it is the constant staple of the human diet. Regarding this, he says, **and bread sustains the heart of man**.

**And wine makes glad.** He also brings wine forth from the earth, for it is to the benefit of man to gladden his heart. If mixed in the proper measure, it improves his intellect, for with a glad heart, the mind functions better. **And making the face shine with oil.** He also brings forth oil to be used by man, which makes his face appear radiant. While it has many uses, he mentions the primary benefit: it makes the face shine. This could mean the oil physically brightens the skin, or perhaps it refers to the light produced by oil lamps at night. Since he mentioned the benefits of wine, oil, and bread—the three main staples—he notes their high utility. He says **it sustains the heart of man**, for wine gladdens and bread supports, as it is said elsewhere, "Take a morsel of bread and sustain your hearts."

**The trees of the Lord are satisfied.** They are satisfied by the rain mentioned earlier. These are the wild trees of the forest. He attributes the trees to God <note>original: "atzei Hashem"</note> because they grow to great sizes and produce abundantly without human help. It is the way of the scripture to attribute great and mighty things to God, such as "mountains of God" or "cedars of God." Alternatively, they are called "trees of the Lord" because their growth and height involve no human partnership. Since he previously mentioned herbs and trees that require human cultivation, he now mentions those that grow by divine power alone. Therefore, he says **He planted**—specifically the "cedars of Lebanon which He planted"—to show that no man planted them for his own livelihood. Nature itself brought them forth, watered by His "upper chambers" until they were satisfied and strong. Furthermore, they provide a benefit beyond food: they serve as homes for the birds and the stork.

**Where the birds make their nests.** Now he mentions their specific benefit. In their creation, there is a benefit for the birds to have shelter. Among them is the **stork** <note>original: "chasidah"</note>. The name *chasidah* implies she performs acts of kindness <note>original: "chesed"</note>. The scripture notes that while humans plant fruit trees for themselves, God provided these great trees for the birds. He created the world to be an inhabited dwelling for all living things. He mentions the stork specifically because it is a large bird that usually nests in high places like cypresses. **Her home** means her nest.

**The high mountains are for the wild goats.** Just as he mentioned the dwelling of birds in high trees, he notes that the high mountains are the dwellings of wild animals. He specifies the wild goats because they are found on high peaks. **The rocks are a refuge for the hyraxes.** The rocks also serve the animals; they contain caves and crevices where the hyraxes find shelter. This shows that everything was created for a purpose by the Great Compassionate One, and ultimately for the benefit of man, who is superior to them all.

**He made the moon for seasons.** Now he mentions the creations of the fourth day: the luminaries. First, the moon. Although it is the "lesser light," it is mentioned first here regarding the night. **He made the moon for seasons**, as it is written, "they shall be for signs and for seasons." This refers to the calculation of months and festivals based on the moon's cycle. We benefit from its light and its role in marking the passage of the year.

**The sun knows its setting.** Sages have understood that the moon is a dark body that only reflects the sun's light based on its proximity or distance. The moon "does not know" its own light, so to speak, but the sun's light is its own. **Its setting** <note>original: "mevo'o"</note> refers to its shining and its setting. Some explain that the sun "knows" the setting of the moon. Others say the sun's path is precise, whereas the moon's path involves "crooked ways" <note>original: "orchot akalkalot"</note> that are harder to calculate.

**You make darkness and it is night.** Now he mentions the benefit of the night. When He places darkness in the world, it is a benefit for the survival of the animals—the beasts of the forest that are predators. God gave them the ability to hunt, but He did not give them permission to harm man. He placed a "fear of man" upon them, so they stay in their dens during the day and only come out at night to seek their prey. This is what is meant by **all the beasts of the forest creep**. "Creep" <note>original: "tirmos"</note> means to walk. Thus, the night allows the predators to eat while allowing man and his domestic animals to rest safely. Darkness also has a cooling effect on the air. **The young lion...**

### Psalms

**Aramaic Interpretive Translation** | **Hebrew Masoretic Text**

Man goes out to his work and to his labor until the time of evening. | Man goes out to his work and to his labor until evening.
