<margin>Common Commentary</margin> **The young lions roar.** Young lions are those in the peak of their strength and the predatory animals. "And to seek their food from God"—for He has given them strength through the "chain of causes" <note>A medieval philosophical term referring to the natural order of cause and effect established by God.</note>. The animals seek their sustenance through the wisdom God placed in them when they hunt. **The sun rises, they gather.** This is for the sake of man, so he may go out to work his field. "And in their dens"—this is like saying "within their dwellings." **The sun rises, they gather** in their dwellings, in safety. **Until evening.** When man returns to the city, the animals return to seek their food. All of this is sustained by the power of the Creator and the wisdom of the Wise One. **How great are Your works, O Lord.** "How great" here means how numerous and how significant. Just as one might say of a nobleman, "over all the greatness <note>original: "rav"</note> of his house." Or, it refers to the literal number of works. Thus, the text follows with "Your possessions," as if to say the wisdom of the Creator is told through the variety of creatures. At the end of the psalm, he concludes with this verse to say that those who know and recognize the power of God all their days see that His work is full of wisdom. **The earth is full of Your possessions.** Everything in the entire world is Your possession and Your handiwork; nothing happens by chance. This means there is no empty space in the world that does not contain the works of God. The meaning of "Your possessions" <note>original: "kinyanekha"</note> is like "the Maker <note>original: "koneh"</note> of heaven and earth." **This great and wide sea.** Now he speaks of those created on the fifth day—the fish and creeping things of the sea. It is great in length and wide in "hands" <note>A Hebrew idiom for "reaches" or "breadth"</note>. He mentions this because the sea is distant and known to all. Even though birds were also mentioned as being created from the waters, the "great sea" is specified here for the creeping things that are without number. They are more fruitful and numerous than land animals. Furthermore, they are changed by every ship... therefore he says "without number." **There the ships go.** He mentions that even in the sea, which is not a natural habitat for man, God gave man the wisdom to travel in ships as if on dry land. This is like the blessing, "and rule over the fish of the sea." **This Leviathan You formed.** Everything is as nothing compared to it. This is like the verse, "What is man that You are mindful of him?" **Leviathan You formed to play with.** This is the great sea monster described in the Book of Job for its strength and essence. He mentions this to contrast it with everything else we have seen. According to the scriptural narrative, "to play with it" means that compared to all other sea creatures, it is like a king among subjects; it has no fear and finds its sustenance as if "playing." Every movement of the beast seems like a game or a mockery. It is also possible that it refers to the Leviathan "playing" in the waters. He mentions all the creatures sustained in the water and their qualities, as man was already mentioned above. **They all look to You.** He speaks of all the creatures mentioned, both on land and in the sea. They all live by Your providence, and their sustenance is created for them every single day. "They look to You to give them their food in its time"—as it is written, "He gives to them." This refers to the observation of the wise. He says **in its time** because every living thing has a known lifespan and a set time for its food. "They look to You"—even though animal life is lower than human life, the instinct God placed in them makes it as if they are seeking God. Through the wisdom with which they were created, they recognize their sustenance and they all rejoice. **You give to them, they gather.** The verse repeats the idea for emphasis. He does not say "he gathers" (singular) but "they gather" (plural), for they gather a little here and a little there at the proper time. Then "You open Your hand, they are satisfied with good." **You hide Your face, they are dismayed.** When You turn Your face away, meaning when You withhold sustenance, they are terrified, for they have no power to help themselves without You. **You take away their breath, they die.** "Take away" <note>original: "tosef"</note> is like "consume" <note>original: "tasof"</note>. Every living thing is sustained by God. When the soul, which allows them to exist and be distinct, is removed, they return to dust. This does not mean the soul returns to the same physical material, for animals do not have a human soul. The philosophers <note>Likely referring to medieval Aristotelian philosophers like Maimonides or Al-Farabi.</note> say the soul does not return to the body forever, as Job said, "Until the heavens are no more, they shall not awake." However, other verses suggest that the soul *will* return to tell of His wonders. This refers to the **Resurrection of the Dead** <note>original: "Techiyat HaMeitim"</note>, which every Israelite believes in. This will be a miracle and a new creation, not according to the natural order. Regarding this, it says, **You send Your breath, they are created, and You renew the face of the earth.** Even though the previous verse spoke of all living things, this verse refers specifically to man, who is the primary purpose of the lower creations. The resurrection will be for man, as is held by our Sages. Some in the Talmud believed resurrection was only for the righteous and not the wicked. It is also possible to explain this verse as referring to all life: "You send Your breath, they are created"—as some die, others are born in their place. As it is written, "A generation goes and a generation comes." The species remain while the individuals perish. "You renew the face of the earth" refers to the new creatures that come into the world. **May the glory.** When he finishes the description of the work of Creation, he says this. It is like the Torah saying, "And God saw everything that He had made, and behold, it was very good." Everything He made is His glory, and it shall remain in the world forever. "May the Lord rejoice"—everything shall rejoice in its Creator. **Who looks at the earth and it trembles.** This refers to the time of the **Redemption** <note>original: "Geulah"</note>. He says that even though His works are His glory and He rejoices in them, there are times when He is angry with the world, as in the generation of the Flood, or the generation of the Dispersion, or Sodom and Gomorrah. In those times, He does not rejoice in His works. But in the days of the Messiah, it is written that the Lord will be One and His name One, and all will serve Him with one accord. Then, the wicked will be removed from the world, as it is written, "all the arrogant and all who do evil shall be stubble." Then the glory of the Lord will be forever and He will rejoice in His works after the destruction of the wicked. This is why he says, "May sinners be consumed." "The earth trembles" is a metaphor; God's "rejoicing" is not like human joy, but a way to describe the perfection of His works. **Who looks at the earth and it trembles** is a metaphor for the destruction of the wicked, as if the earth itself trembles. He mentions the mountains as if they feel His wrath, meaning the pride of the wicked will be brought low. **I will sing.** This is the voice of the people of Israel who serve God. While the wicked perish, I will sing. **May my speech be sweet to Him.** My prayer, Torah study, and praise shall be sweet to Him. "I will rejoice in the Lord"—just as He rejoices in His works, we shall rejoice in Him. **May sinners be consumed.** They will be finished and no others will take their place. In this world, sinners are never finished, but in the days of the Messiah, when the wicked are gone, there will be no more evil. This is why he says "and the wicked be no more." Therefore, I return to my soul: "Bless the Lord, O my soul." This occurs twice in the psalm. The Sages explain that "May the glory of the Lord be forever" refers to the natural world. "May the Lord rejoice" refers to the unity of the species. "Who looks at the earth" refers to His power to destroy. "May my speech be sweet" means that when the world is perfected, human actions will be aligned with Divine joy. **Bless the Lord** follows the destruction of the wicked. David did not say **Hallelujah** <note>literally "Praise the Lord"</note> until he saw the downfall of the wicked. We have written in the introduction to this book that "Hallelujah" is the greatest of all praises, for it includes both the act of praise and the Divine Name in one word.

<summary>This page concludes Psalm 104, detailing the natural order from lions and the sea's Leviathan to the cycle of life and death. The commentary by Radak explores themes of Divine joy, the Resurrection of the Dead, and the ultimate removal of evil from the world during the Messianic age.</summary>

### **The Hebrew Text**

**Give thanks** to the Lord, call upon His name; make His deeds known among the nations.
Sing to Him, play music to Him; speak of all His wonders. Glory in His holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice. Seek the Lord and His strength; seek His presence always. Remember His wonders that He has performed, His miracles, and the judgments of His mouth. O seed of Abraham His servant, O children of Jacob His chosen ones.
He is the Lord our God; His judgments are in all the earth. He remembers His covenant forever, the word He commanded for a thousand generations. Which He made with Abraham, and His oath to Isaac. # ## Give Thanks (Hodu)

**Give thanks to the Lord, call upon His name, make His deeds known among the nations.** This psalm was composed by David when he brought up the Ark from the house of Obed-Edom the Gittite to the City of David. He gave it to Asaph and his brothers to sing before the Ark, as it is written in the Book of Chronicles. There, this psalm is recorded until the verse "do My prophets no harm." However, the conclusion of the song there differs slightly in its wording, though the theme remains the same. When David compiled this Book of Psalms, he included this psalm here and added to it the account of the seed of Abraham until they arrived in the Land <note>Israel</note>. It appears that when the exiles returned, they would not recite this in the morning and evening except before the Ark in the Temple.

**Call upon His name:** This means to pray to Him, as in the phrase "called upon the name of the Lord." Alternatively, "calling in His name" refers to giving thanks in the way of the Lord, as it says "And there Abraham called upon the name of the Lord." This is the meaning of "make His deeds known among the nations"—the deeds revealed by His wonders regarding the Ark. **Sing to Him, play music to Him:** With the voice and with instruments. **Speak of all His wonders:** You should also tell one another about the miracles regarding the Ark and the wonders He performed for others in their days. **Glory in His holy name; let the heart of those who seek the Lord rejoice:** You shall praise the Lord and boast over all the nations in His holy name, and they shall fear you. Just as you received a blessing, so may it be. Therefore, let your hearts rejoice because you are seekers of the Lord. You have been privileged to seek Him, and unlike the other nations, your heart shall rejoice in the name of the Lord through seeking Him.

**Seek the Lord and His strength; seek His presence always:** This refers to seeking the dwelling place of the Ark and praying there before Him. "Seeking His presence" means praying before Him continually. As in the Midrash of Rabbi Ishmael: "Do not be dismayed or wonder; all the days of your life you seek to behold the Divine Presence (Shekhinah) in this world." <note>Radak interprets 'strength' as a reference to the Ark of the Covenant.</note>

**Remember His wonders:** Remember in your heart His miracles and wonders that He performed in Egypt and in the desert, and the judgments He executed. The subject is the same: the miracles performed in the land of the Philistines <note>meaning the surrounding regions</note>. He says to remember the ancient miracles. This is why he says **which He performed... the judgments of His mouth.** The "mouth" refers to the plagues He brought upon Egypt, which He spoke through Moses, so to speak, at the beginning. These were the judgments against the Egyptians. In Chronicles, it says "seed of Israel His servant," but the meaning is the same. Whether it says "seed of Abraham" or "seed of Israel," it refers to the specific lineage chosen for Abraham. As it was said to Abraham, "for in Isaac shall your seed be called," and Isaac said to Jacob, "And may He give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and your seed with you." This is the unique seed of Abraham: the children of Israel. Thus he explains, **children of Jacob His chosen ones**—meaning, who is the seed of Abraham? They are the children of Jacob who were truly chosen to serve Him.

**His judgments are in all the earth:** Though He is our God and we are His people, His judgment governs the entire world. As the Midrash says: "He is our God"—you do not find Him except in goodness and joy. Even in punishment, He is the Mighty One. He is the Judge, He is the King. **He remembers His covenant forever:** As explained in the verse "the word He commanded for a thousand generations." This refers to the decree He made to Abraham. Though they were exiled from the land, they will return and dwell in it forever. This is the meaning of "forever" and "a thousand generations." In the Midrash, "a thousand generations" refers to the Torah, which was envisioned a thousand generations before creation.

**Which He made with Abraham:** As it says, "On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your seed I have given..." **and His oath to Isaac:** Meaning, for the sake of Isaac, or the oath made at the Binding of Isaac (Akedah), where God said "By Myself I have sworn." **And He established it for Jacob:** That same covenant and oath were confirmed for Jacob as a statute and for Israel as an everlasting covenant. This emphasizes that the covenant was for this specific lineage, not for all of Abraham's descendants.

**To say, "To you I will give...":** He said this to each of the Patriarchs. **The lot of your inheritance:** Addressing the collective Israel. **When they were but few in number:** This refers to the Patriarchs and their children. Jacob himself said, "and I am few in number." **Hardly any, and strangers in it:** For a short time they were strangers in the land because they had to wander from it, like Abraham going to Egypt because of famine, or Isaac and Jacob's travels. **And they wandered from nation to nation:** Even though they stayed in the land, they were not settled. They went from Canaan to Egypt and the land of the Philistines.

**He allowed no man to oppress them:** Referring to kings like Pharaoh and Abimelech. **Touch not My anointed ones:** They were esteemed like "anointed" kings or priests. For example, the sons of Heth said to Abraham, "You are a prince of God among us," and Abimelech sought to make a peace treaty with Isaac. **And My prophets:** The Patriarchs were prophets to whom God spoke in visions and dreams. As He said regarding Abraham: "Return the man's wife, for he is a prophet."

**And He called a famine:** He mentions the reason the family of Jacob went down to Egypt. "He called" means He commanded the famine to come upon the land. **Every staff of bread:** Bread is the support of life. **He sent a man before them:** Joseph. Even though Joseph was sold through the jealousy of his brothers, it was God's plan. As Joseph said, "God sent me before you." **They afflicted his foot with a chain:** When he was put in prison. The Hebrew text says "his foot" (singular) but we read it as "feet" (plural), for both were bound. **His soul was placed in iron:** His soul suffered through the affliction of his body.

**Until the time that his word came to pass:** Until the interpretation of Pharaoh's dream was fulfilled. **The word of the Lord refined him:** He was tested and purified. The Midrash explains: One opinion says "until the word of Joseph" (his interpretation) was fulfilled, and another says "until the word of the Holy One, Blessed be He" was fulfilled—for Joseph had to wait two extra years in prison because he put his trust in the chief cupbearer rather than God alone.

# 106
->**Hallelujah! Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good; for His mercy endures forever.**<-
->**Who can express the mighty acts of the Lord, or make all His praise heard?**<-
->**Blessed are those who keep justice, who perform righteousness at all times.**<-
->**Remember me, O Lord, when You favor Your people; visit me with Your salvation.**<-
->**That I may see the prosperity of Your chosen ones, that I may rejoice in the gladness of Your nation, that I may glory with Your inheritance.**<-

---

**The king sent.** As it is written: "And Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they brought him hastily out of the dungeon" <note>Genesis 41:14</note>. The verse repeats the idea using different words. **He made him lord.** As it is written: "You shall be over my house" <note>Genesis 41:40</note>.

**To bind his princes by his soul.** The explanation is that there were high-ranking officials there, as if Pharaoh agreed to the "binding" or authority of Joseph. For so he said to him: "According to your word shall all my people be ruled; only in the throne will I be greater than you."

**His elders he made wise.** This means the sages would learn and become wise from him, and he would remove their confusion. This was because his wisdom was like the wisdom of God in Joseph. This is the explanation: when he was in the prison house, the sages of Pharaoh said that according to the calculations, Joseph was wiser than they were. And so Pharaoh said to him: "There is none as discreet and wise as you." This is written here as a song of praise. Its meaning is that Joseph was the wisest of the young men, for he had strength. Perhaps all of Egypt was included in this.

**And He increased His people.** This refers to the period after Joseph, when His kindness was extended to all of Israel among the people in the land of Egypt. As it is written: "They were fruitful and increased abundantly." **He turned their heart.** This means He changed the heart of the people to hate. **To deal craftily.** This refers to the nations plotting, though I do not see it exactly as the sages say. It refers to the change in the heart of the people from kindness to hatred.

**They set among them.** As it is written, He placed among them all the wonders He requested. **He sent darkness.** This means He sent it to darken, so they could not even see a black hole. He mentions the opening of the darkness. In the Midrash <note>Traditional Jewish homiletical interpretation.</note>, it says "they rebelled not against His word" because of the honor of the plague; even the angels of the chariot did not rebel against His word.

**He turned... and slew their fish.** The blood was in the living creatures in the water, and every living thing there died. **Their land swarmed.** He mentions the land because the plague was everywhere, as it says "in the chambers of their kings." This is also written regarding the firstborn and the plagues—they reached even the kings in their bedrooms.

**He gave them hail.** Even though it is written "with flame," it is as it says "fire ran along the ground." **He smote their vines.** He mentions the vine and the fig because they are the primary products of the land.

**He spread a cloud for a covering.** This means it was like a protective covering. This is the secret of the "pillar of cloud by day." The meaning of "covering" is not that it was dark above, but like a canopy to protect them. It is possible that "covering" includes protection for their possessions and their strength.

**He opened the rock.** Like a fountain. **They ran in the dry places like a river.** In a place of drought and wasteland, the waters went like a river. This was so great that the waters were many, even enough to carry a boat from one place to another.

**For He remembered.** He did all this for them in the merit of Abraham.

**And He brought forth His people with joy.** They were happy, and those coming after them were many. **His chosen ones.** Because of their excellence. **He gave them.** He did not do this only for honor, but so that they would be servants. He gave them the lands of the nations **that they might keep His statutes.** This is the ultimate purpose: He gave them the land so they would observe the Torah. As it is written: "To bring them to the land which I swore to their fathers." If they do not keep the statutes, they will be removed from the land.

**Who can express the mighty acts of the Lord.** This means, who can make them heard? In the previous psalm, he mentioned the work of the kingdom and what happened with Israel in Egypt. In this psalm (106), he mentions what He did with them in the wilderness and their rebellions. All these are signs for us. We are obligated to call out: "Who can express His mighty acts?" even for what was done in the wilderness. Who has the knowledge to tell all His praises? One should tell them in every generation. The poet comes to bless what the Holy One, blessed be He, did for us. **Blessed are those who keep judgment.** Every day one should tell of them. For a person does not always recognize the good done for him until after the fact. David said "all Your praises" because through the revealed miracles, His great name was sanctified. A person should realize the righteousness God does with them every day—even when a person goes to bed and the earth is hard, he wakes up and does not know what wonders the Holy One performed for him. Before the poet begins his story, he says:

**Blessed** are they who observe justice, who perform righteousness at all times. Remember me, O Lord, with the favor shown to Your people; visit me with Your salvation. To see the goodness of Your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of Your people, to glory with Your inheritance. We have sinned with our ancestors, we have acted perversely, we have done wickedly. Our ancestors in Egypt did not understand Your wonders; they did not remember the abundance of Your goodness, and they rebelled against Your <term>Memra</term><note>Aramaic for "Word," often used in the Targum to refer to God’s manifest presence or command without implying a physical form.</note> at the sea, the Sea of Reeds. <td width="50%">

<center>### **The Hebrew Masoretic Text**</center>

**Happy** are those who observe justice, who do righteousness at all times. Remember me, O Lord, in the favor of Your people; visit me with Your salvation. To see the goodness of Your chosen ones, to rejoice in the joy of Your nation, to glory with Your inheritance. We have sinned with our fathers, we have acted perversely, we have done wickedly. Our fathers in Egypt did not understand Your wonders; they did not remember the abundance of Your kindnesses, and they rebelled by the sea, at the Sea of Reeds. Yet He saved them for His name's sake, to make His power known. He rebuked the Sea of Reeds and it became dry; and He led them through the depths as through a wilderness. He saved them from the hand of the hater and redeemed them from the hand of the enemy. The waters covered their oppressors; not one of them remained. Then they believed His words; they sang His praise. They hurried and forgot His works; they did not wait for His counsel. They craved a craving in the wilderness and tested God in the wasteland. So He gave them their request, but sent a wasting disease into their soul. They were jealous of Moses in the camp, and of Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. The earth opened and swallowed Dathan, and covered the congregation of Abiram. A fire burned in their congregation; a flame consumed the wicked. They made a calf at Horeb and bowed down to a molten image. They exchanged their glory for the image of an ox that eats grass. They forgot God their Savior, who did great things in Egypt: wonders in the land of Ham, awesome things by the Sea of Reeds.

---

**Happy are those who observe justice**. This means: happy are you, O Israel, if you were to keep the laws of God which He commanded, for in the time that they did good, He did good with them. Even in the wilderness, though they sinned time after time, He would return and forgive them; "remember them for good at all times," meaning always. And so we find an interpretive tradition <note>original: "midrash aggadah"</note> in the *Torat Kohanim* <note>The Halakhic Midrash on Leviticus.</note>: Is it really possible for a person to perform righteousness "at all times"? Our rabbis in the center <note>likely referring to the scholars of the Babylonian academies</note> said: "This refers to one who raises an orphan within his house." Because of this, the text follows with: *Remember me, O Lord, in the favor of Your people*.

**Remember me, O Lord**. That is to say: remember for me and for my people that goodness and gift which You were accustomed to doing for Your people for their benefit. Note that in the Psalms, the word "at all times" is sometimes written without the letter *vav* or *yod* <note>Rabbinic commentary often notes small spelling variations in the Hebrew scrolls, which were believed to hold deeper meanings.</note>. These variations in spelling across the text often hint at specific times or conditions, such as the time of monarchy or the time of rest.

**To see the goodness of Your chosen ones**. This refers to seeing the well-being of the select of the people. This entire section is repeated often because the matter is clear: even in this long exile, whatever passes over us is not for nothing. Therefore, this is a matter of pride—even though in the majority of our deeds we transgressed in our security, we ask Him to remember us.

**To glory with Your inheritance**. There is a midrashic interpretation regarding the missing letters here. This "gift" refers to His rest, and that the youths did not stray. Similarly, our rabbis of blessed memory noted that "in your life" or "in your understanding" are sometimes written with missing letters to signal the Sabbath of your chosen one, whom You promised to teach Torah. Thus, they called the Temple a place of "walking" or "going," as in the verse "her virgins did not go."

**We have sinned**. The Psalmist mentions this on behalf of the children of the exile. **With our fathers**: we sinned in Egypt and in the wilderness. Every sinner eventually regrets it, but we did not merit our inheritance because of the iniquity in the wilderness.

**They did not remember the abundance of Your kindnesses**. For the kindnesses and wonders You performed with them in Egypt—the house of their kindness—and the protection of His judgments against the Egyptians, You made a distinction between them and the Egyptians. This was known throughout all the land. Yet they were like those who "repay evil for good."

**They rebelled by the sea, at the Sea of Reeds**. This is the plain meaning <term>peshat</term>. Regarding the merit of the children of the exile, they returned to the lack of order in these kindnesses. According to the children of Israel, they sinned among your people and in the writing of Jacob. They were called "the face of the poor" and "the root." After their sin, as the midrash on Egypt says, they were diminished.

**They rebelled by the sea, at the Sea of Reeds**. There are those who are in danger and do not remember. For one for whom all these wonders were performed in Egypt—how could they tremble and shake before the Egyptians and sink into such a state? This rebellion at the sea was because they were worried, saying, "Perhaps they will come upon us," etc. Some explain that they rebelled *inside* the sea itself. In the words of our Sages of blessed memory, they had doubts even as they descended into the Sea of Reeds. The Midrash says they rebelled against their very lives through hard labor with mortar and bricks, and even when they went down to the sea, they were fighting in the mud within the sea while the rest of Israel walked on dry land.

**He saved them for His name's sake**. He saved them from the Egyptians to make His kindness known before His people. That is to say, strengthen the Name that was rebelled against by our ancestors, so that it might be known to those who come after, to make His power known—just as He destroyed Pharaoh and all his army.

**He rebuked the Sea of Reeds and it dried up**. The "rebuke" is a hint at the way He moved the sea so that it became like a wilderness. He led them through the depths as through a wilderness, as it is written: "In the depths of the sea as in a desert."

**He saved them from the hand of the hater**. As it is written: "And the Lord saved Israel that day from the hand of the Egyptians."

**The waters covered their oppressors**. That is, the waters covered the Egyptians, as it is written: "And the waters were a wall for them on their right and on their left."

**Then they believed His words**. They believed in His Word <note>original: "Memra"</note>. As it is written: "And Israel saw the great hand... and they believed in the Lord and in Moses His servant." Now, this was a great good for my people Israel. They should have waited and anticipated what God would do for them, and not blocked their hearts, for He acted with a "wide hand and a high hand." As it says in the Psalm: "My Torah goes before my people." They should have sought out what God would do and not been stubborn. This is the meaning of "they did not wait for His counsel." They should have waited for the voice of their people, as we explained regarding the "mouth" at the mountain.

**He gave them their request, but sent leanness into their souls**. This refers to the strength of those who were sent. It uses the term "leanness" for their glory, because they thought to satisfy their souls and fatten them, but the result was the opposite.

**They were jealous of Moses**. As occurred in the wilderness during the rebellion. The jealousy mentioned here refers to the dispute of Korah. It was revealed to us that in all those days they suffered. There were also those from the tribe of Reuben with them, and therefore it mentions Israel and the sages waiting at Sinai. The reason Aaron is called "the holy one of the Lord" is because the rebels claimed "all the congregation are holy," but the Lord chose who was truly holy—and that was Aaron.

**The earth opened**. The future tense is used here in place of the past <note>A common feature in biblical Hebrew poetry</note>. It mentions the destruction of Korah's followers. Korah himself is remembered because he was among those swallowed up or consumed. Dathan and Abiram are mentioned as the leaders of the faction of the dispute. One of them, On son of Peleth, is not mentioned afterward because he regretted it and withdrew from the dispute.

**A fire burned**. It consumed the sinners among Israel, as it is written, "A fire came out from the Lord and consumed..."

**They made a calf at Horeb**. Again, the future tense is used for the past. They made a calf at the very place where they received the law of the Torah from Him at Sinai.

**They exchanged their glory**. They traded the Divine Presence for the image of an ox. They forgot God their Savior who did great things in Egypt—wonders that broke the very laws of nature. By the power of the water and His might, He showed the children of Ham His strength.

**And he said** <note>Catchword for the next page</note>

And He said by His Word <note>original: "Memra," the manifest Word of God</note> to destroy them, were it not for Moses His chosen one, who stood and strengthened himself in prayer before Him to turn back His wrath from destroying. And they grew distant from the desirable land; they did not believe in His words. And they murmured in their tents; they did not accept the Word of the Lord. And He lifted His hand in an oath not to cast them down as slain in the wilderness. And to exile their children among the nations and to scatter them among the lands. And they attached themselves to the error of Peor <note>The idol Baal-Peor</note> and ate the sacrifices of the dead <note>Idols, which are lifeless compared to the living God</note>. Many times He saved them, but they rebelled in their counsels and were brought low by their sins. And He saw their distress when He heard their prayer. And He remembered for them His covenant and relented from His anger in the abundance of His kindness. And He gave them over to mercy in the sight of all those who took them captive. The redeemed of the Lord shall say, those whom He redeemed from the hand of the oppressor, and from the lands...

And He said He would destroy them, had not Moses His chosen one stood in the breach before Him, to turn away His wrath from destroying. And they despised the pleasant land; they did not believe His word. And they murmured in their tents; they did not listen to the voice of the Lord. And He lifted His hand to them, to make them fall in the wilderness. And to make their descendants fall among the nations, and to scatter them among the lands. And they attached themselves to Baal-Peor, and ate the sacrifices of the dead. And they provoked Him with their deeds, and a plague broke out among them. And Phinehas stood up and executed judgment, and the plague was stayed. And it was accounted to him for righteousness to all generations forever. And they angered Him at the waters of Meribah, and it went ill for Moses on their account. For they embittered his spirit, and he spoke rashly with his lips. They did not destroy the peoples, as the Lord had commanded them. And they mingled with the nations and learned their works. And they served their idols, which became a snare to them. And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons. And they shed innocent blood, the blood of their sons and their daughters, whom they sacrificed to the idols of Canaan; and the land was polluted with blood. And they became unclean through their deeds, and played the harlot in their practices. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against His people, and He abhorred His inheritance. And He gave them into the hand of the nations, and those who hated them ruled over them. Their enemies also oppressed them, and they were brought into subjection under their hand. Many times He delivered them; but they were rebellious in their counsel, and were brought low through their iniquity. Nevertheless He regarded their distress, when He heard their cry. And He remembered for them His covenant, and repented according to the multitude of His mercies. He made them also to be pitied by all those who carried them captives. Save us, O Lord our God, and gather us from among the nations, to give thanks to Your holy name, and to triumph in Your praise. Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, from everlasting even to everlasting. And let all the people say: "Amen." Hallelujah.

### Give thanks 
to the Lord, for He is good; for His mercy endures forever. Let the redeemed of the Lord say so, whom He has redeemed from the hand of the adversary.

---

**And He said He would destroy them.** This means He specified the details of their sins, and Moses stood before Him, and so on. **And they murmured.** This is like "they turned about" and grumbled. **And He lifted His hand to them.** This refers to an oath, as in the phrase "For I lift up My hand to heaven." The meaning of "to them" is "on their account." **And to make their descendants fall among the nations, and to scatter them among the lands.** It is likewise written in Ezekiel: "I also lifted up My hand to them in the wilderness, that I would scatter them among the nations." This refers to this Psalm, and the intention was to say they were worthy of exile. Similarly, when it says "to make their descendants fall" regarding the future, it means: I did not lift My hand merely to bring them down, but to kill them in the wilderness—"in this wilderness your carcasses shall fall," etc. The explanation is that when it says "He lifted His hand to them to make them fall in the wilderness," it implies it was also fitting to say "and to make their descendants fall," etc. **And they attached themselves to Baal-Peor.** This is a term of attachment and joining. It means they were stuck to idolatry as if someone had fastened <note>original: "tzimid," like a bracelet or fastener</note> two things together. This is also found in the Torah portion regarding this event. **And ate the sacrifices of the dead.** Meaning the sacrifices of idols, which are dead and have no breath of life in them. **And a plague broke out among them.** Like a breach; the matter of the plague was like a breach of water, for the plague swept over them like a great river. **And Phinehas stood up and executed judgment.** He stood for judgment <note>Hebrew: "Palal," often translated as prayer, but here interpreted as a judicial act</note>. A term of judgment and law. **And it was accounted to him for righteousness.** As the Holy One, Blessed be He, explicitly said: "Behold, I give to him My covenant of peace; and it shall be to him and to his descendants after him the covenant of an everlasting priesthood." **And they angered Him at the waters of Meribah.** They provoked God until evil came upon Moses because of them. **For they embittered his spirit.** They embittered the spirit of the Holy One, Blessed be He. **And he spoke rashly with his lips.** An error came out of Moses' lips, for they lacked the strength of the glory of God, may He be blessed, and did not sanctify Him at the rock first, as the commentators say... **And they sacrificed their sons and their daughters to demons.** As it says in the Law of the Priests <note>Leviticus</note>: "And of your seed you shall not give to pass through to Molech," etc. The Psalm says this because they were sacrificing everything to demons and to idols, and it calls them "demons." **And the land was polluted with blood.** It became impure and soiled, for they were shedding innocent blood within it. **And they were brought low through their iniquity.** This also refers to the evil because of which they descended into poverty <note>Hebrew "Ani" / "Maku" linked to being brought low or impoverished</note>. On the great day of judgment, their merit will be seen alongside their sins... **Many times.** The Holy One, Blessed be He, explained that they would be saved from the Egyptians in war. **And He gave them over to mercy.** This explains that He will humble the hearts of their enemies and grant them mercy in their eyes. The Psalm covers every matter of the exile and the conclusion of the commandment of the Sukkah. **Blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel.** The Psalm concludes with giving thanks to the Lord's holy name and praising His glory. Since the Psalm is written in the language of exile, redemption, and supplications that the Holy One, Blessed be He, should gather us from among the nations to give thanks to His holy name. The fourth section is completed. This Psalm is a praise for the future redemption, and it is fitting to give thanks to the Lord, for it is the redemption that is greater than all others... The four who are required to give thanks and bless God, may He be blessed, on their journeys: those who have recovered from illness, prisoners, and so on. This Psalm calls them in the language of the humble, for this is to give thanks because His mercy is an eternal mercy. **Let the redeemed of the Lord say so.** Let the redeemed speak, and let it return to them... for in distress they shall speak.

<summary>This page concludes Psalm 106, recounting Israel's sins and God's mercy throughout the wilderness and early settlement periods, ending with a prayer for gathering the exiles. It then begins Psalm 107 (Book Five), which introduces the theme of the "four who must give thanks" for deliverance from various perils.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the historical retelling of Israel’s rebellions in Psalm 106 to the opening of Psalm 107. This new psalm introduces a liturgical framework for four specific groups of people—wanderers in the desert, prisoners, the sick, and seafarers—to offer thanks to God for their deliverance.</meta>

<center>### **The Hebrew Scripture**</center>

<margin>In distress</margin> and from the north: and from the lands He gathered them, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea. They wandered in the wilderness in a desert way; they found no city to dwell in. Hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them.

And they cried out to the Lord in their trouble; He delivered them from their distresses. And He led them by a straight way, to go to a city of habitation. Let them give thanks to the Lord for His goodness, and for His wonders to the children of men!

For He satisfies the longing soul, and the hungry soul He fills with good. Such as sit in darkness and in the shadow of death, being bound in affliction and iron; because they rebelled against the words of God, and condemned the counsel of the Most High. Therefore He brought down their heart with labor; they fell down, and there was none to help. And they cried out to the Lord in their trouble; He saved them from their distresses.

He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and broke their bonds asunder. Let them give thanks to the Lord for His goodness, and for His wonders to the children of men! For He has broken the doors of bronze, and cut the bars of iron in sunder.

<margin>Distresses</margin> Fools, because of their transgression and because of their iniquities, are afflicted. Their soul loathes all manner of food; and they draw near to the gates of death. And they cry out to the Lord in their trouble; He saves them from their distresses.

He sends His word and heals them, and delivers them from their destructions. Let them give thanks to the Lord <margin>Him</margin> for His goodness, and for His wonders to the children of men! And let them sacrifice the sacrifices of thanksgiving, and declare His works with rejoicing.

<margin>Work</margin> Those who go down to the sea in ships, who do business in great waters; these see the works of the Lord, and His wonders in the deep. For He speaks and raises the stormy wind, which lifts up the waves thereof.

<center>### **The Aramaic Translation (Targum)**</center>

And from the lands He gathered them, from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea of the south. The people of the House of Israel wandered; they were forgotten and hidden in the desolate desert; the path to the daughter of the city <note>original: "Berata," often used to refer to a daughter-city or suburb</note> of the habitation that is built <note>referring to Jerusalem</note> they did not find. In the evening they saw that they were thirsty; their souls were desolate. And they prayed before the Lord when they had trouble; from their distresses He delivered them. And He led them in a straight path to go to Jerusalem, the city that is built.

They shall give thanks before the Lord for His kindness, and His praise to the sons of men. For He satisfied the empty soul, and the hungry soul He filled with good. Concerning Zedekiah and the nobles of Israel he prophesied and said: those who were exiled and the skulls <note>meaning the individuals</note> of Israel who were exiled to Babylon and sat in darkness and the shadow of death, and were bound in shackles of iron. Because they rebelled against the Word of God <note>original: "Memra"</note> and the word of the Most High they pushed away. And He broke their heart with labor; they stumbled and there was no helper. And they prayed before the Lord in the time they had trouble; from their distresses He redeemed them.

He brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death, and their chains He shall snap. They shall give thanks before the Lord for His kindness and His praise to the sons of men. For He broke the doors of bronze and the bars of iron He cut. Concerning King Hezekiah <note>The Targum applies these verses to King Hezekiah of Judah</note>, who praised because the house of Judah was saved, he prophesied and said: for the leaders of the house of Judah saw that they rebelled by taking a woman of inheritance <note>referring to a specific historical/legal dispute regarding marriage and property</note>... like this they shall be judged, and for their iniquities they shall be afflicted. All food their soul pushed away, and they reached until the entrance of death. And they prayed before the Lord when they had trouble; from their distresses He redeemed them.

He shall send the words of His healing and heal them, and rescue from their destruction. They shall give thanks before the Lord for His kindness and His praise to the sons of men. And they shall sacrifice sacrifices of thanksgiving and tell of His works with praise. Concerning the sailors who went out into the sea, he prophesied and said: sailors in ships who perform service in great waters. They saw the works of the Lord and His wonders in the depths. And He said by His Word and raised the storm and the whirlwind, and its waves were lifted up.

<column-break/>

**And from the lands He gathered them.** He begins with these because they are gathered as more than just a family. It is the nature of human feet to walk the paths of the way, and those who cross the ways of the wilderness and sands will be gathered by His kindnesses from the East and the West, where they went to dwell, and he returns them to Jerusalem, a place of safety. He mentions the edges: East, West, North, and "the Sea," which is the Western Sea for all the Land of Israel; "the Sea" is mentioned in place of the South because the sea stops one from walking there... he mentions the Great Sea, called the Sea of Sand, for in its way is a place of sand, not the open sea for ships... and he says "and the sea" because the Easterners call the South "the Sea." Thus he begins by mentioning that from the four winds they shall be gathered from every place.

**They wandered in the wilderness.** He mentions that everyone went not just through the wilderness: this is one of the groups he counts. He mentions "in a desert way," for the desert paths are covered by the blowing wind and mud, and they cannot find a path to go to a city of habitation to settle there.

**Hungry and thirsty.** Because they are seeking shelter in the desert ways and were lacking bread and water according to the journey's needs. For in the wilderness one finds neither life nor food to eat. And behold, while they were toiling... they were hungry and also thirsty, their soul fainted from the event of hunger and thirst...

**And they cried out to the Lord.** As is the way, for men when they are on the road... he reveals to them the way they had wandered from.

**And He led them by a path.** When He hears, He establishes them toward a city of habitation and distances them from obstacles, and a crooked path He makes straight for them... these are the groups who are under the kindness of the Lord, may He be blessed.

**For He satisfies the longing soul.** This refers to a lack of Torah and wisdom, for the Torah is compared to water. A lack of wisdom is worse than a hunger for water, for it is a hunger to hear the words of the Lord. Similarly, a wise man who is full of wisdom is satisfied...

**Dwellers in darkness and the shadow of death.** Now the verse mentions the second group: those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death and iron, meaning prisoners of affliction and iron. "Dwellers in darkness" refers to a pit or a prison, and he calls it "the shadow of death" because it is dark... and iron refers to the chains and copper that would bind their feet and hands. And why? "Because they rebelled against the words of God." Behold, they suffer because of their sins according to their rebellion... Know that these afflictions, all of them in iron, are because they rebelled against the commandments... and they despised the word of the Lord. And this perversion of theirs he mentions as being in the place of the blow. Because of their rebellion against the Tablets <note>The Ten Commandments</note>... they are caught in the obstacles of iniquity... and they cry out to heaven...

**And He humbled their heart with labor.** Our sages established this verse and wrote that their heart was humbled with labor, like the labor of the surroundings...

**And they cried out to the Lord.** To call unto the Lord, blessed be He, to save them...

**And He brought them out.** He rescued them... sometimes from a pit and sometimes from the outside.

**He brought them out of darkness.** He continues the general rule and mentions the time of Hezekiah and the mighty wise men and his scribes... He sends His word and heals them...

**Let them give thanks... and sacrifice sacrifices of thanksgiving.** He mentions the conduct of the upright and the pious of the Name... they should bring burnt offerings... so that they may live with a good heart...

**Let them give thanks to the Lord for His kindness.** When they give thanks from the book <note>The Torah or Psalms</note>, they shall tell to the children of men of the wonders He did for them. And what are the wonders? **For He has broken the doors of bronze, etc.** Men, to strengthen their defenses in a fortified city, use doors and bars. But through His strength... He brings about the breaking of the prison and even if the doors of iron and the bars are strong.

**Fools.** Now he mentions the sick. And he says that from the way of their transgression and their iniquities they are afflicted and worn down. He calls them "fools" <unclear>...</unclear> because their sickness is heavy day after day. They are sick in brain and temperament... and they do not conduct themselves [properly] like those whose brains are sickened by the evil they brought on themselves... until the sickness overwhelms them...

**Their soul loathes all food.** <unclear>...</unclear> as one who draws near to the gates of death... for the smell [of food] does not help them, nor the doctor or investigation.

**He delivers their soul from the pit.** As those who are sick <unclear>...</unclear> His word will be their cure... "He delivers them from their destructions," he mentions this because they caused this through their own sin.

**Let them give thanks.** Explanation: publicize it. And they shall sacrifice sacrifices of thanksgiving... he concludes that this is a law for those who received kindnesses... so that they may complete their days in health. And they shall tell of it with their mouths...

**And declare His works with rejoicing.** They shall tell the children of men of the acts of kindness He performed, with a voice of rejoicing and a great voice.

**Those who go down to the sea in ships.** One who goes on dry land is called a traveler, but one who comes in a ship is called "one who goes down" <note>Hebrew: "Yorei Hayam"</note>... as it says "those who go down to the sea"... they saw and confessed and feared the Lord... and the sea is called "great waters" because it is vast.

**These see.** In the "deep," in the depths of the sea, a place that is clear, there they see the works of the Lord and His wonders. For in the breadth of the colors they recognize the sea... This is the explanation.

**He spoke and raised.** God said: meaning He willed and decreed, and He raised a storm wind... the wind raises the waves of the sea... and then the ship goes up and down.

<center>### **The Hebrew Scripture**</center>

They mount up to the heavens, they go down to the depths; their soul melts away in their misery. They reel and stagger like a drunkard, and all their wisdom is swallowed up. Then they cry to the Lord in their trouble, and He brings them out of their distresses. He stills the storm to a calm, and the waves thereof are hushed. He turns rivers into a wilderness, and watersprings into a thirsty ground; a fruitful land into a salt waste, for the wickedness of them that dwell therein. He turns a wilderness into a pool of water, and a dry land into watersprings. And there He makes the hungry to dwell, and they establish a city of habitation; and sow fields, and plant vineyards, and yield fruits of increase. 

He blesses them also, so that they multiply greatly, and He suffers not their cattle to decrease. Again, they are diminished and brought low through oppression, evil, and sorrow. <column-break/>

->From the emergence of the separated "I shall be" <note>This likely refers to a mystical or grammatical interpretation of the divine name</note> and they shall understand His mercies.<-

**They mount up to the heavens, they go down to the depths.** The "sages of the ship" <note>The sailors or navigators</note> rise from it. That is to say, when the sand is high, the wave lifts the ship, and afterwards, as the wave passes, they go down to the depths. And the descent is difficult upon it. 

**Their soul melts away in their misery.** Meaning, their soul dissolves from the fear of drowning and the descent into the great waters, for the ship spins in a circle in the sea. **They reel and stagger like a drunkard.** They circle and move in every direction during the festival <note>The commentator links the Hebrew word for "reeling" (*yahogu*) with the word for "festival" (*hag*), suggesting a circular movement or dance</note>. For "to reel" is a matter of movement. Like the phrase "it shall be a festival for your generations." The ship is tossed and circles in the sea, and because of it, those in the ship are moved and they <unclear>struggle</unclear> to stay steady. The "sages of the ship" and the weak sailors are unable to stand before the stormy wind that grips the ship and moves it up and down. 

**And all their wisdom is swallowed up.** All the wisdom of the captain and his tactics, and the wisdom of those who watch the storm. For with all their wisdom and tactics, they cannot keep the ship steady because the storm surrounds them. **And they cry.** They are able <note>meaning, they have no other recourse</note>. The explanation is: from the sea to the dry land. They cry out from their poverty and their affliction. 

**He stills the storm to a calm.** "Stills" <note>original: yakem</note> is like "He restores." The storm that He raised, He returns to silence. **And the waves thereof are hushed.** This refers to the sailors. The **waves** that were rising against them were silenced and quieted from their lifting and moving. 

**Let them exalt Him in the congregation of the people.** They shall exalt His name. This refers to the gathering of the masses. **And in the seat of the elders.** The sages and those who sit in judgment. They shall praise His kindness and His dominion. 

**He turns rivers into a wilderness.** The moral of the psalm was a desert of acquisitions. He turns the waters into salt land because of the wickedness of the inhabitants. **He turns a wilderness.** Behold, He will turn the desert into a place of water. **And there He makes the hungry to dwell.** Those who were hungry in another place, He settles them in this place which has become good. **And they establish a city of habitation.** They build a city there because the hungry have come and settled there. 

**And sow fields.** They sowed fields and vineyards and produced fruit, for the blessings were made. **And He blesses them.** Through the harvest. **And their cattle did not decrease.** Everything increased. **Again, they are diminished and brought low.** Behold, when they forget God, there will be a lack of money/property. This is the "evil" mentioned above: "because of the wickedness of them that dwell therein." They are diminished, the opposite of "multiplying greatly." **And brought low.** The opposite of being happy. **Through oppression, evil, and sorrow.** From the lack of goodness. **He pours contempt upon princes.** Upon the wealthy and honored man who once was great and is now poor. He wanders in the waste. 

**Yet He sets the needy on high.** He elevates the poor and the humble. **And makes families like a flock.** The opposite of being diminished. He will give them families as numerous as a flock. 

**The upright shall see.** They shall see the punishment of the wicked and rejoice. **And all iniquity shall stop her mouth.** Every man of iniquity will have his mouth closed when he sees the hand of God striking the wicked. **Whoso is wise, let him observe these things.** Whoever is wise will keep these things in his heart and recognize that this is from the hand of God. **And they shall consider the loving-kindness of the Lord.** They will understand and be glad in this understanding.

---

**A Song, a Psalm of David.** This psalm is written at the end of Psalm 60. There it is written about the war with Aram-Naharaim and Aram-Zobah. And from those verses, he remembered God. This psalm refers to the future. Therefore, he did not mention the great war here. The sages say this psalm refers to the gathering of the exiles. David rejoiced over the portions that the kings of the nations had taken from them. This is why he mentions Shechem and the Valley of Succoth and Gilead and Manasseh, which refer to the Kingdom of Joseph, written as a future promise under the King of Judah. As it is written in Ezekiel: "And I will make them one nation... and my servant David shall be king over them."

<center># Psalms</center>

### 108

**The Aramaic Translation (Targum)**

A praise, a song, and a hymn at the beginning: I will praise You before the nations, O Lord, and I will sing to You among the kingdoms. For Your goodness is great above the heavens, and Your truth reaches the skies. Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and Your glory over all the earth. So that Your beloved ones may be delivered from before You, save with Your right hand and answer me. God spoke in the place of His Divine Presence <note>original: "Beit Shekhinteh," the Temple</note>: I will bring forth, I will divide Shechem, and the valley of Succoth I will measure. Gilead is mine and Manasseh is mine, and the house of Ephraim is the strength of my head, and from the house of Judah comes my scribe. They serve before me like spears. Moab is like the basin of a wash-pot. On the kingdom of Edom I will pull off my sandal; over the Philistines I will shout. Who will lead me to the city of <unclear>Uvli</unclear>, even to the fortress of Rome the wicked? <note>The Aramaic translator identifies Edom with the Roman Empire</note> Who will lead me even to Constantinople <note>original: "Konstantina"</note> of Edom? Have You not, O God, distanced us? And Your Presence does not go out with our armies. Give us help from the oppressor, for the redemption of man is nothing. Through God we shall do valiantly, and He will tread down our oppressors.

For the praise by the hand of David: A hymn. O God of my praise, do not be silent. For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit they opened against me; they spoke with me with a lying tongue. And words of hatred they turned against me, and they fought with me without cause. In exchange for my love, they accused me, but I pray. And they placed evil upon me in exchange for good, and hatred in exchange for my love. Appoint a wicked man over him, and an adversary <note>Satan</note> shall stand at his right hand. In his judgment, let him come out guilty, and let his prayer be for a debt. Let his days be few, fewer than his years; let another inherit his position. Let his children be orphans and his wife a widow. And let his children be wanderers, wandering and asking from their ruins. Let the creditor entrap everything he has, and let strangers plunder his toil. Let there be no one to extend kindness to him, and let no one have pity on his orphans. Let his end be... they shall be...

---

**Commentary**

**Awake, harp.** This is a metaphor. Does the harp wake by itself? Is there any force in it? It is strengthened for all. The dawn is a form. Mercy wakes everything. Wake the lyre at the time of waking from the city <note>perhaps referring to the early morning prayers in Jerusalem</note> to say "hurry" and "quickly." This is prepared for the time when the kings of the nations benefit from wine... and I will praise You among the nations, O Lord. Through your poverty they will be strengthened in wars, like the families of Israel. As it is written, "Nations shall call to the mountain." I will praise You with melodies among Your people. In this psalm, all the nations are explained, for all nations will take their portion at the time of the Redemption. As it is written: "And many nations shall go to the Lord, to the house of our God." Among the peoples: between the nations and the kingdoms they shall live...

...The mercy is greater than any nation can describe. Even though they have served in this exile for many years and all the sects are against you, the Lord will establish the redemption from under their hands, and they shall inherit their portion and their property against their will. Furthermore, the merit of Israel and all the glory of Israel is Your light and Your strength... This mercy is great, from tomorrow until forever...

**For the leader. A psalm of David. O God of my praise, do not be silent.** David composed this psalm when he was fleeing from Saul. And in those days, there were wise men who spoke evil against him... He said, "O God of my praise, do not be silent," meaning: in You I trust, my God, do not be quiet while they blaspheme... I call to You all night. **For the mouth of the wicked and the mouth of deceit have they opened against me.** The mouth of Edom is deceit. They opened their mouths against me with evil and spoke with tongues of deceit against my honor... **And they fought against me.** Like those who fight with me, yet I am for peace. **But I am prayer.** I am a man of prayer. Just as one might say "I am all peace" or "I am all song." Meaning, when they are angry with me, my heart is turned to prayer... **Appoint a wicked man over him.** Let a wicked person rule over him. **And let an accuser stand at his right hand.** An angel of accusation shall stand at his right hand to accuse him, meaning his plans for redemption will fail. He speaks in the singular about the chief of the enemies who pursued him...

**When he is judged.** If he has a trial with another person, let him come out guilty... **And let his prayer become a sin.** When he prays for his people, let it not be considered a merit for him, but a sin... **Let his days be few.** His "office" (the thing entrusted to him) is either his money or his wife. **Let his children be orphans.** Young orphans. **And let his children wander.** Like a nomad who wanders for bread... **Let the creditor strike.** Like a trap that takes everything from him... Because he said "let them beg for bread," they will be prevented from the kindness usually shown to children... **Let his posterity be cut off.** Meaning his children. Let them be cut off from every place... therefore it says: **Let the iniquity of his fathers be remembered.** Let the sins of his ancestors be visited upon him, as it is written: "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children."

## A Psalm of David. The Lord says to my lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet."
### The Lord shall send the rod of your strength out of Zion; rule in the midst of your enemies.
### Your people shall be willing in the day of your power, in the beauties of holiness from the womb of the morning: you have the dew of your youth. <margin>In beauties</margin> <margin>Your youth</margin>
### The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek."

"Let the iniquity of his fathers be"—and let the iniquity and the sin be before the Name [God] as it says "let it be remembered." This matter is doubled for emphasis. And so "let them be before the Lord continually," and likewise "the iniquity of his fathers." The explanation of this psalm: my heart almost says that it is possible to interpret it regarding the Patriarchs and the generation of the desert. It is explained that this wicked person and his fathers did not learn from their ancestors to remember to perform kindness, but instead pursued the poor and needy. The phrase "broken-hearted" refers to a person standing up for himself, his children, and his pious ones, and thus is his heart. The statement is about himself and his company. He considered this a curse and therefore desired it as a blessing. The past tense is used here in place of the future. The explanation is that it shall "come upon him like water in my inward parts." Water goes to the place of those who descend. Such is the statement: "war, etc." "And he wrapped himself," because he wrapped himself and put on a garment. "Like his mantle," his clothing—meaning the measurements of the wrap that surrounds his body. And so "it shall come into him," like water in the midst of the intestines. "Like oil in his bones"—these are like the fluids of bone wounds caused by a cessation in the bones from a blow. Thus they are like a kind of oil in his bones. "Like water"—in the intestines. "Like water from the hearts." And in its midst, like water in his bowels. It lacks the letter *Vav*. Just as you would say "let them be a blessing upon us," like the sand of the sea. Kindnesses shall come, and from them the bones instead of water and oil. Like the order of companions. Behold, kindness is upon him. As the statement moves through four levels, descending and ascending. That is to say, behold, this will be in bitterness. "As a covering," like a wrapping garment. That is to say, behold, it will be like the belt, like the cloak that occupies the place of the "measure" of the thing due to a curse. "As the waters of kindness" of the pious of the Lord, from the kindness of Your name rescue me. And because of the Queen, for so shall be the kindness; Your kindness is good for me, "wounded in my midst"—meaning my heart is profaned and torn within me from the multitude of my troubles. And so all my bones. "Like a shadow," "as it declines"—like the stretching of the afternoon shadow, which is a complete walking in vain, similar to the matter of "like a passing shadow." "And he shall fly," "as the locust"—from place to place in a jump, as they push the locust from place to place by the wind. The letter *Kaph* from "and like a bird wandering." For since he has no dwelling in the evening in the place of residence, he is hollow in the wind, etc., like a locust from place to place. Everything is regarding moving from place to place. Due to fasting, from much pain and distress, and "my flesh, etc." and it became thin from the fat and regarding the oil. That is to say, behold, from the fatness his face became haggard. The fat "they shake their head" in mockery, Heaven forbid. They shall recognize that in this trouble of mine, it came upon me because of Your kindness. "Through it, into the gate for me," for because of You, Your mercies reached me, "open for me." Your pious ones opened the holy covenant and established it for me, and they arose and were blessed. They are the ones judged, and not the Lord who performed all this. Words of joy and my glory. What is a curse from a blessing in the service of the heart to them; they shall be ashamed and they shall be "he shall rejoice." Instead of the reproach, to bind them, and as their comforter, milk in blessing like meditating on myrrh. "Disgrace"—and how shall they be clothed? What is this kindness? And do good from the ruins of sin. "Your reproach." Be muzzled, etc., and the matter is for them to be comforted. "And they shall sing" is missing a letter. And like a gift to a scorpion from which strength is taken for their blessings and for their places. What is with them? "And they fought me" is missing a letter. "And my palate is prayer." Visions... the palate close to the surroundings of his image. And life is divided among them. From His hand in the psalm. A hole instead of the knife, silence and my filters.

### For David
A psalm founded upon Joshua <note>Or "Salvation"</note> until "at my right hand, until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet." This psalm was previously interpreted by our Rabbis of blessed memory as referring to Abraham our father, as written elsewhere. "With your army in the day of your power." They explained it as a supreme sheath, for the priesthood was worthy to belong to Melchizedek. "My strength is lacking," a priest to the Most High God. "Profaned," the mouth here sanctifies with his blessing to Abraham, not to this high one. The judgment opened... the priesthood was taken from him and given to Abraham. Support: "You are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek"—concerning the word spoken by Melchizedek. According to the plain meaning of the verses, they refer to David. One of the singers said it about him, and taught to say "to my lord." So too "A Psalm for David" is written later. Like "our dismissal to the king." A wise man said it about David, for the Lord will see comfort at the beginning of his kingdom, according to its literal meaning—his kingdom because of the generation for the king, and vines shall grow... And He promised him that His house should rest and His hand be given over the Persians, and when Rephaiah dies. And for him is the kindness of the psalm. "The Lord said to my lord"—meaning, the Holy One, blessed be He, said to my lord David, "Sit at my right hand." For it shall be... behold, he was in the promise at His right hand. "For My right hand shall support you," and the sword of your trained men shall not depart. "The rod of your strength He shall send, etc." For in His refuge, the power of David was partitioned in the congregations of his kingdom. The rod and the staff are from the side of the Lord. From it, He began to build the generation of the kingdom of kindness, strong and visionary to achieve... the land... "the dew of your youth." "In the midst of your gods" <note>Hebrew: *Eloheicha*</note> between gods, for in the midst of the kingdom which is appointed with great priesthood... "Your people are willing in the day of your power"—on the day you shall be a force to fight... "In the beauties of holiness"—explanation: that holy place is like congregations to descend to the sanctuary. "Beauties" is a matter of majesty and beauty. And so "in beauties" shall be the girdle, the power of majesty. For in many ways, the power of majesty is good. And the Lord will add... kindness to you, the dew of your youth. Some skip "from the womb of the morning, to you the dew of your youth"—meaning, your youth taught you. The language "the dew of your youth" refers to them living as the dew... meaning from the womb it goes out to the kingdom, and the dew of blessing is yours... in the strengthening of the rod... to revive them. "A priest"—just as it is written, David's sons were priests <note>referencing 2 Samuel 8:18</note>. The priest leads the psalm among the many and in peace. "Forever"—for life was forgiven him for his rule. "After the order of Melchizedek"—and for him the bitterness of your covenant, a king forever, because he was first a king of righteousness <note>Melchizedek means "King of Righteousness"</note>. As it is written of him: "And David executed judgment and righteousness for all his people." And this is "my word" and "my king" in these places.

- 1: Hallelujah! I will praise before the Lord with all my heart, in the secret of the upright and in the assembly.
- 2: Great are the works of the Lord, to be sought out for all His desires.
- 3: Splendor and praise is His work, and His merit stands for the world of worlds.
- 4: He made a memorial for His wonders; the Lord is gracious and compassionate.
- 5: Sustenance He gave to those who fear Him; He will remember His covenant forever.
- 6: The strength of His works He told to His people, to give them the inheritance of the nations.
- 7: The works of His hands are truth and judgment; all His commands are faithful.
- 8: Sustained for the world of worlds, they are made in truth and uprightness.
- 9: Redemption He sent to His people; He commanded His covenant forever; holy and awesome is His name.
- 10: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord; a good mind to all who do them; His praise stands for the world of worlds.

# Hallelujah

->The Lord at your right hand: The Lord is at your right hand as a comforter in wars. He shatters kings on the day of His wrath: This refers to the shattering of the kings of Canaan who rose up to fight against you. On the day of His wrath: meaning that day was a time of fierce anger against them, and He cut them off and uprooted them. He will judge among the nations: Jacob <note>likely referring to the nation of Israel</note> will judge and pass sentence among the nations who survived the war. Full of corpses: meaning dead bodies. Shatters the head over a broad land: He shatters the many kings over the land. And "head" refers to a king. From the brook by the way: mention is made of a miracle of strength, like the first of the holy ones. And some specify "great" <note>Hebrew: *rabbah*</note> as referring to a specific king of the Ammonites. Regarding this war, this verse was said: From the brook by the way he will drink. His kingdom is so strong that even when he travels through the desert, he drinks on the way from a brook—meaning God's protection follows him. Therefore he will lift up his head: Therefore, when all the wars that destroy the wicked are concluded, He will lift up our heads. So too it returns to the generation and its house... to lift up his head like a prophet and an elder, etc.<-

# Hallelujah

->I will thank the Lord with all my heart in the counsel of the upright and the congregation: This psalm is arranged according to the letters of the alphabet <note>original: *Aleph-Bet*</note>... because this psalm already established its theme in recounting the words of the Creator, to constantly mention His commandments, testimonies, and mighty deeds. It is said that Isaac <note>possibly Isaac Caro or another commentator</note> labored in this. Every psalm said in alphabetical order... "Hallelujah" is part of the melody... With all the intention of the heart. In the counsel of the upright and the congregation: In the assembly of the upright. The upright ones are those who occupy themselves with the Lord and the houses of study. Great are the deeds of the Lord: This is the beginning of the psalm. All the works of creation are great. Sought out by all who delight in them: Meaning, for anyone who desires to reflect upon them, they are found to be worth seeking and are accepted. Upon them falls the desire of the elders... Majesty and splendor: Just as His work is eternal, so is the strength of His majesty and splendor. He made a memorial: He made a memorial of His graciousness to teach those who see His wonders... He tells of His deeds... and tells that He made a memorial for His people for His wonders... and those were the beginning of the wonders. These wonders were so great they are remembered in every generation. The Lord is gracious and compassionate: For He was gracious to them and had mercy on them. One may also interpret "He made a memorial" to mean that He acts with them in every generation as a reminder of the wonders He performed in Egypt... He gave prey: For He provided their sustenance... He remembers His covenant forever: He remembers the covenant made with Abraham... The power of His works: To tell the wisdom of His turns <note>likely cycles of nature or history</note> to them, to know His wonders and His might... giving them the inheritance of nations. For His strength was so great... the sages said that it is more powerful for a king to rule over Israel... He told them before it happened. And so He did... The works of His hands: These were done in the wars of the nations... it was all truth and judgment. Truth, because He promised it to Abraham our father. Judgment, because it was a just sentence against the inhabitants of the land due to their evil deeds... for the sin of the Amorites was not yet full... faithful are all His precepts: Not only these, but all His commandments are faithful and without injustice. Sustained forever and ever: For they will never pass away or falter, because they are established in truth and the path of uprightness... Redemption He sent to His people: He sent them redemption and commanded His covenant forever... Therefore they shall praise Him and be holy, for He is holy... The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord: The first step of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. He tells them this... The fear of the Lord is the price of the Torah and the commandments. Wisdom is the wisdom of investigation and the knowledge of the work of creation, which is the service of God, for through it man recognizes his Creator. Therefore he said "to all who perform them." When one joins wisdom with the specific commandments... he will cling to the blessed God... for one who does not know Him cannot truly fear Him. This verse places the fear of the Lord before wisdom to say that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. It means that one who intends to occupy his heart with wisdom should first occupy himself with the fear of the Lord and make it his root and essence. On this path, the wisdom he learns will draw him closer. As our Rabbis of blessed memory said: "Whosoever's fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures; but whosoever's wisdom precedes his fear of sin, his wisdom does not endure." If a man says he will study the wisdom of investigation or philosophy first... he might misunderstand the great secrets in the Holy Scriptures. Therefore, one must first learn the Torah, which is the "fear of the Lord," and establish in his heart to believe everything written in it regarding the creation of the world and the changing of nature through signs and wonders. Then he may reflect on the Torah and see the ways of wisdom within it, as it is written: "For this is your wisdom and understanding in the eyes of the nations." For it is unnecessary to say that the Torah and commandments are in accordance with reason, for even the statutes <note>original: *chukim*, laws without obvious rationales</note>... the wise man who reflects on them will find their reason clear and selected. After the wise man reflects on the words of the Torah and rejoices... he can then learn philosophy, and it will not damage his faith because he learned the Torah first. He will recognize the guidance of the Creator... Therefore it is said: The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. And "good understanding to all who perform them" means a good result and a good find for the soul... His praise stands forever: For the one who acts uprightly and keeps the Torah... his praise will be in the mouths of the wise, a memory for generations, and finally it stands for the world to come. This verse has been further explained in the beginning of the commentary on the book. Hallelujah.<-
