# Proverbs

->Page 155<-

**Aramaic Translation (Targum)** | **Hebrew Source Text**
:--- | :---
Why then is this price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, when he has no heart or wisdom? | Why is there a price in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, when he has no heart?
At all times a man is beloved, and a brother is born for trouble. | At all times a friend loves, and a brother is born for adversity.
A man lacking in reason <note>original: "ra'yona," meaning thought or mind</note> shakes hands and becomes a guarantor for his companion. | A man void of heart <note>In biblical Hebrew, "heart" (lev) refers to the seat of intellect and will.</note> strikes hands and becomes a guarantor before his friend.
He who loves sin loves strife, and he who raises his gate seeks destruction. | He who loves transgression loves strife; he who makes his gate high seeks destruction.
He who has a crooked heart finds no good, and he who is perverse in his tongue falls into evil. | He whose heart is perverse finds no good, and he who is wayward in his tongue falls into calamity.
He who begets a fool, it is a bitterness to him; and the father of a fool <note>original: "tapsha," a dullard</note> has no joy. | He who begets a fool does so to his sorrow, and the father of a churl has no joy.
A joyful heart makes the body beautiful, but a broken spirit dries the bones. | A merry heart does good like a medicine, but a broken spirit dries the bones.
A wicked man receives a bribe from his bosom to pervert the paths of justice. | A wicked man takes a bribe out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.
The face of the understanding man rejoices in wisdom, but the eyes of a fool are in the depths of the earth. | Wisdom is before him who has understanding, but the eyes of a fool are in the ends of the earth.
A foolish son causes his father to weep and is bitterness to her who bore him. | A foolish son is a grief to his father and bitterness to her who bore him.
Even to punish the righteous is not good, nor to strike the noble who maintain uprightness. | Also to punish the righteous is not good, nor to strike nobles for their uprightness.
He who spares his words knows knowledge, and he of a cool spirit is a man of understanding. | He who has knowledge spares his words, and a man of understanding is of a precious spirit.
Even a fool, when he is silent, is considered wise; and he who shuts his lips is discerning. | Even a fool, when he holds his peace, is counted wise; and he who shuts his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.
Desire seeks the simpleton, and in every reproach he is exposed. | He who separates himself seeks his own desire; he quarrels against all sound wisdom.
A fool does not desire understanding, but only to reveal his heart. | A fool has no delight in understanding, but only that his heart may reveal itself.
When the wicked comes, contempt and lack come, and with the bosom <note>likely a scribal error for "disgrace"</note> comes deficiency. | When the wicked comes, then comes also contempt, and with ignominy comes reproach.
The words of a man’s mouth are deep waters; a flowing stream is the source of wisdom. | The words of a man's mouth are as deep waters, and the wellspring of wisdom as a flowing brook.
To favor the wicked is not good, nor to pervert the judgment of the righteous. | It is not good to accept the person of the wicked, to overthrow the righteous in judgment.

<column-break/>

<margin>
At all times a lover and a heart...
</margin>

### Commentary

**Why is there a price?** This describes the utility of money, which is a tool to acquire all virtues. The <term>price/merit</term> <note>original: "mekhes," usually meaning tax or customs, but here used by the commentator to mean the value or money in hand</note> that is in the hand of fools is a void thing, for they do not intend to buy wisdom with it, since they lack a "heart" for true knowledge. Their material substance is weak and only strong in the trait of physical desire. The wisdom of thought and the substance of actions must be constant despite the many accidents that befall the human species.

**At all times a friend loves.** This refers to the wisdom of wealth and its substance, and this <term>price</term> is among the constant matters in human life. It refers to the commerce that depends on human relationships. The <term>price</term> that stands for a man in his time of trouble is his money. This is the law described above regarding the traits of commerce, friendship, and peace.

**A man void of heart.** This refers to the fool who involves himself in things that have no utility. He "strikes hands" <note>a gesture of closing a deal or guarantee</note> to guarantee his friend's debt. The writer notes that he gives himself over as a guarantor for his companion, yet the text says one who loves transgression loves strife. When the fool brings his own shame, it stems from these guarantees. He seeks strife because he is arrogant and avoids paying what he owes.

**A merry heart.** "Medicine" <note>original: "gehah"</note> is a term for healing. When the heart is joyful and strong, any wisdom or medicine applied to the body is accepted more readily, and the body finds utility in it. **But a broken spirit.** This dries the "marrow of wisdom." If a person is constantly in a state of mourning or brokenness, their physical substance wastes away and they cannot attain intellectual perfection.

**A bribe from the bosom.** This refers to one who perverts justice in secret. The wicked man takes the bribe "from the bosom," meaning in a hidden manner, so as to pervert the <term>commerce of justice</term>.

**Wisdom is before him who has understanding.** The understanding man has his wisdom prepared and ready to be taught; it is found in every place. But the **eyes of the fool** look to the ends of the earth; he thinks wisdom is something rare and distant from him, and thus he never begins to learn.

**A foolish son.** He is a "provocation of bitterness." Just as "bitter" is used for the tongue, the foolish son causes a cooling of the father’s heart and bitterness to his mother.

**To punish the righteous.** Even if a judge punishes a righteous man for a minor infraction, it is not good, for it diminishes his honor. There is no lack in the nature of many who are born with a tendency toward error, but those who turn their natures toward many matters are the ones who strike the noble for their uprightness. He who is "sparing of words" is like a master of knowledge who speaks with deliberation.

**He who separates himself seeks his own desire.** This refers to one who isolates himself from the community to follow his physical lusts. He separates himself from the path of Torah and seeks only worldly desires; in all sound wisdom, he will be "exposed" or entangled in shame.

**The words of a man's mouth are deep waters.** Just as deep waters have no visible end, so too the words of a wise man have no end or limit to their depth. Wisdom is a source that never stops, but constantly adds more. Alternatively, the words of the wise are like "deep waters" because one can only draw understanding from them with great effort.

# Proverbs

### Chapter 18

**Hebrew Source Text** | **Aramaic Translation (Targum)**
:--- | :---
The lips of a fool enter into strife, and his mouth calls for blows. | The lips of a fool lead him to judgment, and his mouth brings him to a beating.
A fool’s mouth is his ruin, and his lips are a snare for his soul. | A fool’s mouth is a change <note>original: "shinya," perhaps meaning a transformation for the worse</note> for him, and the lips of a sinner are a snare for his soul.
The words of a whisperer <note>original: "nergan," a grumbler or slanderer</note> are like delicious morsels; they go down into the innermost parts of the body. | The words of a deceptive man are like a groan <note>original: "brangana"</note> and they descend to the depths of the belly.
One who is slack in his work is a brother to a master of destruction. | Even one who is lazy in his work is a companion to a destructive man.
The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous run into it and are safe <note>literally: "set on high"</note>. | The name of the Lord is a tower of strength; into it the righteous shall run and be protected.
A rich man’s wealth is his strong city, and like a high wall in his own imagination. | A rich man’s possessions are his city of strength, and it grows higher than a wall.
Before destruction, a man’s heart is haughty, but humility comes before honor. | Before a break, the heart of a man is exalted, and before honor is humility.
He who gives an answer before he hears—it is his folly and shame. | He who returns a word before he hears—it is his stupidity and disgrace.
A man’s spirit will sustain him in sickness, but a crushed spirit, who can bear? | The spirit of a man sustains him in his illness, but a bubbling <note>troubled</note> spirit, who can support it?
The heart of the discerning acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks knowledge. | An understanding heart acquires knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks wisdom.
A man’s gift makes room for him and brings him before the great. | A man's gift broadens his way and leads him before the great.
<margin>3 and comes / and contentions</margin> | <column-break/>
The first to plead his case seems right, until his neighbor comes and examines him. | The righteous man is first in his judgment, then his companion comes and investigates him.
The lot puts an end to disputes and decides between the powerful. | The lot <note>original: "pisa," a casting of lots</note> nullifies contentions and separates between the mighty.
A brother offended is more unyielding than a strong city, and quarrels are like the bars of a castle. | A brother who is distanced from his brother is like a city of strength, and an ear <note>perhaps a scribal error for "strife"</note> is like the bolt of a fortress.
From the fruit of a man’s mouth his stomach is satisfied; he is satisfied by the yield of his lips. | From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly is filled, and from the produce of his lips he shall be satisfied.
Death and life are in the power <note>literally: "hand"</note> of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit. | Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and he who loves it shall eat of its fruit.
He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord. | He who finds a good wife finds goodness and brings forth mercy from before the Lord.
The poor man speaks entreaties, but the rich man answers roughly. | The poor man speaks supplications, but the rich man speaks impudently.
A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. | There are friends who associate, and there is a lover who clings closer than a brother.
Better is a poor man who walks in his integrity than one who is perverse in his speech and is a fool. | Better is a poor man who walks in his simplicity than one whose lips are crooked and who is a fool.

***

**The lips of a fool.** A fool is unable to speak except in words of strife and war, because by the very word of his speech, strife arrives. His words are a reminder of words of blows and wounds. **Blows** <note>original: "mahalumot"</note> are ultimately hidden things originating from the mouth, like wounds and bruises; the fool’s words are considered words of contention, blows, and wounds. This verse says that the fool's lips bring the blows and wounds upon himself. This is because when a dispute flares up among wise men, the fool mixes into that strife, and his strength is spent in receiving the blows. The matter is that he causes himself harm through this involvement.

**A fool’s mouth.** The mouth brings destruction to the fool; by the very words of a fool, he is broken. He is like one crushed by his own words, as the fool's power is explained. So too, the fool's lips begin a ruin that lasts until it results in the contempt of his body and his possessions. Thus, a fool's lips are a snare for his soul.

**The words of a whisperer.** This refers to one who incites and brings down the cloak of slander. **Like delicious morsels** <note>original: "mitlahamim"</note> means they are drawn from the house of the person being defamed, like the phrase "and they struck Sisera." From the words of a talebearer, the slander is smoothed over, and the victim is made to look evil in the eyes of others. This is a bad blow delivered in secret by the tongue; the words descend to the innermost chambers of the heart—a blow that is not recognized except by the tongue. Some interpret this as words that are accepted like merchandise; thus the words of a slanderer are spoken in secret.

**Even one who is slack.** We learn that those who shrink from doing their work, living in a state lacking wisdom, eventually lose their livelihood. Because of his lack of sustenance, he turns to harming others, and thus he destroys himself. Because of this evil and the loss of his reputation, he acts as a destroyer.

**The name of the Lord is a strong tower.** His name is a tower of strength and a secret of might. In their time of trouble, the righteous do not merit to be gathered and hidden away, but they merit this tower. When they run to keep the statutes, they are sustained. He mentions the "secret of the Lord" in the place of His dwellings. Some interpret "he runs" <note>original: "yarutz"</note> as a matter of "surrounding," meaning the righteous man runs around it in an act of kindness, and in it is his defense, and no one can overcome him.

**And a high wall.** This is compared to the strong city mentioned with this tower. The righteous man walks in it, dwelling in security, and his refuge allows him to flee from the tower—the righteous man runs into it and is exalted in it.

**A rich man’s wealth.** This returns to the idea of the man's confidence in his money. The rich man thinks his wealth is a city of strength for him. It is like a high wall in his **imagination** <note>original: "maskito," meaning imagery or thought</note>. He acts with his money as if it were a wall, walking in the ways of violence, thinking his money is the voice of his strong city. In his inner chambers, he feels safe and relies on it. **Maskit** is a term for a "form" or "image," like the language of "covering" in the Targum.

**Before destruction.** Before a person suffers a collapse, his heart becomes haughty and he prides himself. But before honor comes to him, he must have humility. The verse mentions what factors cause the break—pride—and what causes honor—humility.

**He who gives an answer.** One who responds to a matter before he has heard it and analyzed it properly—his response is a folly to him and a disgrace, for the speaker will frustrate him. From this we learn the trait of the wise.

**A man's spirit will sustain.** This refers to his entire strength and the spirit of the soul, which sustans the body during its toil and labor. The body, being material, receives the illness, but the spirit gives it strength to endure through the words of the soul. Thus the spirit can sustain the body's sickness.

**The heart of the discerning.** This means the intellect of the discerning person is excessive; he is unique in his preparation. The ear of the wise seeks to hear knowledge, and they are worthy of acquiring it. Some explain that the intellect of the discerning man asks for everything, and he does not let knowledge slip from him, for the wisdom of the researcher and the unique individual is found in their knowledge. As it says regarding the spirit of the intellect, the concealed things are found in the seal of the Torah to clarify every path of understanding. Knowledge is also said regarding general wisdom, and "knowledge" is its permanence. Thus the wise man seeks knowledge to hear gathered insights, for partial wisdom is a received tradition.

**A man’s gift.** One who brings a gift to his friend—that gift will broaden his way. The matter is that for the wise, his "gift" is his wisdom and his honor, which brings him before the great—kings and judges. Some say this refers to the wisdom and perfections that were given to him, which help him in his honor before people.

**The first to plead his case seems right.** When two people have a dispute, the first one to present his arguments seems strong, but contentions arise when the second arrives.

**A brother offended.** This verse connects to what was said above. It says a fool causes a quarrel between brothers, and only a lot can separate them from their strong cities and their portions. Because of the offense of the brother, he is like a stranger. **Contentions are like the bars of a castle.** Quarrels and strifes are as strong as the bolt of a king's palace, which is strong so that no man can enter. The lot is what separates and settles it. This also warns against strife between brothers, which is stronger than strife between the wise and the righteous. The natural bond and the closeness are more powerful than a strong city, and the offense between them is harder than the bars of a castle.

**From the fruit of a man's mouth.** From the fruit produced by the words of a man's mouth, his belly is satisfied. Since the purpose of speech is that a person eats by it, he calls whatever happens to him as a result of his speech "his fruit." According to his speech, so it will happen to him: if it is good, good will occur, and vice versa. He is satisfied by the produce of his lips.

**Death and life.** By the power of the words a man uses with his tongue, he may die or have life for his soul. Good speech can sometimes save one from death. Each person eats the fruit of what he loves—if he loves to speak well or poorly, he will face the consequences.

**Finds a wife.** He who finds a good wife has found a good thing for himself and will receive favor from God, who has granted her to him.

**The poor man speaks entreaties.** The poor man speaks with supplications and soft words because he is low in status, unlike the rich man.

**A man of many companions.** A man who loves many friends just to associate with them may come to ruin. It is better for a man to have a few true friends, for there is a lover who is more devoted than a brother. Some interpret this as meaning one should associate with the wise so that they might connect him to their ways.

**Better is a poor man.** It is better to be a person who is poor in money but walks in his integrity—meaning his perfect traits—than a person who is crooked in his speech. Even if he has money, he is a fool. 

**Until here is the knowledge.**

A brother offended is harder to win than a strong city, and disputes are like the bars of a castle. | A brother who is distanced from his brother is like a strong city, and a sign is like a fortress bar.
From the fruit of a man's mouth his belly is satisfied; he is satisfied by the product of his lips. | From the fruit of a man’s mouth his belly is filled, and from the harvest of his lips he is satisfied.
Death and life are in the power <note>literally: "hand"</note> of the tongue, and those who love it will eat its fruit. | Death and life are in the hand of the tongue, and those who love it shall eat from its fruit.
He who finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favor from the Lord. | He who finds a good wife has found [a treasure], and receives his will from God.
The poor man speaks entreaties, but the rich man answers harshly. | The poor man speaks with supplications, but the rich man speaks with strength.
A man of many companions may come to ruin, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother. | There are friends who join together, and there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother.
Better is the poor man walking in his integrity than one who is perverse in his lips and is a fool. | Better is the poor man who walks in his simplicity than one who perverts his ways and is a fool.

<column-break/>

---

**Commentary**

**The lips of a fool.** This entire verse revolves around the matter of illness and the matter of strife and war, for by the word of his mouth, strife begins, and the words of his mouth call for and compel words of blows and wounds. **Blows** <note>original: "mahalumot"</note> is associated with the idea of hidden things and heat <note>the commentator is exploring a phonetic or linguistic link between "blows" and "heat/fever"</note>, because from the fool's speech, the words of strife, blows, and wounds emerge. It says "into strife" to mean that the fool’s lips enter and join the conflict. This is because in his poverty of mind, when he enters into a dispute between wise men, he mingles the strife within himself, and through his mouth, he calls for blows. The meaning is entirely plain, as I intended.

**A fool’s mouth is his ruin.** All the power of his destruction is because of the words of his mouth. **And his lips are a snare for his soul.** The seductions and deceptions by which he is misled are a snare and a trap for him.

**The words of a whisperer.** The voice of the wicked man who entices and stirs up strife, who calculates with his tongue; his words prepare internal ruin and the degradation of his heart. Whoever hears him would say that the ingredients of death are right here. **Like delicious morsels** <note>original: "mitlahamim"</note>. This refers to a strong, frequent, and permanent illness caused by the "whisperer" <note>the slanderer</note>. The connection between these verses and "blows" refers to those who act with understanding, and the sick are those who... <unclear>broken text</unclear>. The general rule is that from the flight of the "whisperer," the sick descend to the gaps of death and the ruin of the ranks of the eloquent. For the words of the enticer—the one who spies in secret and with deceit—are wounds to wisdom; they are called "morsels" for his brain and return as an illness of death and burns at the opening of the pit. Upon him come wars and the illness of strange hearts... from death and life.

**The name of the Lord is a strong tower.** A tower that is superior and of great might. He strengthens himself in his spirit so as not to be crushed, but rather they focus on this mentioned tower, the Name of the Lord, as a dwelling for His laws and His strength. It mentions "The Name of the Lord" in place of strength and excellence. **The righteous runs into it** with swiftness, and the action decides for him, as it is written "and he shall be safe/exalted" through the power of kindness. Listen to the prophet: "The Lord is high" <note>Isaiah 33:5</note>. All the words of this narrative and learning are part of rising above the "blows" of the mouth... <unclear>fragmentary manuscript</unclear>.

**A rich man’s wealth.** He holds onto his imagination <note>original: "maskit"</note>—the imagination of days—placing his trust in [his wealth]. He does not run to God in his time of trouble because he thinks the rich man is not [at risk]. He thinks his wealth is a strong city and a wall, and he has a vision of it as a wall exalted in the chambers of his imagination. The Targum says: "The rich man covets his city of strength." He walks in the ways of his own vision and the noise of his strong city, and there the fool prepares... and stands in the secret chambers of his cover, for he is supposedly secure in his trust and nothing terrifies him. The translation of "maskit" is "his strength."

**Before destruction, a man’s heart is haughty.** It means that before a break comes to a man, his heart becomes haughty; whereas honor is preceded by humility. Humility does not cause a man to break, but rather leads to honor.

**He who gives an answer.** He who returns a word before the other has finished speaking—before he has heard it—will be ashamed and will be caught in his own rebuke. It is a folly and a disgrace for him because of his words. This is a folly because he thinks he has heard enough to answer.

**A man's spirit will sustain.** A man's wisdom and his nature will sustain and support him against the "ferment" and the folly and the constant illness of the soul, which is harder than the illness of the body. The spirit sustains the soul and the body and the life... but if the spirit itself is crushed, who can support it?

**An intelligent heart.** This refers to the heart of the righteous. It says it will "acquire knowledge," which is the knowledge of wisdom. **And the ear of the wise seeks knowledge.** They follow the path of acquisition. It tells us that the receiving of wisdom is not only from others, but one can acquire knowledge from within himself, for the wisdom of the soul is found by every person who is influenced by it, and they know it without a teacher. This is the knowledge of the intellect imprinted in the nature of man's birth, in the way of wisdom... and also knowledge of divine wisdom... as long as one does not lack an "ear" to receive the wisdom heard from the words of experts, for divine wisdom requires reception from others.

**A man’s gift.** One who is generous with a gift to another; the gift "makes room" for him. The meaning is that the wise and his honor will increase because of his disputes <note>perhaps meaning his ability to settle them</note>, and they will provide him with room in the assembly and bring him before the great—the kings and the officers of high rank. Similarly, if a man is perfect in his heart, a "gift" from wisdom and perfection will increase his standing before kings and the wise, and he will be honored by men.

**The first to plead his case.** This is connected to the wise. In order to be far from sin, he increases his humility... and afterward his opponent comes and examines him and proves him wrong. Or, he returns to the judgment and examines the matter in light of the opponent's argument.

**The lot puts an end to disputes.** Many quarrels are ended by the lot, for it is a thing of heaven. And between the "powerful" wise men, it separates the dispute. It means that the quarrels and strife will not be explosive.

**A brother offended.** A brother who is transgressed against by his brother. It says that even a small quarrel between two brothers, even if a lot is cast to separate them, it is harder than a strong city because of the transgression he committed against his brother.

**Disputes are like the bars of a castle.** These quarrels and contentions are as strong as the bars of a king's palace, which are strong so that no man may enter. The lot ends the rebellion. It informs us that a dispute between brothers is stronger than a dispute between strangers... and a quarrel between them is stronger than the bars of a palace.

**From the fruit of a man's mouth.** From the fruit of his deeds—the words of a man's mouth—his belly is satisfied. Because the result of speech is the "fruit" of his soul, whatever happens to him because of his speech... if it is good, good will happen to him; and if the opposite, then from the "harvest" of his speech his belly will be satisfied, and he will bear the weight of his folly. It mentions "fruit of the mouth" as a hint toward eating <note>physical results</note> and "harvest of the lips" as a hint toward the speech itself.

**Death and life.** Death and life are not literally in the hands of the tongue, but they depend on the speech a man makes with his tongue; for he can speak and bring death upon his soul. And conversely, good speech sometimes saves those taken to death. Every person is a "lover" of the tongue—not that he is accustomed to speaking, but that he follows the words—and he will eat the fruit of his words, whether good or bad.

**He who finds a wife.** This refers to the "harvest" of a good woman. When a man takes a good wife for himself, it is a "good thing." And he will receive the "will" <note>favor</note> of the Lord because of his faithfulness, and God will increase his gift to him. Conversely, a bad wife is a "bad companion."

**The poor man speaks entreaties.** The poor man speaks with supplications, but the rich man speaks with "strength" <note>harshly</note>, because he is arrogant in his voice.

**A man of many companions.** This does not mean a man who *loves* many friends, but one who seeks to associate and join with them for his own ruin. It gives the reason that a man should choose a few friends and trust in them in times of trouble more than in his own brothers. Some interpret this to mean that a man who buys many friends with his money will end up broken, for his money will fail. A "friend who sticks closer than a brother" refers to those who are joined in their souls.

**Better is the poor man.** The poor man is better than the "rich" who is "perverse," for the poor man walks in his "integrity"—meaning his perfect traits—while the one who is perverse in his lips speaks crookedly. Even if he is not poor in his family, he is "poor in knowledge" and is a fool.

<summary>This page contains Proverbs 18:6-24 and 19:1, contrasting the destructive nature of foolish speech and slander with the security of the divine name. The commentary emphasizes the psychological depth of "whispering" (slander) as an internal illness and explores the social value of humility and wisdom over material wealth.</summary>

# Proverbs

### Chapter 19

<column-break/>

<margin>
S <note>Likely a scribal marker for a new section</note>
Rebellious
</margin>

**Aramaic Translation (Targum)** | **Hebrew Source Text**
:--- | :---
One who does not know his own soul, it is not good for him; and he who is hasty with his feet is a sinner. | Also, without knowledge a soul is not good, and he who is hasty with his feet sins.
The foolishness of a man upends his path, and against God his heart rages. | The folly of a man perverts his way, and against the Lord his heart frets.
Wealth adds many companions, but the poor man is separated from his friend. | Wealth adds many friends, but the poor man is separated from his friend.
A false witness shall not be acquitted, and he who speaks lies shall not escape. | A false witness shall not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies shall not escape.
Many serve before a prince and see his splendor and are comforted. | Many will entreat the favor of a generous man, and every man is a friend to him who gives gifts.
All the days of the poor are evil to him, and even his friends distance themselves from him; the wicked man turns away with unreliable words. | All the brothers of a poor man hate him; how much more do his friends go far from him! He pursues them with words, but they are gone.
He who acquires a heart <note>meaning wisdom</note> loves his soul; he who guards understanding finds good. | He who gets wisdom loves his own soul; he who keeps understanding will find good.
A false witness shall not be acquitted, and he who speaks lies shall perish. | A false witness shall not go unpunished, and he who breathes out lies shall perish.
Luxury is not fitting for a fool, nor for a servant to rule over princes. | Luxury is not fitting for a fool, much less for a servant to rule over princes.
A man's wisdom draws out his path <note>meaning patience</note>, and it is his glory to overlook an offense. | A man’s discretion makes him slow to anger, and it is his glory to overlook a transgression.
The wrath of a king is like the roaring of a lion, but his favor is like dew upon the grass. | A king’s wrath is like the growling of a lion, but his favor is like dew upon the grass.
A foolish son is a hardship to his father, and the contentions of a wife are like a constant dripping. | A foolish son is ruin to his father, and a wife's quarreling is a continual dripping of rain.
House and wealth are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from God. | House and wealth are an inheritance from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the Lord.
Laziness brings on a deep sleep, and an idle soul will go hungry. | Slothfulness casts into a deep sleep, and an idle person will suffer hunger.
He who keeps the commandment guards his soul; he who despises His ways shall die. | Whoever keeps the commandment keeps his life; he who is careless in his ways will die.
One who is kind to the poor lends to God, and He will repay him a good reward. | Whoever is generous to the poor lends to the Lord, and He will repay him for his deed.
Chasten your son while there is hope, and do not set your heart on his destruction. | Discipline your son, for there is hope; do not set your heart on putting him to death.
A man of great wrath shall bear the punishment; for if you rescue him, you will have to do it again. | A man of great wrath will pay the penalty, for if you deliver him, you will only have to do it again.

<column-break/>

<margin>

---

**Also without knowledge.** The pious one <note>Refers to a specific commentator, possibly Rashi or a contemporary sage</note> explained: Without the knowledge of the Torah, even if one rises up, it will not lead to any good, for he will live without the fear of sin. Moreover, the fool will sin many times and not even know he has sinned. **Alternative reading:** The verse means a soul without knowledge is not good. Some explain this in the context of one's trust in the Holy One, Blessed be He. If a person acts without knowledge and is foolish—meaning his mind is on his own strength rather than trusting in God—his path is like robbery <note>meaning illegitimate</note> and he is a sinner in this matter. Others say: one who is hasty in his actions and thinks he is safe from stumbling, yet sins. This is like a marksman who aims but misses the target <note>Hebrew: *yachti*, related to the word for "sin"</note>. Our Rabbis explained "without knowledge" as referring to those who engage in intimacy without proper preparation or consent. **And he who is hasty with his feet sins.** This refers to one who walks over deep pits in the darkness.

**The foolishness of man perverts his way.** Meaning, through his own iniquity he ruins his life, and when things go poorly in his portion, his path is twisted. He commits transgressions, and they are held against him. Then his heart **rages against the Lord**, grumbling against the Divine attribute of Justice for his misfortune. 

**Wealth adds many friends.** He who has money finds that companions gather toward him because they hope to benefit from him. But if his wealth fails, his friend **separates from him** and does not desire his company. Even a poor man's relative will distance himself from him.

**A false witness.** One who testifies falsely against his neighbor is disqualified. One who speaks lies will be trapped by his own words when they demand he swear to a lie or a robbery; he will not escape from the punishment of Heaven. **He breathes out lies.** This means he makes his lies known, and his eyes will not see the light. There is a traditional teaching regarding the letters of the word for "Falsehood" (שקר - *Sheqer*): each letter stands on only one leg, making it unstable, whereas the letters of "Truth" (אמת - *Emet*) each have two legs or a firm base to stand upon. This teaches that truth stands forever, but falsehood has no "legs" to stand on. Because falsehood has no foundation, its practitioners will eventually be found in "distant places," meaning they will be removed from society because a lie cannot be sustained. 

**Many entreat the favor of a prince.** Many are those who seek the favor of the judge, hoping for a gift from his hand. And all are friends to the man who gives gifts. Some interpret this in the context of charity, others in the context of the "givers" of Torah.

**All the brothers of a poor man.** All the relatives of a poor man hate him because they are afraid he will ask them for support. Not only do they not help him, they distance themselves even further. He pursues them with words, perhaps begging or reminding them of family ties, but they have no desire for his words. 

**He who acquires a heart.** One who acquires knowledge and wisdom loves his own soul, protecting it from all harm. Also, such a man will find that "goodness" fills him. To **guard understanding** is to find the "good" that is stored away for the wise—the reward given in this world and the world to come.

**A false witness.** This verse was written previously <note>referring to verse 5</note>, but here it replaces "shall not go unpunished" with "shall perish." This teaches that while he may not be punished immediately by a human court, he will eventually perish by the hand of God, both in this world and the world to come.

**Luxury is not fitting.** It is not beautiful or appropriate for a fool to live in luxury and honor, for he does not know how to handle it. It is even less fitting for a servant to rule over princes. When a fool is given honor, he is like a "servant who becomes a king," ruling over people with harshness and lack of character. The wise man, however, through his wisdom, gains a higher status.

**A man's wisdom.** The understanding a man possesses makes him **slow to anger**. The wisdom he contains prevents him from being quick to rage. It is his glory to **overlook an offense**, for this act of forgiveness comes from a place of inner strength and beauty. One who does not overlook a transgression shows a lack of such inner "glory."

**The roaring of a lion.** When a king is in a state of rage against a man, he is as terrifying as a lion. But when the king is pleased, it is a benefit and a source of peace, like dew falling on the grass, which saturates the earth and brings life. This is mentioned to teach a person to fear the King of Kings even more than a flesh-and-blood king.

**Ruin to his father.** This refers to a son who acts wickedly and brings grief to his father. Even if he does not physically harm others, his bad reputation is a "ruin." Furthermore, the **contentions of a wife** are compared to a constant dripping of water through a leaky roof; just as a man cannot live in a house with a constant leak, he cannot find rest in a house of strife.

**House and wealth.** Even though a leaky roof and a contentious wife are mentioned, do not think that a "prudent wife" is merely a matter of luck or inheritance like a house. A prudent wife is a gift directly **from God**, granted according to a person's merit and destiny.

**Laziness.** Neglect of work and study brings a "deep sleep" upon a person. He becomes even more lethargic, falling from one level of idleness to another, until he is like a dead man. This leads to hunger, both physical and spiritual. 

**He who keeps the commandment.** One who guards the path of the commandments guards his own soul from the "accidents of time" and spiritual ruin. He who **despises His ways**—ignoring the proper path—will die a premature or spiritual death.

**Lends to God.** One who is gracious to the poor is as if he is lending to the Creator. God becomes, so to speak, his debtor. And God will surely repay the reward for this kindness, because the person gave from his own to help the poor man in his time of need.

**Chasten your son.** Discipline your son while he is young and there is still "hope" to change him. If a father waits too long, the son's character will be set, and he will not be able to turn back. Do not let your mercy prevent you from correcting him, for failing to discipline him is like "putting him to death" by allowing him to ruin his own life.

**A man of great wrath.** One who is habitually angry will suffer the consequences. If you save an angry man from the trouble his temper caused, you will only have to do it again, for his nature will soon lead him into a new conflict.

A notable linguistic discussion compares the physical stability of the Hebrew letters in the word "Truth" versus "Falsehood."</summary>

# Proverbs

### Chapter 20

**Aramaic Translation (Targum)** | **Hebrew Source Text**
:--- | :---
A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure <note>original: *mitqala* and *kilya*</note> are distanced before God, even from His sight. | Diverse weights and diverse measures, both of them are an abomination to the Lord.
Even by his childhood deeds a youth is known, whether his work be pure and whether it be right. | Even a child is known by his doings, whether his work be pure and whether it be right.
The hearing ear and the seeing eye, God made them both. | The hearing ear and the seeing eye, the Lord has made even both of them.
Do not love sleep, lest you become poor; open your eyes and you shall be satisfied with bread. | Love not sleep, lest you come to poverty; open your eyes, and you shall be satisfied with bread.
"It is bad, it is bad," says the buyer; and when he has gone out and is happy, he shall boast and say [it was good]. | <margin>And he goes on</margin> "It is bad, it is bad," says the buyer; but when he is gone his way, then he boasts.
There is gold and a multitude of fine stones and precious vessels, but the lips of knowledge [are more precious]. | <margin>A strange woman</margin> There is gold and a multitude of rubies, but the lips of knowledge are a precious jewel.
Take his garment because he was surety for a stranger, and because of a strange woman, take a pledge from him. | Take his garment that is surety for a stranger; and take a pledge of him for a strange woman.
Sweet to a man is the bread of deceit, but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel. | Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel.
Thoughts are established by counsel, and with strategies make war. | Every purpose is established by counsel; and with good advice make war.
He who reveals a secret is a slanderer, and one who entices with his lips—do not mix with him. | He that goes about as a talebearer reveals secrets; therefore meddle not with him that flatters with his lips.
He who curses his father and his mother, his lamp shall be extinguished as in a furnace of darkness. | <margin>In the pupil [of the eye]</margin> Whoso curses his father or his mother, his lamp shall be put out in obscure darkness.
An inheritance that is hurried at the first shall not be blessed at its end. | An inheritance may be gotten hastily at the beginning; but the end thereof shall not be blessed.
Do not say, "I will repay evil"; wait for God, and He will save you. | Say not, "I will recompense evil"; but wait on the Lord, and He shall save you.
Diverse weights are distanced before God, and a weight of deceit and evil is not good before Him. | Diverse weights are an abomination to the Lord; and a false balance is not good.
From before the Lord are the steps of a man; and a son of man, how can he understand his own way? | Man's goings are of the Lord; how can a man then understand his own way?
It is a snare for a man to be consecrated to the Holy, and after he has vowed, [he seeks] his soul. | It is a snare to a man to devour that which is holy, and after vows to make inquiry.
A wise king scatters the wicked and turns the wheel over them. | A wise king scatters the wicked, and brings the wheel over them.
The lamp of God is the soul of man, searching all the chambers of the belly. | The spirit of man is the candle of the Lord, searching all the inward parts of the belly.
Mercy and truth shall guard the king, and his throne is established by mercy. | Mercy and truth preserve the king; and his throne is upholden by mercy.
The glory of young men is their strength, and the beauty of old men is the gray head. | The glory of young men is their strength; and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
And the bruises and the sword of evil are a cleansing and like the wounds of the inner parts. | The blueness of a wound cleanses away evil; so do stripes the inward parts of the belly.

<column-break/>

**Diverse weights:** This means one who acquires for himself two different weights, a full one and a deficient one, so that he may buy with the full and sell with the deficient. Both are an abomination to the Lord. Why does the text say "both of them"? It is to include even the one who possesses them but does not use them, for even having them is an abomination before Him. **Even by his doings:** All the actions and deeds of a youth are recognizable, showing whether his work will be pure and upright when he grows up. This is close to the spirit of the ancients who said that during youth, habits are formed that carry weight later. Or, the word *yitnaker* <note>original Hebrew: "be recognized" or "make oneself a stranger"</note> is from the sense of "becoming a stranger," meaning a youth might act contrary to his true nature, but eventually his true character will be revealed in the end, whether for good or evil.

**The hearing ear:** The one who created the ear to hear and the eye to see—He made the human being complete. This teaches that a person should not think their actions are hidden from the Holy One, blessed be He, for He who planted the ear, shall He not hear? The verse comes to say that the people should use their senses for life—to hear and to see the path of God.

**Love not sleep:** This means it is proper for a person to be diligent and involved in their affairs. This does not mean one should never sleep, but rather that one should not be lazy, for diligence is what God blesses. He who opens his eyes early will be satisfied with bread. Knowledge is more precious than gold and rubies; "lips of knowledge" refers to speech that is weighed with wisdom and understanding.

**It is bad, it is bad:** This refers to the buyer who, at the time of purchase, belittles the item to the seller to get a lower price. But after he has bought it and gone his way, he boasts and says that what he bought is worth much more, and he rejoices in his cleverness.

**Take his garment:** This means take a pledge from someone who has entered into a guarantee for a stranger or a foreign woman. It warns of the danger of becoming a surety <note>a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt</note> for those who are untrustworthy or immoral, which leads to the loss of one's own property.

**Sweet to a man:** One who acquires bread or wealth through deceit and theft—it seems sweet to him at first. But in the end, it will be as if his mouth is filled with gravel, and the sin will turn bitter.

**Thoughts by counsel:** One should prepare one's plans through the advice of the wise. Whether in physical war or in the internal war against the "Evil Inclination" <term>Yetzer Hara: the innate impulse to do evil in Jewish thought</term>, a person must consult the Torah and the Sages.

**Revealer of secrets:** One who goes about as a slanderer or a gossip will eventually reveal the secrets entrusted to him by his friends. Do not associate with such a flatterer; stay away from those who speak with "open lips" and have no self-control over their speech.

**Cursing father and mother:** One who curses his parents—it is right that his light be extinguished in the darkness of the night. This implies a spiritual darkness and a loss of the person's merit.

**A hastened inheritance:** One who is greedy to take his portion of an inheritance before the proper time, like the tribes of Gad and Reuben who hurried to take their land. In the end, such wealth will not be blessed and will dwindle away.

**Do not say "I will repay evil":** Do not seek revenge, for you do not have the power to truly judge. Instead, wait for the Lord, and He will save you through your righteous actions.

**The lamp of the Lord is the soul of man:** The human soul is like God's candle, for it is a spirit taken from His glory. It acts as a light that examines the secrets of the body and the heart. Some interpret "the chambers of the belly" as the "Good Inclination" <term>Yetzer Hatov: the impulse to do good</term> which is hidden within, guiding the person toward wisdom.

**Mercy and truth:** The mercy that a king performs—providing for those who do not strictly deserve it—and the truth of his word, these are the things that protect his throne and sustain his kingdom.

**The glory of young men:** Youth boast of their physical strength, but the true glory of the elderly is the gray head, representing the wisdom and experience they have gathered through the years.

<summary>This page covers Proverbs 20, focusing on the importance of honest weights, the dangers of laziness and gossip, and the concept of the human soul as a divine lamp that searches the conscience. The commentary emphasizes that both physical and spiritual diligence are required for a blessed life.</summary>

# Proverbs

### Chapter 21

**Hebrew Source Text** | **Aramaic Translation (Targum)**
:--- | :---
<margin>Measures 2</margin> **The scouring** of a wound cleanses away evil, and strokes reach the inner chambers of the belly. **The king’s heart** is like streams of water in the hand of the Lord; He turns it toward whatever He desires. **Every way** of a man is right in his own eyes, but the Lord weighs the hearts. **To do righteousness and justice** is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice. **Haughty eyes** and a proud heart—the lamp of the wicked is sin. **The thoughts of the diligent** tend only to plenty, but everyone who is hasty comes only to want. **The getting of treasures** by a lying tongue is a fleeting vapor of those who seek death. **The violence of the wicked** shall drag them away, because they refuse to do justice. **The way** of a guilty man is crooked and strange, but as for the pure, his work is right. **It is better to dwell** in a corner of the housetop than with a contentious woman in a shared house. **The soul of the wicked** desires evil; his neighbor finds no favor in his eyes. **When the scorner is punished**, the simple is made wise; and when the wise man is instructed, he receives knowledge. **The Righteous One** considers the house of the wicked, overturning the wicked to their ruin. **Whoever stops his ear** at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry and not be answered. **A gift in secret** pacifies anger, and a bribe in the bosom subdues strong wrath. **It is joy to the righteous** to do justice, but it is destruction to the workers of iniquity. **The man who wanders** out of the way of understanding shall rest in the assembly of the shades. <note>original: *Rephaim*, referring to the spirits of the dead or the inhabitants of the underworld.</note> **He who loves pleasure** will be a poor man; he who loves wine and oil will not be rich. | The scouring and cleansing hits the evil one and strikes the inner parts of the belly. Like the flow of water is the heart of the king in the hands of the Lord; to the place He desires, He inclines it. Every path of a man is straight in his eyes, but God prepares the heart. One who performs charity and justice is more pleasing to God than a sacrifice. Lofty eyes and a boastful heart, the lamp of the wicked is sin. The thoughts of the industrious are for profit, and everyone who is hasty brings about loss. Whoever gathers treasures with a lying tongue, his life is a vapor that is driven away, and they are prepared for those who seek death. The robbery of the wicked shall cast them down, because they refused to perform judgment. Crooked is the way of a man who is a stranger, but the pure one's works are straight. It is better to sit on the corner of a roof than with a quarrelsome woman in a common house. The soul of the wicked meditates on evil and does not trust his friend in his eyes. Through the palm of the mocking one, the simple man becomes wise, and through the insight of the wise, he will receive knowledge. The righteous man looks at the house of the wicked and tosses the wicked into evil. He who shuts his ear to the sound of the cry of the poor, he too shall call to God and not be answered. A settlement in secret subdues anger, and a bribe in the bosom subdues strong wrath. It is joy for the righteous to do justice, and destruction for those who do wrong. A man who strays from the path of wisdom shall dwell with the sons of the earth in the underworld. A man who is lacking and loves joy, and loves wine and oil, will not become rich.

<column-break/>

**The scouring of a wound.** There is something missing from the phrase "scouring of a wound"—it means that from the depths, it removes the "moist evil," and the strokes reach the inner chambers of the belly, going down to the bowels of death, for it has no strength forever, because he [God] spares the death of the wicked. And if it were said that "scouring of a wound" is the removal and destruction that will befall him, he spares the death of the wicked... it would be "scouring," a healing and a bandage, like the phrase "and with his stripes we are healed." For him, wounds that are feared in the soul are met with the healing of the wise through suffering with strong words, with strokes of discipline and chance strokes.

**Streams of water.** This is compared to the "streaming of water," and according to how one can incline them to one side or another, he has a path of conduction... with wisdom they go here and there. So too, the heart of the king is in the hand of God; He takes his heart toward whatever He desires... the hearts of kings without any diminishment of their stature.

**Every way of a man.** This says that all the ways and actions that a person does are right in his own eyes, and sometimes they are a "right way" before God, yet its end is the ways of death.

**But the Lord weighs the hearts.** This is the language of "adjustment" or "leveling." Judgment adjusts them according to His will. He weighs the thoughts of the heart according to the input of the soul and the state of the standing of the hearts of men, whether he knows evil or whether it is the intention of good.

**To do righteousness.** Like kindness. Behold, the preference for an altar is better than bringing a sacrifice for sins. Righteousness and justice are lacking if God does not intend the direction of the heart in the charity.

**Haughty eyes.** One who raises his eyes in his trust upon his strength and becomes haughty in his heart, holding onto his thoughts of pride and expanding his heart toward the desires and thoughts of the wicked—this is sin... just as "a lamp for you" refers to the thoughts of the world. And some explain "two haughtinesses," for every facet of greatness that happens to the wicked, the world thinks it is all for the wicked, but the correct view is... the violence of the wicked.

**The thoughts of the diligent.** The thoughts of the industrious and the clever to act and to plot for high plowing bring advantage. And if it were said the thoughts of the one who fears the loss, they are for lack... the affairs of the world that happen as well, and these are repaid from his pain... for the majority of chances are not secure from stumbling.

**Getting treasures.** Meaning wealth collected by a lying tongue and deceit, which will be on a path toward death. A bad and fleeting status... seekers of death, for their sins against the kingdom will necessitate death because of their lies. And to interpret this as a rebuke from wisdom regarding the high path: since the Torah is a stabilizer of good, it [deceitful wealth] is a fleeting vapor. And those who gather injustice are seekers of death, meriting strange blows to their souls.

**The violence of the wicked.** "It shall drag them" means the robbery and the business that the wicked engage in will bring fear upon them, because they refused to do justice and did not want to return and restore to their neighbors. Their violence will be the trade of the violent... the matter of the verse is that the wicked will be separated and go down...

**Crooked.** The path of a person is crooked and strange... but the pure one will always follow the discipline of all his actions in righteousness and justice.

**It is better to dwell.** He says it is better for a man to dwell in a narrow and orderly place, in a dwelling on the corner of a roof, even if he is exposed to heat and cold and open to the elements, than to have a big wide house as a "shared house"—meaning sharing it with a companion in that house—while the house's standing is full of strife.

**The soul of the wicked.** He says that the soul of this person—evil will be profaned by it... because his mouth profanes the work of his body and he covets the acquisitions of this world... and he does not spare his neighbor. To interpret the verse: the one who does evil holds on to achieve his desire, and the wicked one is a loather of the wicked, and he finds no grace in his eyes.

**When the scorner is punished.** The explanation is: when the simple man turns away from the scorner being punished for his actions, the person becomes wise, for he says, "I should not be like him."

**And when the wise man is instructed, he receives knowledge.** That is to say, when a wise man gains insight from his wisdom, he takes the knowledge into his heart to understand and gain even more insight than what prevents him from evil... Just as one acquires wisdom by seeing the end of a transgressor, so it happens to the wise when they see their colleagues receiving a large measure of wisdom due to their diligence and effort to acquire it. The matter of the verse is: "when the wise man is instructed," meaning at the time he receives insight from God... He subverts and strikes the ways of the wicked so that they do not choose the good path... and this happens to prevent them from their evil and to prevent from them the paths of repentance. Or it says that when the righteous man is insightful in the house of the wicked and deals with it, this subverts him [the wicked] to strengthen his wickedness.

**Whoever stops his ear.** One who is tested by his station... on his lack or on the depth of his explanations, he too will cry out to God in his distress and will not be answered. Or it means he is always crying out before him until he is choked by lack... and if he does not have mercy on him, he too will cry out to the Blessed Name... and he will not be answered. To interpret the verse regarding the trait of the wise: one who is "blocked" and his obligation is present... he will bend to the path of life... "a gift in secret subdues" [anger].

**Subdues wrath.** Silver and gold are like horses, and regarding the gift given in secret to a judge who is troubled by him, it will double and humble his anger and fury—meaning it will break it. And if the wrath is not hidden in secret but remains only in the bosom, the judge will set it... a gift of life in the judge's bosom subdues strong wrath. Or it says that at the time of giving in secret, it subdues the judgment; but at the time when the judge's fury is in the bosom and not revealed to the judge, the wrath he has against you will be strong. Also, this verse can be explained regarding charity and kindness with the previous verse: one should not give to the poor as a "gift in secret" so as not to embarrass him...

**It is joy to the righteous.** Joy is in the eyes of righteousness and justice, and not as others say, "to do straightness and justice is a terror to him." Or it causes him terror and fear... whereas it is a terror to the workers of iniquity... for they fear it and cannot diminish it. The sages interpreted this as the one who subverts the paths of merits...

**The man who wanders out of the way of understanding.** It says to the one who counts himself among the scholars of the Torah... he will rest with the "shades" <note>the dead</note> in the trouble of their world.

**He who loves pleasure.** One who is involved in desires and banquets and wine—because it is only for his own pleasure and lust and to seek the world—he will experience lack and become poor... or it says a man who is occupied with "lack" for himself, sufficing with necessary things, that is his joy... and he will merit all the traits of wealth...

<column-break/>

<margin>It will be shortened; He will be blessed</margin>

**Commentary**

**A ransom for the righteous is the wicked.** <note>Referring to Proverbs 21:18</note> If the righteous lacks anything, God will give the wicked as his ransom and substitute. This is similar to the verse: "I have given Egypt as your ransom" <note>Isaiah 43:3</note>. The wicked man takes the place of the righteous, and the betrayal intended for the upright shall return upon the head of the treacherous. This follows the principle of justice: the troubles the wicked cause shall befall them, while God provides a way for the righteous to escape.

**It is better to dwell.** It is far better for a person to live settled alone in the wilderness than to have a wife who is a mistress of strife and anger constantly. The "center of the desert" <note>original: "מרכז מדבר"</note> is a place of solitude, far from the social gatherings of the city, the bathhouses, and the pressures of society that often lead to conflict and the pursuit of unnecessary luxuries. Such luxuries often lead us to neglect the laws of God.

**Desirable treasure.** In the home of a wise man, one finds a "desirable treasure." This refers to both spiritual and physical acquisitions that are sweet to the soul. The wise man uses his resources carefully, whereas the fool "swallows it up"—meaning he consumes everything impulsively without regard for the future. Some philosophers suggest that wisdom itself is the greatest oil, more nourishing to the soul than actual oil or wine. The fool, however, cannot wait to learn; he wants to "swallow" knowledge without the proper process of study and reflection.

**He who pursues righteousness.** One who directs his heart toward helping the poor and performing acts of kindness will find that his life is enriched. His deeds do not harm him; rather, they grant him strength. Life is mentioned here because the physical life of a person is sustained by these spiritual foundations.

**A wise man scales the city of the mighty.** A wise man achieves through his intellect what a warrior cannot achieve through strength alone. Wisdom allows one to "ascend" and overcome even the most fortified defenses of the "mighty" (which can represent physical strength or the physical body's impulses). The wise man conquers his own physical nature and the obstacles placed by others.

**He who guards his mouth.** A person should guard his mouth and tongue from speaking evil. Both are mentioned because they are the physical instruments of speech. Additionally, some interpret this as guarding the mouth from harmful foods that damage health. One should only speak that which brings benefit—either in terms of practical life or in service to the Torah, teaching others, or prayer.

**Proud and haughty.** A person who acts with malice and arrogance deserves the title of "scorner." His actions are born of "overflowing pride." This is the opposite of the "pass over a transgression" mentioned elsewhere. 

**The desire of the sluggard.** The unfulfilled cravings of the lazy person eventually destroy him, because he refuses to use his hands for productive work that would sustain him. While the lazy man spends all day wishing for things, the righteous man is busy giving to charity, and he never finds himself lacking.

**The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination.** God rejects the offerings of those who intend to continue their wicked plots. The word "plot" <term>zimmah: a calculated evil plan</term> implies that even while they are performing a religious act, their hearts are focused on sin. The Aramaic translates this as "strength of possessions" <note>original: "עבת תחסין"</note>, suggesting that they think their wealth can buy God's favor.

**A lying witness.** A witness who speaks lies will eventually be caught and his words will perish. However, a "man who listens"—one who only speaks what he has truly heard and verified—will be able to speak with confidence forever. The word "forever" <note>Hebrew: "lanetzach"</note> also implies strength and endurance.

**A wicked man hardens his face.** The wicked man shows a brazen face when giving false testimony. But the upright man "understands his way," meaning he reflects carefully on his path and ensures his testimony is true.

**There is no wisdom... against the Lord.** No human wisdom or strategy can stand against God's decree. Where there is a desecration of God's name, we do not show honor even to a great teacher if they oppose the Divine will.

**The horse.** A horse may be prepared for battle, but the actual "victory" <note>original: "teshuah"</note> or salvation comes from the Lord. A rider should not trust in the strength of the horse but in the blessing of the Creator.

**A good name is to be chosen.** A good reputation is more valuable to a person than great wealth. Grace and favor in the eyes of others are better than silver and gold. Wealth can be used for evil, but a good name stays with a person and opens doors that money cannot.

**The rich and the poor.** They "meet" because they depend on each other for the world to function. If everyone were rich, there would be no one to do the necessary work; if everyone were poor, there would be no one to provide employment. God made them both to create a balanced society.

**A prudent man sees evil.** A wise person anticipates trouble before it arrives and hides himself (either physically or by avoiding the situation). The "simple" or "fools," however, walk blindly into danger and are punished for their lack of foresight.

**The reward of humility.** Humility and the fear of God lead to wealth, honor, and life. Humility is the "heel" <note>a play on the Hebrew word "ekev" which means both "reward/consequence" and "heel"</note>—it is the foundation upon which spiritual life is built.

**Thorns and snares.** A collection of thorns and snares, a net of traps, to say that the way of the crooked person is full of thorns and snares. <column-break/> **The Aramaic Tradition (Targum):** Thorns and traps are in the crooked path, and he who guards his soul stays far from them. Train a child according to his way, so that even when he grows old, he will not forget it. The rich man shall rule over the poor, and the borrower is a servant to the man who lends. He who sows injustice shall harvest calamity, and the rod of his anger shall be finished. One who has a good eye shall be blessed, because he gives of his bread to the poor. Cast out the mocker and the quarrel will leave, and judgment and suffering will settle. God loves the pure of heart, and the grace of his lips joins him to the king. The eyes of God guard knowledge, and he misleads the words of the liar. The lazy man says in his laziness, "There is a lion outside, and I might be killed in the middle of the markets." The mouth of the stranger is a deep pit, and he who is angry before God will fall there. Foolishness is tied to the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will distance it from him. He who oppresses the poor to increase his own, or gives to the rich, it is for his own lack before God. Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise, and set your heart to my knowledge. Because they are sweet when you keep them in your belly, and they shall be established as one upon your lips. So that your hope may be in God, I have informed you this day. And behold, I have written for you three times <note>The Aramaic translates "shalishim" as "three times" or "triplicate," emphasizing the importance of the teaching</note> with counsel and knowledge.

**Thorns and snares.** A collection of thorns and snares, a net of traps, meaning the way of the crooked person is full of thorns and snares. All troubles are prepared and traps are set on the path of transgressors. If there be thorns and snares on the way of the person, do not walk in that path lest you be trapped and prepared for evil; therefore, he who guards his soul stays far from the path of crookedness. **Train up a child, etc.** As long as the child is small, train him; he should be trained in matters of strength, discipline, and goodness. There were lines and corrections... the intention is to spread and distribute discipline to the child at all costs in his youth. The training should be a good discipline leading the child at the beginning of his learning toward the good path, with strength and discipline as the child is trained and rebuked according to the capacity of the student. Everything he is trained in during his youth will be like lines engraved on a new vessel. **Train up a child.** Teach the child and train him at the beginning of his way with rebuke according to his capacity; everything he is trained in during his life will be lines like the brightness of a new vessel. Learning in the days of childhood is like engraving on sand <note>meaning easily received</note> or rather, like a permanent mark on a clean page. Another explanation: provide the child with wisdom and discipline, for everything that passes in his youth is like writing placed on the heart of a scribe upon the tablet of wisdom; as he grows stronger, that writing remains strong and will not be erased. **The rich rules over the poor.** The powerful rich man, by his foundation, tramples the poor who are lacking, and his words are heard and accepted; therefore, he is able to rule. Thus, the status of the rich and the ruler is such that the poor must receive from them... **He who sows injustice.** He who sows injustice intends a punishment... for he who sows evil and bad schemes, the rod strikes him according to his injustice and he will be destroyed... **A generous eye.** The person who is generous in all matters is good and gracious, and his character brings him to wisdom... he will be filled with the blessing of the LORD because he gave his bread to the poor. **Drive out the scorner.** Remove the powerful scorner who causes others to sin... and when the mocker is removed, strife and shame vanish. **He who loves purity of heart.** One who desires the company of people and is forgiving and pure in heart, through the grace of his lips, he is chosen. He will find favor in the eyes of the king... **Incline your ear.** Turn your ear to the eyes... to receive knowledge so you do not stumble. **For it is pleasant.** It is pleasant to receive these words of the wise... they will be kept and established in your heart to benefit others as well... they will be ready on your lips as a response. **That your trust may be in the LORD.** These things I have made known to you today so that you will trust in God with all your heart and not rely solely on your own understanding... **Have I not written for you thirty.** Meaning many times, or "thirty" as a number representing abundance. Or perhaps these are "excellent things" <term>shalishim</term> <note>The Hebrew "Shalishim" can mean "thirty," "officers," or "excellent things." Historically, this is linked to the "Thirty Sayings" of wisdom literature</note> which are the primary things that guide a person in counsel and knowledge.

Do not desire his delicacies, for it is bread of lies. **Do not** weary yourself to become rich; from your own understanding, cease. <margin>Fly away</margin> Will you fly your eyes toward it, and it is gone? For it surely makes for itself wings, like an eagle, and flies toward the heavens. <margin>Fly, fly</margin> **Do not** eat the bread of one with an evil eye, and do not desire his delicacies. For as he calculates <note>original: "sha'ar," also meaning a gate or a price/value</note> in his soul, so is he; "Eat and drink," he says to you, but his heart is not with you. <margin>70</margin>

---

<column-break/>

**To make you know the truth.** This means to make you know the truth of the words of truth. According to the Midrash <note>Homiletic interpretation</note>, it is to bring back an answer to the One who sent him. "Truth" <note>Aramaic: "Kosht"</note> was given at Sinai together with "Truth" <note>Hebrew: "Emet"</note>, and this is the translation of "truth." All this I have written for you today to make you know the truth of the matters, so that the commandments might be established as foundations of wisdom. To return truth to those who sent you—referring to those who come from abroad to trade. Or, let the fear of your Sender be upon you... it will be a strength to share with those who sent you. He has already mentioned this many times. **Do not rob the poor because he is poor.** Do not rob him because he lacks strength, being poor and having no helpers against those who rise up against him. Do not say, "He lacks a portion of what a man needs to eat and drink," lest they eat and... **Do not rob the poor because he is poor.** This is a secret: do not rob, whether for existence or to remove the gift of his poverty. **And do not crush the afflicted at the gate.** At the time of judgment, for the gate is where the court sits. This is the plain meaning. Let not the judgment be weakened at the gate, like the elders of the gate of his city who sit to pour out the grace of the law... and the wise man says do not crush the poor with your hand... and his way is in vanity... **For the LORD will plead their cause.** Like the strength of anger, He will take and despoil. A language of robbery. God will take vengeance... **Do not befriend.** Do not be a friend or companion to a person of low status whose intellect is anger... and why should you not? Lest you learn from him and forget wisdom. The wise are honored, but those who learn from him bring shame to their souls. For bad traits are a snare in the soul of a man. Even if they are not permanent, "lest you learn his paths" and find the well-known snare of wisdom. Afterward it is written: **Do not be among those.** Do not be a person who makes agreements to return a debt, like they say regarding "guarantors." For can a person be trusted to pay back a debt that is beyond him? **If you have nothing to pay.** If you have no power in your hand to honor the guarantee... for those who are wise will take... **Do not remove.** A warning for generations to follow the prohibitions and the boundaries of the land, which the children of God <note>ancestors/saints</note> established in the past, and they took the commandments to pursue the ways of the ancients. It is not fitting for a man to break through and change the boundaries that the giants of wisdom set. And so the Sages said: "Establish a fence around the Torah." And all the ways which the great ones of wisdom set... one should not dream of changing them... this will be a security against sorcery and straying. And it is possible that this refers to the gathering of wisdom... **Will you fly your eyes...** meaning the movement of the eye... if you remove your eyes from wealth, it disappears. For it makes for itself wings like an eagle... The one who makes himself rich is like one whose eye flies... And some say "cease" <note>Hebrew: "hadal"</note> in the sense of the beginning, meaning it is not fitting for you to begin with an evil eye... **For as he calculates.** This "gate" <note>Hebrew: "sha'ar"</note> is the measure he prepares in his toil... for the man with an evil eye is a stranger... for what he calculates in his soul, so is he. "Gate" is a language of estimation <note>as in a market price</note>. And some interpret it from the end of the matter... he will say to you "eat and drink" with his mouth, but in his heart it is not so...
