# Proverbs

The scheming of foolishness is sin, and the scoffer is an abomination to men. If you faint in the day of adversity, your strength is small. Deliver those being taken to death, and those stumbling toward slaughter—if you can hold them back. If you say, "Behold, we did not know this," does not He who weighs hearts understand? He who keeps your soul knows it, and He will render to man according to his work. My son, eat honey because it is good, and the honeycomb which is sweet to your palate. So shall the knowledge of wisdom be to your soul; if you find it, there is a future, and your hope shall not be cut off. Do not lie in wait, O wicked man, against the dwelling of the righteous; do not spoil his resting place. For a righteous man falls seven times and rises again, but the wicked stumble in calamity. <margin>Your enemy</margin> When your enemy falls, do not rejoice, and when he stumbles, do not let your heart be glad. Lest the Lord see it and it be evil in His eyes, and He turn away His anger from him. Do not fret because of evildoers, nor be envious of the wicked. For there will be no future for the evil man; the lamp of the wicked will be put out. Fear the Lord, my son, and the king; do not associate with those given to change. For their calamity will rise suddenly, and who knows the ruin of them both? These also belong to the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not good.

<column-break/>

The intention of the sinner is sin, and the distancing of a man is a sufficient sin <note>The Aramaic Targum emphasizes the social and spiritual distancing caused by sin</note>. If you are weak in the day of distress, your strength is weakened. Save those who are led to death, and those led to slaughter, spare them; and if you say, "We did not know this," God knows this in His heart; He knows your soul, and He pays man according to his deeds. My son, eat honey, for it is as good as the honeycomb that is sweet to your palate. Thus, let wisdom be fitting in your soul, for if you find it, there is a future before Him, and your hope will not cease, and your expectation will not end. Do not lie in wait, O wicked one, for the dwelling of the righteous, and do not disturb his place of rest. For seven times the righteous man falls and rises, but the wicked are tripped up by evil. At the fall of your enemy do not rejoice, and when he is tripped up by evil, let not your heart be glad. Lest it be bad in the eyes of God, and He turn His anger away from him. Do not be angry with the wicked, and do not be jealous of the sinner. For there is no good future for the evil one, and the lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished. Fear God, my son, and the king, and do not mix with those who change. Because their destruction comes suddenly, and the end of both of them, who knows? These things I say to the wise: To show partiality in judgment is not fair. ->Darkness<- <note>original: "אופלא" (Opla); likely a catchword referring to the following page</note>

---

**The scheming of foolishness.** This comes to tell you that what you might "carve out" of foolishness through wisdom is a small matter <note>original: "זמת אולת", often translated as "the thought of foolishness"</note>, for wisdom is a great thing, and sin resulting from folly is a cause for distancing from God. Those who cling to Him—He is their life, and folly removes that life. It says "the scheming of foolishness is sin" to teach that even the intent of a fool is considered sinful. And some explain "abomination" <note>original: "תועבת"</note> as something even more repulsive than sin. Some commentators say the "scoffer" is an abomination to men because he disturbs the peace. **If you faint.** If you have trained yourself to be lazy, you will not find the strength in a day of trouble to stand against it. Your strength will be as small as your effort was during your training. If you do not restrain your eyes from seeing a person in trouble, you will be repaid accordingly. <gloss>Some say: if one's hands are weak from performing commandments, his strength will be small when he needs it.</gloss> And according to the Midrash: "If you are faint in the Torah <note>i.e., lazy in its study</note>, in the day of trouble your strength will fail against the accusing angels." **Deliver those taken.** It is a man's duty to save those being taken to execution or being judged unfairly. For one who says, "We did not know," and hides his soul from his fellow's suffering, God knows the heart's truth. He knows if you truly were ignorant or just lazy. **My son, eat honey.** This is a metaphor for the sweetness of the Torah and wisdom. Just as honey provides nourishment for the physical body, wisdom provides the food and life for the rational soul. If you find wisdom, you have a "future" (acharit), because while the wicked are cut off, the wise soul is eternal. **Do not lie in wait, O wicked man.** This is a warning to the wicked not to ambush the righteous man's home, for though the righteous man may fall many times, God will raise him up. Seven is not a literal limit, but signifies "many times." **When your enemy falls.** This is a high moral standard: do not rejoice in another's downfall. If you rejoice, God may see your pride as worse than the enemy's original sin and "turn His anger from him"—perhaps even onto you. **Do not fret.** Do not be jealous of the apparent success of evildoers, for their "lamp" <note>their life or legacy</note> is temporary and will be extinguished. **Fear the Lord, my son, and the king.** One is obligated to fear God first, and then the earthly authority He has appointed. "Those given to change" refers to those who rebel against the laws of God or the king. Their ruin comes suddenly. **These also belong to the wise.** This refers to the following section on judicial integrity. A judge must be blind to the status of the people before him, acting as if he does not recognize them, so that his judgment remains pure and true.

# Proverbs

Even to not say to the wicked, "You are righteous"; nations shall curse him and peoples shall despise him.
And to those who rebuke, it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come a good blessing.
The lips of those who return words of rebuke shall be kissed.
Prepare your work outside and make it ready for yourself in the field, and afterward build your house.
Do not be a witness for nothing against your neighbor, and do not be misled by your lips.
Do not say, "As he did to me, so I will do to him; I will return to him according to his deeds."

And behold, it was all overgrown with thistles, its surface covered with nettles, and its stone wall was torn down.
And I saw, and I set my heart; I looked and I received instruction.
A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest.

Also these are the proverbs of Solomon which the friends of Hezekiah, king of Judah, transcribed.

**He who says to the wicked** — One who is a liar will say of the evil that it is good. This lacks the refinement of speech and brings a bad reputation. When one says to the wicked "You are righteous," the peoples curse him in his disgrace. **And the loathing of people in general** — for they will speak against the lie, and thus all nations will loathe him. **But to those who rebuke, it will be pleasant** — and the fear of the Lord will be within them. Through this, blessing will come from the mouths of princes. As it is written: "a good blessing," for they merit the good portion prepared for those who uphold justice. **To those who rebuke, it will be pleasant** — This refers to those who protest against transgressors because the fear of God is in their hearts. They will not dispute the attribute of the Uprightness of God, blessed be His name, by calling a wicked man righteous. **A good blessing** — every good blessing a man can be blessed with will be given to these rebukers, because everyone acknowledges their excellence in doing good and supporting the right.

**He kisses the lips** — This refers to one who speaks right and straight words. They are like a kiss of the lips that restores the spirit. These are lovely and beloved words, like one who kisses another's mouth; through this, the listener rejoices and finds peace of mind. Those who give legal counsel are the ones "returning right words," and of this it is said: "he kisses the lips." **He kisses the lips** — that he should speak right and good words so that all will rejoice in him and he will restore the spirit of all. The deeper meaning of "kissing the lips" is that he brings back the words of the evil person and returns them to the company of the "good lips," thereby instilling moral discipline in the hearts of the listeners.

**Prepare your work outside and make it ready for yourself in the field** — Here he warns a person to first acquire land and a vineyard, for from them comes sustenance, and only afterward build a house. If he has a source of livelihood, he can sustain himself; but if he builds a house before acquiring land, he will fall into poverty and be unable to maintain the house. This is the <term>wisdom of the ways of the world</term> <note>practical financial management</note> to guard the reward of one's labor.

**Prepare your work outside... and make it ready in the field** — These are words of moral instruction teaching a man to train his household for the service of God and to prepare his heart for divine service and the management of upright character traits that point toward God. The scripture means: before you build your "house"—which is the body and the soul—prepare from the "outside"—which are your character traits—so that they are clean from any blemish. Likewise, the "field" in which you work represents the one who plows and sows and brings forth fruit; from these you will have sustenance for the soul's needs and be able to serve the Lord with a whole heart.

**Do not be a witness for nothing** — This refers to one who testifies against his fellow "for nothing," meaning not by the command of a judge or according to our <term>Holy Torah</term>. It is a man's duty to testify truthfully regarding everything he knows in a dispute between people, and he must not withhold himself from testifying if he knows anything. **Do not be a witness for nothing** — Do not bear false witness against your neighbor's words, not by the command of the <term>Beth Din</term> <note>Rabbinical Court</note>, but by your own will and heart's desire. False testimony will be revealed, and many troubles and evils will come upon him.

**And do not deceive with your lips** — This warns one to pursue compromise and peace between litigants, rather than inciting or "deceiving" them into speaking perversely or lying about one another. Such actions destroy the peace of society. It is a great evil in human nature to incite people with words in matters of strife and contention.

**Do not say** — A man should not say that just as his fellow did to him, so he will do in return, paying back evil for evil. This is a bad trait. Regarding this, it is said: "You shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge." The Torah warns us to conduct ourselves with good traits and distance ourselves from evil ones. On this, <note>Rashi: Rabbi Shlomo Yitzchaki, 11th-century commentator</note> **Rashi, of blessed memory**, says: "Do not say 'as he did to me so I will do,' for if he did you evil, the Judge is the one who will exact justice from him."

**By the field of a lazy man I passed... and by the vineyard of a man lacking heart** — Here he warns a man to be diligent in Torah and wisdom, and to guard himself from laziness and idleness. Idleness destroys the intellect and wisdom and every good virtue, bringing a person to poverty and "lack of heart" <note>lack of sense or moral center</note>. The Torah has warned in many ways to distance oneself from laziness and the bad traits that lead to poverty and lack. **By the field of a lazy man I passed** — This is because he previously mentioned the attribute of uprightness in the ways of God—to walk in His ways and the ways of wisdom. Therefore, he adds a warning against laziness, which ruins all matters of wisdom. All wise men are diligent and toil in Torah and wisdom, while the opposite is true of the lazy and the "heartless." For the little wisdom he might acquire, he loses through the ways of laziness and idleness.

**And behold, it was all overgrown with thistles** — The meaning of the text is that because the lazy man refrains from working his field and tending the vineyard, not only does he fail to produce benefit or enjoyment, but he even loses his previous labor. So it is with one who turns his heart away from wisdom; not only does he fail to acquire new wisdom, but even his own wisdom and the wisdom of his teachers is forgotten from his heart, for laziness is the great enemy of the intellect.

**And behold it was all... and I saw, and I set my heart; I looked and I received instruction** — He says this to make known that "because I knew in myself that the soul of the wise is like clay receiving a form," the intellectual soul is that which receives moral instruction. From this evidence, I learned a lesson for myself: not to fall into this state. After I saw the great loss that befell this man due to his laziness and lack of heart, I resolved in my soul to discipline myself with the instruction of the Torah and not to waste my time in idleness.

**And your poverty shall come as a traveler** — This means: see now, the sword of necessary action is drawn against the "heartless" man, and he will always lack, as will all those of his kind. Conversely, he will increase in strength, for one who holds fast to wisdom and intellect will always go on increasing, and a full lot of favor will be in his hand, his destiny set on the upright path.

**Also these** — Little commandments shall stand before him, and the moral stories of the wise regarding the past and the future shall be told. His heart shall be awake and ready for wisdom; he shall not slumber or sleep—God forbid—from any of the commandments or wisdom. This is the core principle that sustains all creation: to keep the commandments of the Lord, may He be blessed and exalted. The scripture states this general rule: wisdom is the foundation of the body and the soul. If one separates from the practical application of these words, life departs quickly. This is why it says, "Also these are the proverbs of Solomon..."

The power that sustains the merit of Hezekiah continues in life, the King of Judah. Through him, the King of Kings, who is established through the generations, judges with a shield. **Also these are the proverbs of Solomon** — We learn that "Also" includes many sages, like those who shared in the service of King Solomon and the kingdom of King Hezekiah (peace be upon him) who merited these traits. Hezekiah transcribed from the language of the kingdom into upright deeds. These are the words of Solomon, which are all words of the <term>Holy Spirit</term>, so that they would be unsealed and revealed to all people. It is proper to add them into the books of kings that are worthy of God's glory, to remember the chosen ways... **The glory of God is to conceal a matter, and the glory of kings is to search out a matter** — He connected this to the "glory of God" to hide matters of inner wisdom, called "the face of the heart," and to see the attainment of action. In our Torah, there is the revealed and the hidden... those who train their hearts in wisdom will merit miracles and signs. In the "glory of kings," they search out matters to understand their standing and nature, and to understand the reward destined—the hidden and wonderful reward... The doubt is removed when royalty and wisdom go with the wise. **The glory of God...** in the pleasantness of the order, wisdom, and research that strengthens the lacking. May our testimony be with you.

The law of the pious and the great is explained above and below. Through it, they return from the lack of discipline by way of absolute reconciliation, for they will know all. Especially concerning righteous kings who research the ways, for they prepare and seek... and what is proper to observe... the fear of the kingdom... the inhabitants of their house... to increase their merit and their trust, and the life of all in the "Zohar of the worlds" <note>the radiance of the hidden realms</note>...

# Proverbs

<columns>2</columns>

The heavens for height and the earth for depth, and the heart of kings is unsearchable. Remove the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the refiner. Remove the wicked man from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness. Do not glorify yourself in the presence of the king, and do not stand in the place of the great. For it is better that it be said to you, "Come up here," than that you should be put lower in the presence of the nobleman whom your eyes have seen. Do not go out hastily to strive, lest you know not what to do in the end, when your neighbor has put you to shame. Debate your cause with your neighbor himself, and do not reveal the secret of another. Lest he who hears it put you to shame, and your ill repute never turn away. Like apples of gold in settings of silver is a word spoken in its proper place. Like an earring of gold and an ornament of fine gold is a wise rebuker to a listening ear. Like the cold of snow in the time of harvest is a faithful messenger to those who send him, for he refreshes the soul of his masters. Like clouds and wind without rain is a man who boasts of a false gift. By long forbearing is a ruler persuaded, and a soft tongue breaks the bone. Have you found honey? Eat only what is enough for you, lest you be filled with it and vomit it up. Make your foot rare in your neighbor’s house, lest he be weary of you and hate you. A maul, a sword, and a sharp arrow is a man who bears false witness against his neighbor. Like a bad tooth and a wavering foot is trust in a faithless man in the time of trouble. Like one who removes a garment on a cold day, or like vinegar upon soda, so is he who sings songs to a heavy heart. If your enemy is hungry, give him bread to eat, and if he is thirsty, give him water to drink.

<column-break/>

The heavens are high and the earth is deep, and the heart of kings cannot be searched out. Remove the sparks <note>original Aramaic: *sulhava* - referring to the impurities or dross</note> from the silver, so that a vessel may emerge from the refiner. Let the wicked be removed from before the king, and his throne shall be established in righteousness. Do not boast before the king, and do not stand in the place of the great. For it is better that it be said to you, "Come up here," than that they lower you before the ruler because of what your eyes have seen. Do not go out to a quarrel in haste, so that you do not end up in judgment when your friend shames you. Judge your case with your friend, and do not reveal the secret of another. Lest the one who hears shames you, and your reputation does not return. Like a vision of gold in silver carvings is a word spoken in its proper turn. Like a holy ornament of gold and vessels of pearls is a wise man to a listening ear. Like the coldness of snow on a harvest day is a faithful messenger to those who send him; he restores the soul of his master. Like clouds and wind and rain that does not fall is a man who boasts of a false gift. With a patient spirit <note>original: *bingida de-rucha*</note> the wicked is persuaded, and a soft tongue breaks a strong bone. If you have found honey, eat what is sufficient, and do not be sated by it lest you vomit. Make your foot weary <note>meaning "make it rare"</note> from your friend’s house, lest he be sated with you and hate you. Like iron, a sword, and a sharpened arrow is a man who testifies false witness against his friend. Like a bad tooth and a stumbling foot is a deceptive hope in the day of distress. Like a person taking off a garment on a day of cold, or like vinegar on soda, are those who sing songs to a bitter heart.

<meta>Catchwords: "If" (Hebrew) and "Because" (Aramaic)</meta>

---

->On a cold day, vinegar and soda; just as vinegar is to soda, so is the bad heart. If your enemy is hungry, give him bread; if thirsty, give him water.<-

---

<margin>And your enemy</margin>
**Remove the dross.** This refers to all the desires and vanities that distance one from the ultimate height, just as the earth is at the ultimate depth. **The heart of kings.** From him comes the standing of ultimate knowledge. And who can say to him, "What are you doing?" 

Many regret when they see the "vision of grace" <note>an interpretive term for a king's favor</note> has vanished. **Remove the dross.** The word "remove" <note>Hebrew: *hago*</note> means to set aside or take away, as in "removing a sin." By removing the dross from the silver, the vessel becomes pure. **Remove the wicked.** When you remove and set aside the wicked from the king’s presence, his throne is established in righteousness. 

Do not carry yourself with pride or arrogance in your heart in the king's courts; rather, be fearful and restrained, for this leads to honor. **Do not glorify yourself.** It is better for you to be elevated from a lower rank than to lose your honor among the wise by being demoted. **For it is better.** It is much better for you to sit in a lowly place and be told "Come up here" than to be cast down from a high seat of glory. 

**Do not go out to strive.** Conflict leads to destruction. Consider the end of the matter, lest you find yourself shamed in the outcome. **In the end.** If you act hastily, you may find your reputation ruined, like a city in ruins. When you reveal secrets, you lose the trust of the wise. **Debate your cause.** Settle matters directly with your peer; do not reveal private writings or hidden things. **Lest the hearer shame you.** People will speak of your disgrace and your reputation will be sharpened like a sword against you.

**Apples of gold.** The sages describe wise words as being like gold apples inside silver filigree—beautiful both in their inner meaning and their outer expression. **A word spoken in its place.** This refers to speech that is perfectly timed and structured. Wisdom is protected by such careful speech. **An earring of gold.** Just as gold adorns the body, a wise rebuke adorns the listening ear. 

**Like the cold of snow.** Just as a cold wind or snow provides relief to workers during the heat of the harvest, a reliable messenger brings peace of mind to his master. **Clouds and wind.** A person who promises gifts but does not deliver is as disappointing as storm clouds that bring no rain. 

**By long forbearing.** Through patience, even a harsh ruler can be swayed. **A soft tongue.** Gentle words can "break the bone," meaning they can overcome even the hardest and most stubborn resistance. **Have you found honey?** Honey is sweet and good, but one must eat it in moderation. This is a metaphor for all worldly matters: if you overindulge, you will eventually despise it. **Make your foot rare.** Do not visit your friend so often that you become a burden. Too much familiarity breeds contempt. 

**A maul and a sword.** A false witness is as physically destructive as a weapon; he causes death and ruin. **A bad tooth.** Relying on a traitor is like trying to eat with a rotted tooth or walk on a broken foot—it fails you exactly when you need it most. **Removing a garment.** To sing joyful songs to someone who is mourning or "heavy of heart" is as jarring and harmful as pouring vinegar on soda or taking a coat away in the freezing cold. **If your enemy is hungry.** Conquer your enemy through kindness; by providing for his needs, you may turn his heart.

->**Hebrew Text**<-

A stone is heavy and the sand is weighty, but a fool’s anger is heavier than both.
Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood, but who can stand before jealousy?
Better is open rebuke than hidden love.
Faithful are the wounds of a friend, but the kisses of an enemy are profuse.
A sated soul loathes a honeycomb, but to a hungry soul, every bitter thing is sweet.
Like a bird that wanders from its nest, so is a man who wanders from his place.
Oil and incense gladden the heart, and the sweetness of a friend comes from sincere counsel.
Do not forsake your friend or your father’s friend, and do not go to your brother’s house on the day of your calamity; a neighbor nearby is better than a brother far away.
Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart, that I may answer him who taunts me.
A prudent man sees evil and hides; the simple pass on and are punished.
Take his garment, for he has gone surety for a stranger, and take a pledge from him for a foreign woman.
He who blesses his friend with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, it shall be counted as a curse to him.
A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike.
He who would restrain her restrains the wind, and his right hand grasps oil.
Iron sharpens iron, and a man sharpens the face of his friend.
He who tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who guards his master will be honored.
As water reflects face to face, so the heart of man reflects to man.
The grave <note>original: "Sheol"</note> and destruction <note>original: "Abaddon"</note> are never satisfied, and the eyes of man are never satisfied.

<margin>
We say
Better is open rebuke
than love
great
contentions
and a man sharpens
the grave
and destruction
</margin>

**A stone is heavy**. It is heavy for a man to carry. **Heavy and the weight of sand, but a fool’s anger is heavier than both**. The anger of a fool is even more burdensome and difficult to endure than the physical weights mentioned above. **Wrath is cruel and anger is a flood**. We say that wrath is "great" in the sense of being overwhelming and hot, and "flood" refers to a sweeping overflow; yet despite this, a person might withstand them. However, regarding **jealousy, who can stand before it?** The heat of jealousy is the most evil thing of all. **Better is rebuke**. A rebuke from one who loves you, which is spoken openly, is more beneficial than a love that is kept hidden and does not point out faults. For with rebuke, one can improve. Some suggest that "faithful wounds" <note>from a friend</note> cause more pain than others, but are intended for good. Alternatively, it means that open rebuke is better than a love that is hidden in the heart, meaning one who says, "I love you," but does not correct you. **Faithful are the wounds of a friend**. Even the wounds inflicted by a friend are "faithful" because they are intended for the person's benefit. The "profuse kisses" of an enemy are like the deceptive kisses of Esau <note>a reference to the Midrash where Esau's kiss to Jacob was said to be insincere</note>. **A sated soul**. It will loathe <note>original Hebrew "tovus," meaning to trample or despise</note> the honeycomb. When a person is full, even the sweetest things are repulsive to him. But to a **hungry soul**, even the bitterest thing is sweet. This can also be understood as a metaphor for Torah study: one who is "full" of worldly vanity will find the sweetness of wisdom bitter, but one who hungers for truth will find even the "bitter" toil of study to be sweet. **Like a bird that wanders**. Just as a bird is distanced from its life and the safety of its nest, so is a man who must wander from his place; if he has no rest, he will find only weariness. **Oil and incense**. Just as oil and incense gladden the heart through their good scent, so the sweetness of a **faithful friend** provides counsel that settles the soul. **Your friend and your father’s friend**. If someone was a friend to your father, do not abandon that connection. For an old friend is more reliable than a new one. Do not rely solely on a brother in times of trouble, for a **neighbor who is close** to you and helps you is better than a **brother who is far away** from you in heart or distance. **Be wise, my son, and gladden my heart**. This is the plea of a teacher to a student or a father to a son, asking them to excel in wisdom so the teacher may answer those who mock his methods. **A prudent man sees**. One who is wise perceives a coming danger—whether in a city or on a path—and hides himself. But the **simple** pass through blindly and are punished. **Take his garment**. If a man is foolish enough to guarantee the debt of a stranger or a "foreign woman" <note>often a metaphor for illicit desires or strange philosophies</note>, he deserves to lose his cloak as a pledge, for he has acted without judgment. **He who blesses his friend**. One who praises his friend too loudly or too early in the morning may actually be doing him a disservice. Neighbors who hear the loud praise might become jealous or begin to speak of the person's faults to "balance" the praise. Thus, a loud blessing is "counted as a curse." Our sages also taught that one should not greet his fellow before praying. **A constant dripping**. *Delef* <note>dripping</note> refers to water leaking through a roof. Just as a leak on a rainy day drives a man out of his house, so does a **quarrelsome wife**. A man cannot find rest in his own home. **He who would hide her**. Trying to restrain or hide such a person is as impossible as trying to hide the wind or trying to hold oil in your hand; it inevitably slips out and reveals itself. **Iron sharpens iron**. Just as one piece of iron sharpens another, so do two scholars sharpen each other’s minds through debate. **He who tends a fig tree**. The fig tree is unique because its fruit does not ripen all at once; one must guard it daily to eat the fruit as it ripens. So too, one who faithfully serves his master will eventually be honored and "eat the fruit" of his labor. **As water reflects the face**. If you look into the water, you see a reflection of your own face. So too, the heart of one man is reflected in another; if you show love to your fellow, his heart will reflect that love back to you. **The grave and destruction**. Sheol <note>the underworld</note> and Abaddon <note>the place of ruin</note> are never full; they always have room for more. Likewise, the **eyes of man** are never satisfied with worldly possessions; the more he has, the more he desires.

The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, and a man is tested by his praise.
Though you should crush a fool in a mortar among grits with a pestle, yet his foolishness will not depart from him.
Know well the state of your flocks, and set your heart to the herds.
For riches <note>original: חֹסֶן (chosen) - meaning wealth or strength</note> are not forever, and does a crown endure for every generation?
The hay is removed, and the tender grass appears, and the herbs of the mountains are gathered.

Because of the transgression of a land, its princes are many, but by a man of understanding and knowledge, stability shall be prolonged.

<margin>B
Be careful</margin>

The crucible for silver and the furnace for gold; so is a man tested by the mouth of those who praise him.
If you should crush a fool in a mortar in the midst of the mill and the ear <note>This Aramaic translation uses "ear" likely as a metaphor for the pestle or a specific part of the grinding tool.</note>, his foolishness will not pass from him.
Know well the faces of your flock, and set your heart upon your herds.
For strength is not forever, nor is a crown perfected for every generation.
The hay is removed and the grass is seen, and the herbs of the mountains are gathered.
Lambs are for your clothing, and goats for the purchase of a field.
And a sufficiency of goat's milk for your sustenance, for the provision of your house, and life for your maidens.
The wicked flee without a pursuer, but the righteous are like a lion that is confident; he is confident in wisdom.
By the sins of a land, its great ones are many; but by a man of understanding and knowledge, its leadership is extended.
A poor man who oppresses the poor is like a snatching rain that leaves no bread.
Those who leave the law praise the wicked, and those who guard the law contend with them because of their sins.
Evil people do not understand judgment, but those who seek from before the Lord understand everything.
Better is the poor man who walks in his perfection than he who is deceptive in his ways, even if he is rich.
He who guards the law is an understanding son, but he who joins with gluttons shames his father.
He who increases his money with interest and usury—for the one who has mercy on the poor, he shall gather it.
He who blinds his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer is cast away.
He who misleads the straight in an evil path shall fall into a pit, and the perfect shall inherit good things.
The man <note>catchword: גברא - the man</note>

***

**The crucible for silver... and a man according to his praise** • A person is tested by those who praise him to see if he is good or bad, wise or foolish. • If he is wise, when he is tested by words of praise, his heart will not become haughty. • But if he is a fool, he will immediately become arrogant. • Another explanation <note>original: ד"א - דבר אחר (davar acher)</note>: It is common, just as the crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold to test them, a man is tested by what comes from his mouth in praise. • If he praises the righteous, he is righteous; if he praises the wicked, he is wicked.

**The fool in a mortar... his foolishness will not depart** • No amount of suffering cleanses the folly of a fool. He is not like wheat, whose husks fall off in a mortar; for him, the suffering is simply like the pestle in the mortar <note>meaning it strikes him but does not change his inner nature</note>.

**Know well...** • What was seen above, "set your heart to the herds," is because money does not last forever; therefore, be diligent with your livestock.

**For riches are not forever** • Referring to monetary wealth.

**And if a crown [endures] for every generation** • Even a royal crown, if you possess it, does not stand forever. The verse is somewhat hidden regarding "wealth"—perhaps a day will come when you have none, or even if you have it now, it will not last for eternity.

**The hay is removed** • The Teacher <note>likely referring to the commentator Radak or Ibn Ezra</note> explains this in the sense of drying up. The meaning of the verse is: when the hay dries, the grass beneath it appears, for the grass dries after the hay. Once the mountain herbs are gathered, all is revealed. The text is saying: do not trust in wealth or crowns. See how plants return in their season and are renewed every year, but wealth and crowns do not return in their season. Therefore, be diligent with your flocks.

**Lambs for your clothing** • From them, you shall prepare your garments; and from the sale of the goats, you shall prepare to buy and maintain a field.

**And enough goat's milk** • "Enough" <note>original: הדי (hadi)</note> means a sufficient supply. Let the goat's milk suffice for your needs, the food of your house, and the "life of your maidens"—meaning you shall provide for them from the milk and its sale.

**The wicked flee when no one pursues** • Because he feels his transgressions in his heart and fears that people might pursue him. • **But the righteous are as bold as a young lion** • For his heart is at peace with the Omnipresent <note>a traditional name for God</note> and trusts that He will save him. The lion trusts in its strength and fears no man; so too, the righteous trust in the Lord at all times.

**Because of the transgression of a land, its princes are many** • Due to the sins of the land, the rulers are frequently changed and multiplied. But when a man of understanding is in that land, he will prolong his days in tranquility because he understands how to please the princes.

**A poor man who oppresses the lowly** • The verse teaches that a poor person who oppresses the lowly is harsher than a rich king who oppresses the lowly. For a king is rich and does not take everything; but the poor man who has nothing and yet oppresses is like a "sweeping rain" that leaves no food behind. Thus our Sages of blessed memory said: "A wicked man who is the son of a wicked man and has no bread" <note>original: רשיעא בר רשיעא דלית ליה לחמא</note>.

**Those who forsake the law** • Those who rebel against the Torah will praise the wicked. • **But those who keep the law contend with them** • They will argue with the wicked and rebuke them for their wickedness.

**Evil men do not understand justice** • For they lack the sense to understand the judgment of the Lord, as the bribe of the "Evil Inclination" <note>original: יצר הרע (Yetzer Hara) - the internal impulse toward selfishness or sin</note> destroys their intellect. • **But those who seek the Lord understand all** • Meaning, those who seek the Lord will understand His ways in all their actions and will comprehend His justice and His paths.

**Better is the poor who walks in his integrity** • That is, a poor man walking in integrity is better than a rich man who perverts his ways and whose actions are evil.

**He who keeps the law, etc.** • An understanding son guards the law and keeps it. • **But a companion of gluttons shames his father** • Because he squanders his father's money and shames him before other people.

**He who increases his wealth, etc.** • One who grows his money through interest and usury. • **Gathers it for him who is kind to the poor** • Meaning that in the end, his money will come into the hands of someone who is kind to the poor. As our Sages said in the Talmud (Bava Metzia 70b), this applies even to interest taken from gentiles. It is called "for him who is kind to the poor" because whoever takes that interest will distribute a portion of it to the needy. "Gathers it" means it will come into his hands through Divine providence.

**He who turns away his ear** • One who does not want to hear the words of the Torah and despises it. • **Even his prayer is an abomination** • Because the Holy One, blessed be He, does not desire the prayer of a man who rebels against His law. This is "measure for measure" <note>the principle of divine reciprocity</note>.

**He who misleads the upright, etc.** • One who leads the honest away from the straight path. • **Into his own pit** • Meaning, into the very pit he digs for others, he shall fall; as in the matter of "he who digs a pit shall fall into it." • **But the blameless shall inherit good** • The upright and blameless who do not listen to the one trying to mislead them shall inherit good from the Lord in this world and the world to come.

**A rich man is wise in his own eyes**, but a poor man who has understanding sees through him. A man who is wise in his own eyes, he is wise in his eyes, but the poor man of understanding searches him out. When the righteous are delivered, it is a matter of praise; but when the wicked rise, a person is crushed. He who covers his sins will not succeed, but for him who confesses and leaves them, there shall be mercy upon him. Happy is the man who asks <note>original: שָׁאֵל - meaning to inquire or seek out, here implying constant moral vigilance.</note> constantly for himself, but he who hardens his heart falls into evil. A roaring lion and a thirsty bear represent the wicked, and their wickedness is against a poor people. A ruler lacking understanding has many oppressions, but he who hates wealth and extortion prolongs his days. A man who is troubled by the blood of a soul will flee even to a pit; let them not assist him. He who walks in integrity will be saved, but he whose paths are crooked will fall in one of them. He who works his land will be satisfied with bread, but he who pursues vanity will be satisfied with poverty. A faithful man has many blessings, but he who runs after wealth for injustice will not be cleared. To show favoritism is not good, and for a morsel of bread a man will act corruptly. He who hastens to go in evil, his eye is evil, and he does not know that want is coming upon him. He who rebukes a man before him <note>original: קָדָמוֹי - in his presence.</note> will find grace better than the one who is divisive with his tongue. He who robs his father and his mother and says, "There is no sin," is a companion to a destructive man. A man of wide soul <note>meaning greedy</note> stirs up a quarrel, but he who hopes in God will be fattened. He who relies on his heart is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be saved from evil.

***

A rich man is **wise in his own eyes** because of his wealth; he thinks that all his deeds are done with wisdom, and he is wise in his own eyes to say, "The strength of my hand has made me this wealth" <note>original: כוחי ועוצם ידי - "My power and the might of my hand," a reference to Deuteronomy 8:17.</note>. Regarding the rich, he does not know what he has, but a poor man of understanding is wise and understands his flaws, and will search him out to show that he is not truly wise in the matter as he thought. **When the righteous rejoice**, meaning at the time the righteous are in high positions, the world is revealed in its many beauties—all kinds of glory and peace, for they act according to their will. But when the wicked rise—not to a high level of greatness, but simply to exist—man is "searched" or sought out. This means that people are searched for their money or property because of the wickedness of the rulers. If "searched" is from the root "to be hidden," it means a person must hide himself and his face so as not to be noticed or harmed. **He who conceals his transgressions**: one who hides his sins and acts as if he is innocent will not succeed in his ways, for they are revealed before the Creator. However, he who confesses his sins and leaves them, he will find mercy. **Fears always**: one who is always afraid of his sins and the punishment that might return upon him. He is cautious in all his actions and intends them for the sake of heaven. But he who hardens his heart, not fearing anything, will fall into evil. A "roaring lion" and a "greedy bear" refer to a wicked ruler over a poor people who have no help. The commentary likens the wicked ruler to a predator that stalks the poor and helpless. **A leader who lacks**: a ruler who lacks understanding and is a great oppressor will see his house destroyed. The verse means that a wicked ruler is one who lacks the intelligence to rule with justice. One who hates unjust gain will prolong his days. **A man burdened**: like one who is pursued because he has shed blood; he will flee to the pit and no one should support him or sustain his rule. **He who walks blamelessly** will be saved from the troubles of time, but he who is crooked in his actions will fall all at once. **He who tills his land**: one who works and does not pursue vanities will be satisfied with bread. **A faithful man**: one who acts with faith and does not hasten to become rich through injustice will find blessing. **To show partiality**: it is not good for a judge to favor someone, even for a "piece of bread"—meaning even for a small bribe or out of pity for a poor person, a man may transgress. **A man with an evil eye**: one who is greedy for the money of others and hastens to gather wealth through robbery. He does not realize that want will eventually come upon him because of his crimes. **He who rebukes a man**: Solomon says that based on his experience, he found that one who rebukes a man for his own good will find more favor in the eyes of God and man than one who flatters with a "smooth tongue." **He who robs his father and mother**: one who steals from them and says it is not a sin because he will eventually inherit from them—he is a companion to a destroyer. **A greedy man**: one who has a "wide soul" to fulfill all his desires will stir up strife. But he who trusts in God and is not greedy for others' money will be satisfied. **He who trusts in his own heart** to do evil without weighing his actions is a fool and will not escape, but he who walks in wisdom will escape all this.

<column-break/>

**A rich man is wise in his own eyes, but a poor man who has understanding sees through him.**
**When the righteous triumph, there is great glory; but when the wicked rise, people hide themselves.**
**He who conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will find mercy.**
**Happy is the man who always fears, but he who hardens his heart will fall into calamity.**
**Like a roaring lion and a charging bear is a wicked ruler over a poor people.**
**A leader who lacks understanding is a great oppressor, but he who hates unjust gain will prolong his days.**
<margin>Hates</margin>
**A man burdened with the blood of a person will flee to the pit; let no one support him.**
**He who walks blamelessly will be delivered, but he who is perverse in his ways will fall all at once.**
**He who tills his land will have plenty of bread, but he who follows vanities will have plenty of poverty.**
**A faithful man will abound with blessings, but he who makes haste to be rich will not go unpunished.**
**To show partiality is not good; for a piece of bread a man will transgress.**
**A man with an evil eye hastens after wealth and does not know that want will come upon him.**
<margin>In haste</margin>
**He who rebukes a man will afterward find more favor than he who flatters with the tongue.**
**He who robs his father or his mother and says, "There is no transgression," is a companion to a man who destroys.**
<margin>And said: "No..."</margin>
**A greedy man stirs up strife, but he who trusts in the Lord will be enriched.**
**He who trusts in his own heart is a fool, but he who walks in wisdom will be delivered.**

---

**A rich man is wise in his own eyes:** He thinks that because of his wealth, everything he does is done with wisdom. **But a poor man... sees through him:** <note>The Hebrew word *yachkerenu* implies a deep investigation or interrogation.</note> One who has understanding will rebuke him and search him out, showing him that he is not truly wise. This is a common way of the world.

**When the righteous triumph:** At the time when the righteous are in their greatness and the world is led by their word, **there is great glory**. <note>The commentator uses shorthand here.</note> Their actions all day long are glorious and bring favor, unlike the time of the wicked. **But when the wicked rise, people hide themselves:** Human beings hide so they won't be "searched out" by the wicked <note>The text suggests the wicked hunt down the righteous or their property</note>. The good people who are "free" or prominent hide so they won't be discovered, because the wicked will harm them and steal their money. Or it may mean they hide in houses during times of war and violence, for when the wicked rise, the world becomes a place of destruction and their works are hidden.

**He who conceals his transgressions:** One who commits sins and hides them, not repenting for them, will not find atonement through his wealth or his success. This is because his deeds are revealed and known before the Examiner of Hearts and Minds <note>God</note>. He will not prosper. But if he confesses his sins to a wise man who can help him find atonement and repair his ways—as it says, "he who confesses and forsakes them"—he will be shown mercy.

**Happy is the man:** Happy is the one who is always afraid of the consequences of his actions and is <term>tamim</term> <note>Integrity or simplicity</note> in his behavior. He understands every matter and is cautious, for one who is afraid will correct himself. **But he who hardens his heart:** A man who does not fear the word of God and does not learn from his mistakes will fall into evil. 

**A roaring lion and a prowling bear:** <note>Original: *shokek*</note>. This describes a wicked ruler over a poor people. Just as these animals devour, so does the wicked ruler. He is like a lion that roars and a bear that is hungry for prey. Or it refers to the Aramaic translation <note>Targum</note> that explains this as a ruler who takes from the people's sustenance. His way is always to empty the people of their money.

**A leader who lacks understanding:** This refers to a ruler who acts poorly in all things because his house is far from justice. This ruler of the masses is someone who lacks "insight" <note>Hebrew: *tevunot*</note> because he does not understand that the purpose of his kingdom is to do good. Instead, he is a "great oppressor," robbing the poor. **He who hates unjust gain will prolong his days:** Those who do not join him in his greed, or a king who hates such bribes and instead seeks justice and truth, will see their days prolonged.

**A man burdened with the blood of a person:** Someone who has committed murder, whether intentionally or through negligence, and is pursued by the <term>goel hadam</term> <note>Blood redeemer/avenger</note>. He shall flee even to the "pit" (the grave) and no one should support him or prevent his punishment. Or, it may mean he flees from place to place so that the hand of justice does not find him. On the day of his death, his sins will pursue him and the sages will not support him.

**He who walks blamelessly:** One who is consistent and upright in his actions will be saved from the hazards of time. **But he whose paths are crooked will fall all at once:** If his heart is not pure, he will fall into one of the pits he has dug for himself.

**He who works his land / He who follows vanities:** This compares the one who is industrious in his work to the one who follows idle people. The worker will be satisfied with bread, but the idle one will be satisfied with poverty.

**A faithful man:** A man who is naturally honest and faithful in his dealings will receive many blessings in his life. In contrast, the one who **hastens to be rich**, whether through theft or trickery, will not be cleansed from his sin.

**To show partiality is not good:** It is not good to show favoritism in judgment, even for a bribe. Even for something as small as a piece of bread, a corrupt man will transgress.

**A man with an evil eye hastens after wealth:** This refers to a stingy person who is jealous of others and wants to gather money quickly through theft or exploitation. He does not realize that "want" will come upon him because of his sins.

**He who rebukes a man:** One who rebukes his fellow man for his actions will eventually find more favor in the eyes of God and man than one who uses "smooth talk" <note>flattery</note> and refuses to point out faults. The flattery might feel good at the moment, but the honest rebuke leads to lasting favor.

**He who robs his father or mother:** One who takes from his parents' property, saying "it is no sin" because it will eventually be his inheritance, is a companion to a destroyer. He shows that his character is one of destruction.

**A greedy man stirs up strife:** A person with a "wide soul" <note>Hebrew: *rehav nefesh*, meaning greedy or never satisfied</note> causes conflict because he is always trying to take from others. But he who trusts in God and is not greedy for others' possessions will be "made fat" (prosperous).

**He who trusts in his own heart is a fool:** One who relies only on his own impulses and does not seek counsel or follow wisdom is a fool. But the one who walks in wisdom will escape the pitfalls that the "heart" might lead him into.

# Proverbs

<columns>
He who gives to the poor shall not lack, but he who hides his eyes shall have many curses.
When the wicked arise, a man hides himself, but when they perish, the righteous increase.
A man who does not accept <term>rebuke</term><note>Aramaic: מכסנותא (makhsanuta), meaning correction or discipline.</note> and hardens his neck shall suddenly be broken, and there will be no healing for him.
When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when the wicked rule, the people groan.
A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father, but he who associates with harlots wastes his wealth.
A king by justice establishes the land, but a wicked man tears it down.
A man who deals falsely with his companion spreads a net over his paths.
In the transgression of an evil man is a snare, but the righteous sings and rejoices.
The righteous knows the judgment of the poor, but the wicked does not understand with knowledge.
Mocking men set a city on fire, but the wise turn away anger.
A wise man contends with a foolish man; he rages and laughs, and is not broken.
Men of blood hate the innocent, but the upright seek him out.
A fool vents all his spirit, but the wise man stills it with his reason.
A ruler who listens to lying words—all his servants are wicked.
The poor man and the man of middle-rank meet together; the Lord enlightens the eyes of both of them.
A king who judges the poor in truth—his throne shall be established forever.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, but a youth who does not receive counsel shames his mother.

<column-break/>

<margin>Proverbs, Chapter 30</margin>

He who gives to the poor shall not lack, but he who hides his eyes shall have many curses.
When the wicked rise, a man is hidden, and when they perish, the righteous increase.
A man of <term>rebukes</term><note>Hebrew: תוכחות (tokhachot), refers to someone who has been corrected many times but remains stubborn.</note> who hardens his neck shall suddenly be broken, and there is no remedy.
When the righteous increase, the people rejoice, but when a wicked man rules, the people groan.
A man who loves wisdom gladdens his father, but he who keeps company with harlots wastes his substance.
A king by justice establishes the land, but a man of <term>gifts</term><note>Hebrew: תרומות (terumot), literally "heave-offerings," here referring to a ruler who demands excessive taxes or bribes.</note> tears it down.
A man who flatters his neighbor spreads a net for his steps.
In the transgression of an evil man there is a snare, but the righteous sings and is glad.
The righteous knows the cause of the poor; the wicked does not understand such knowledge.
Scoffers set a city ablaze, but wise men turn away wrath.
If a wise man goes to law with a foolish man, whether he rages or laughs, there is no rest.
Bloodthirsty men hate the blameless, but the upright seek his soul.
A fool vents all his feelings, but a wise man keeps them back and stills them.
If a ruler listens to falsehood, all his officials will be wicked.
The poor man and the oppressor meet together; the Lord gives light to the eyes of both.
A king who faithfully judges the poor, his throne shall be established forever.
The rod and rebuke give wisdom, but a child left to himself brings shame to his mother.
</columns>

***

**He who gives to the poor** — One who gives from his money as charity to the poor will not come to a state of lack, as it is written: "He who gives to the poor shall not lack." Conversely, one who hides his eyes from the poor will find that lack and deficiency come upon all his affairs. 

**When the wicked rise** — When the wicked attain greatness and their wickedness and injustice become publicly known, the judges of the land and its princes become "heavy-eyed" <note>An idiom for being biased or ignoring justice.</note>. In such times, the honor of the righteous is diminished, and a man must hide himself from the wicked. This is compared to how material impulses can "kill" the spiritual potential in a person, turning them away from the service of the Torah. However, when the wicked perish, the righteous increase and find the strength to stand firm.

**A man of rebukes** — If a person is repeatedly corrected but ignores the words of the wise and the paths of the intellect, he will eventually be broken suddenly, in a way that allows no healing. This refers to those who distance themselves from the Torah and the wisdom of the sages, which are the true "life" of a person.

**When the righteous increase** — On the day the righteous find joy and greatness, the hearts of all people rejoice. When the masses see the success of the righteous, they too are drawn to pursue wisdom. Thus, scholars and wise men increase naturally, and the danger of living under thoughtless leadership is removed. 

**A king by justice establishes the land** — A "King" <note>This often refers to the Governing Intellect in medieval philosophy.</note> who acts with righteousness keeps the world in its proper state. This means the intellect perceives the truth of things as they are. In contrast, "a man of gifts" <note>original: איש תרומות (ish terumot)</note> tears it down—this refers to one whose only goal is material gain or theoretical speculation that ignores practical morality, thereby removing the "land" (society or the self) from its proper foundation.

**A man who flatters...** — Sometimes the intellect is misled by deceptive thoughts that act as a "net" for its steps. One must be strong to recognize this and purify their will. The text notes that **the righteous knows the cause of the poor**, meaning the refined intellect knows how to extract the truth even from "poor" or material matters, whereas the wicked (the material drive) lacks the capacity for true knowledge.

**Scoffers set a city ablaze** — The masses of the foolish can destroy the upright and true paths, tearing down the "City of the Intellect" or the "City of the Torah." Wise men, however, "turn away wrath" by returning people's focus to wisdom and the Law. This refers to those who uphold the truths clarified through prophecy and philosophy.

**A wise man goes to law with a foolish man** — This describes the struggle between the intellect and the material/animalistic side of man. The fool (the material drive) will either rage or laugh dismissively, making it impossible to reach a peaceful resolution. 

**The poor man and the man of middle-rank** <note>original: איש תככים (ish tekhakhim), interpreted here as a man of deceit or a middle-rank person.</note> — They meet together, and the Lord enlightens the eyes of both. This suggests that even in the struggle between the higher intellect and the lower material state, the Divine light provides the opportunity for perception. 

**The rod and rebuke** — Discipline and correction provide wisdom to the youth, whereas a youth left to his own devices, without receiving counsel, brings shame to his mother.

### Chapter 29-30

<columns>
When the wicked multiply, sin increases, but the righteous will see their downfall. Chastise your son and he will give you rest; he will bring delights to your soul. When the leaders multiply <note>original: "ravlya." The Aramaic suggests a lack of stable leadership causes the people to be "punished" or "unrestrained."</note>, the people are punished, but he who keeps the law is happy. By words a servant is not disciplined, for he knows but it is not absorbed <note>original: "v’la b’li’a" - literally "not swallowed." The instruction doesn't "sink in."</note>. If you see a man hasty in his words, there is more hope for a fool than for him. He who pampers his servant from youth will find him ungrateful <note>original: "mpatach" - an obscure Aramaic term suggesting the servant becomes a burden or a master in the end.</note> in the end. An angry man stirs up strife, and a hot-tempered man has many sins. A man's pride will bring him low, but he who is humble in spirit shall receive honor. He who shares with a thief hates his own soul; he hears the curse but does not reveal it. The fear of man <note>original: "purkana." In this context, it refers to the anxiety caused by people which leads to a snare.</note> causes a stumbling block, but he who trusts in God shall be strengthened. Many seek the face of the wicked <note>The Aramaic Targum here reads "wicked" (rashia) where the Hebrew has "ruler" (moshel).</note>, but a man's judgment comes from before God. An unjust man is a distance <note>An abomination/repulsive</note> to the righteous, and a man of upright ways is a distance to the wicked. For I am more foolish than any man, and the understanding of men is not in me. I have not learned wisdom, nor do I know the secrets <note>original: "chiduta" - riddles or sacred mysteries.</note> of the Holy Ones. Who has ascended to heaven and come down? Who has gathered the wind in his palms? Who has bound the waters in a wrap? Who has established the ends of the earth? What is his name and what is his son’s name, if you know?

Its exact meaning is debated; it may mean a son, a weakling, or a ruler.</note>. <margin>30</margin> **An angry man** stirs up strife, and a master of wrath has many transgressions. **Pride of man** shall bring him low, but the humble in spirit shall uphold honor. <margin>50</margin> **A partner with a thief** hates his soul; he hears the curse but does not tell. **The fear of man** sets a snare, but he who trusts in the Lord shall be set on high. **Many seek** the face of a ruler, but from the Lord comes a man’s judgment. **An abomination** to the righteous is an unjust man, and an abomination to the wicked is the upright in way. **The words of Agur son of Jakeh**, the oracle. ---

**When the wicked multiply:** This means that when the wicked are numerous in the world, they bring evil upon the righteous. **And the righteous shall see their downfall:** They will be comforted and redeemed from them. The <term>Targum</term><note>The Aramaic translation of the Bible.</note> explains "they shall see" as "they shall see their salvation in their downfall." 

**Chastise your son:** This means you should hold him to his discipline so that he provides for your soul. 

**Where there is no vision:** <term>Vision</term><note>original: "chazon" - refers to prophecy.</note> refers to the prophets and sages. Without their guidance, the people are "exposed" or "destroyed," like a king who dies and his people are left without a leader. But he who keeps the Torah will live and listen to the voice of his rebukers.

**By words a servant will not be disciplined:** A servant should be disciplined with a rod, for soft words may not be absorbed into his heart even if he understands them.

**Do you see a man:** If you see a man who is hasty, there is more hope for a fool than for him. He thinks he knows everything and therefore does not fear the consequences of his words.

**He who pampers his servant from youth:** If one treats his servant with too much kindness and does not discipline him, in the end, that servant will attempt to rule over him or become a source of grief. 

**Agur son of Jakeh:** Our sages explain that this is King Solomon. He was called "Agur" because he *gathered* <note>original: "agar" - to collect.</note> wisdom, and "son of Jakeh" because he *vomited it out* <note>original: "heki" - to spit out/vomit.</note> by ignoring the warnings against having too many wives and horses. The names **Ithiel** and **Ucal** are interpreted as Solomon's claim: "God is with me (<term>Ithi-el</term>) and I shall prevail (<term>ve-ukhal</term>)." He thought his wisdom was so great that he could violate the Torah's restrictions on kings without being led astray, but he was proven wrong.

**For I am more brutish than any man:** This is Solomon speaking in humility or after his failure, saying that his reliance on his own wisdom was foolish. **Who has ascended to heaven:** This verse challenges the limits of human knowledge. Can a human understand the secrets of the heavens, the gathering of the winds, or the boundaries of the earth? These are the works of the Creator alone. The question "What is his son's name?" refers to the people of Israel, who are called the "son" of God, or it refers to the next generation of wise men who might attempt to understand these mysteries.

...the way of an eagle in the sky, the way of a serpent upon a rock; so is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, "I have done no wrong." Under three things the earth trembles, and under four it cannot bear up: Under a slave when he becomes king, and a fool when he is sated with food; Under an unloved woman when she is married, and a maidservant when she displaces her mistress. There are four things that are small on the earth, yet they are exceedingly wise: The ants are a folk without strength, yet they prepare their food in the summer; The hyraxes <note>original: "shafanim" — often translated as rock rabbits or coneys; small mammals that live in cliffs.</note> are a folk without power, yet they make their home in the crags; The locusts have no king, yet they all go forth in ranks; The lizard <note>original: "shemamit" — possibly a gecko or a spider.</note> you can grasp with the hands, yet it is in the palaces of kings. ## The Words of Lemuel
The words of Lemuel, king of Massa <note>original: "massa" — can mean a place name or "a burden/oracle."</note>, which his mother taught him: What, my son? And what, son of my womb? And what, son of my vows? Do not give your strength to women, nor your ways to that which destroys kings.

<column-break/>

...and the way of a ship in the heart of the sea, and the way of a man with a young woman. Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, "I have done nothing wrong or foul." Under three things the earth trembles, and under four it cannot endure: Under a servant when he reigns, and a fool who is full of bread; Under an unloved woman who goes to a husband, and a handmaid who inherits from her mistress. Four are they who are small on the earth, yet they are wise and made wise: The ants, who have no strength with them, yet prepare their food in the summer; The mountain-dwellers <note>The Aramaic "tapni" refers to the hyrax/coney mentioned in the Hebrew.</note>, whose folk are not strong, yet they make their home in the caves; The locusts, who have no king, yet they all gather as one; The lizard <note>original: "asmakta" — Aramaic for gecko.</note>, which clings with its hands and dwells in the houses of kings. Three are they whose steps are beautiful, and four whose walking is fine: The lion, the hero among beasts, who does not turn away from anything; The rooster <note>original: "abtsa" — the Aramaic identifies the "girded of loins" specifically as a rooster.</note> who is armed in his loins; the ram that goes at the head of the flock; and the Caesar who stands and speaks among his people. Do not be contentious lest you be exposed, and do not put your hand to your mouth; for as the pressing of milk brings out butter, and as the rubbing of the nose brings out blood, so the friction of the face <note>i.e., confrontation</note> brings out judgment. The words of Lemuel the king, in prophecy and the pleasantness of the prophecy with which his mother corrected him, saying to him: What, my son? What, son of my belly? What, son of my vows? Do not give your strength to women, nor your path to the daughters of kings. <gloss>Warning</gloss>

---

### Commentary

**The way of the eagle:** When it travels across the water or in its flight, it tramples its prey behind it. Because of its swiftness, the air or water closes up and no trace of its path can be found. Thus the King <note>Referring to Solomon, traditional author of Proverbs.</note> compares these matters to things that are sought in vain. For just as in these matters the trace disappears like a dream, so is the fourth thing—the "way of a man with a young woman." In the heat of passion and the signs of youth, the "trace" or record of the act is not easily tracked or proven. Therefore, he follows this with: **"So is the way of an adulterous woman,"** for she hides her tracks and "wipes her mouth" as if nothing happened. This warns that even if sins are hidden from the eyes of people, they are known to God.

**Under three things:** Meaning "because of." Like the phrase "Because (tachat) you did not serve the Lord." He mentions three things because when they occur, they upset the natural order of the land, being strange and unfitting. He mentions seven in total <note>3 + 4</note> to emphasize how the land's behavior is disrupted. **Under a slave:** For a slave usually lacks the refined nature or the habit of leadership; when he rises, his sudden power and the arrogance of his change in status lead to the destruction of the people. **A fool sated with bread:** A "fool" (navat) refers to a person of low character. When such a person is blessed with wealth and success, his low nature causes him to act out. **Under an unloved woman:** A woman who is rejected for her bad deeds or rebellious nature; if she eventually finds a husband, her elevation is seen as a social disturbance. **A maidservant:** This refers to a servant who becomes a mistress, a reversal of status that is often perceived as an unbearable social chaos.

**Four are small:** Meaning they are small in body and low in status, yet they possess greater wisdom than other creatures. **Ants:** They are not strong, yet they prepare their food in the summer to last through the winter. **Hyraxes:** They find safety by making their homes in the rocks to hide. **Locusts:** Though they have no leader, they act with perfect coordination like a gathered army. **Lizard:** Some say this is a small crawling creature found in the palaces of kings. Despite being small enough to be "grasped by hands," it manages to reside in the most secure and grandest locations.

**Three are stately:** These are noted for their wisdom or the beauty of their movement. The fourth is the **King**, whose gait is the most superior. **Lion:** It is the hero of the beasts and never retreats. **Strutting rooster:** Some say this is a dog, some say a rooster, or a creature that is quick and agile in its walk. **He-goat:** It leads the flock with a light step. **King Alkum:** This means a king whom no one can stand against. These are metaphors for stability and confidence.

**If you have been foolish:** This is an intransitive verb. If you have acted wickedly or even if you have only *thought* to exalt yourself and be arrogant, stop yourself; "put your hand to your mouth." **For the churning of milk:** Just as physical pressure on milk or the nose produces butter or blood, so does the "pressure" of anger between people produce strife.

**The words of Lemuel:** These are the words spoken *to* Lemuel. Who is Lemuel? The Sages say it is Solomon, called Lemuel because he "belonged to God" <note>Hebrew: Lamo-El - "to Him is God."</note>. His mother corrected him when she saw him tending toward the ways of the world, such as taking many wives. **What, my son?** She is asking: "What are you doing, my son? This is not how you should act." She reminds him that he is the son of her vows—prayers she made that she might have a son who would be fit for the throne. She warns him not to waste his "strength" (wealth or vitality) on women who destroy the focus and success of kings.

<meta>This page concludes the final chapter of the Book of Proverbs. Having previously recorded the wisdom of Agur and the warnings given to King Lemuel, the manuscript now presents the famous alphabetic acrostic poem known as "Eshet Chayil" (A Woman of Valor). This section (Proverbs 31:22–31) concludes the entire book. The layout follows the pattern of the Hebrew verse in bold, followed by its Aramaic translation (Targum), and then a lengthy medieval commentary.</meta>

# Proverbs

### Chapter 31

**She makes covers for herself; her clothing is fine linen and purple:**
She made blankets for herself; fine linen and purple are her clothing.
**She makes linen garments and sells them, and supplies sashes to the merchants:**
She made wraps and sold them, and she gave sashes to the merchants.
**She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the teaching of kindness is on her tongue:**
She opens her mouth with wisdom, and the law of kindness is on her tongue.
**Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praises her:**
Her children arose and praised her; her husband arose and praised her.
**Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised:**
Grace is a lie and beauty is empty; a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised.

<column-break/>

**Her husband is known in the gates, when he sits among the elders of the land:**
Her husband is distinguished in the gates, and he surrounds himself with the glory of garments for her husband. <note>The Aramaic Targum adds a specific nuance here regarding the quality of his attire as a reflection of her work.</note>
<margin>Her ways... [illegible]</margin>
**Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laughs at the time to come:**
Strength and splendor are her clothing, and she rejoices for the final day.
**She watches over the ways of her household and does not eat the bread of idleness:**
She oversees the conduct of the house, and the bread of laziness she does not eat.
**Many daughters have done valiantly, but you excel them all:**
Many daughters have performed with strength, but you have risen above them all.
**Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates:**
Give to her from the fruits of her hands, and her deeds shall be praised in the gate.

---

->The total number of verses in the Book of Proverbs is nine hundred and fifteen, and the sign is *Ya-hatz*<- <note>The Hebrew letters Yod (10), Heh (5), and Tzadi (900) serve as a mnemonic for the total verse count of 915.</note>

---

**Covers** — an expression meaning a covering, or *cobertura* <note>original: "kubirtul" — a vernacular Romance/Old French gloss used by medieval commentators like Rashi to explain the Hebrew word "marvadim".</note> in the vernacular. Some interpret "covers" as golden jewelry for daughters. Regarding the "fine linen," it refers to the honored and beautiful garments. **Known** — an expression of recognition, as in being acquainted with the elders; he speaks of her praises and her diligence to her husband. **Linen garment** — meaning a sheet of flax, *linteolo* <note>original: "litol" — another vernacular gloss.</note> in the vernacular. **Merchant** <note>original: "Kena'ani" — literally "Canaanite," but used in Biblical Hebrew to mean a merchant or trader.</note> — meaning a merchant or trader, for the kindness is shown to those who assist her. **Strength and dignity are her clothing** — This refers to the seal of the kingdom. She does not fear the "later day" (the future) or hunger, for she has prepared well. Even when old age comes, she laughs because she is prepared. **She opens her mouth** — She does not open her mouth for vain or foolish words, but only for words of wisdom and knowledge. I do not know the exact lineage of this "law of kindness," but perhaps it refers to the entire Torah which is characterized by kindness. **She watches over the ways of her household** — She gazes and observes the paths followed by the members of her house, ensuring peace in her home and seeing if they lack anything. She is not like those who waste the day in idleness, eating and drinking, but she maintains her health through work. **Her children rise up** — They recognize her valor and the honor she brings them. **And he praises her** — All her glory is for the sake of the Messiah <note>This reflects a common medieval allegorical interpretation where the "Woman of Valor" represents the Torah or the Congregation of Israel.</note>. **Many daughters** — Many have gathered wealth through diligence, but you have surpassed them all in generosity and wisdom. **Grace is deceitful** — One should not praise a woman merely for her beauty if her deeds are not good. True "grace" is the fear of Heaven. Or, as her husband and children say: "Beauty is temporary and vain, but her fear of the Lord is what makes her truly worthy of praise." **Give her of the fruit of her hands** — After mentioning her virtues, the text concludes that she needs no external praise, for her own actions and the wealth she has acquired through her labor speak for themselves in the public gates.

<column-break/>
Blessed be the Merciful One who assisted us from the beginning of the book until now.

It includes a verse count (915) for the book and a medieval commentary that explains the Hebrew text using vernacular glosses and allegorical interpretations.</summary>

<meta>This page is a significant departure from the previous section. While the preceding page concluded the biblical Book of Proverbs, this page serves as a flyleaf or a practice sheet from a much later period—the 19th century. It features penmanship exercises and legal formulas in both Russian and Hebrew, suggesting the manuscript was reused or bound with administrative papers from the Piotrków Governorate (Petrokovskaya Guberniya) in the Russian Empire (modern-day Poland).</meta>

<note>The manuscript page is filled with elaborate calligraphic flourishes and pen-tests. Large, sweeping loops and decorative paraphs (flourishes after a signature to prevent forgery) surround the text blocks. The handwriting is in a formal 19th-century Russian cursive style and a neat Hebrew square script.</note>
